TESTIMONY BEFORE MCDONALD COMMISSION-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43. The former solicitor general, Mr. Fox, at the time the McDonald commission of inquiry was established, with reference to the commission's right to decide what was or was not to be held in camera, said the following:
Whether or not the commission would do it in camera or in public depended on the decision of the commission itself in conformity with those terms of reference and powers.
Considering that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) was quoted in the Ottawa Citizen last Saturday, October 14, as having said, the commission "shouldn't have the right to tell the public what a minister said to me about the operations of the RCMP" both contradicts what the former solicitor general said and completely undermines the integrity of the McDonald inquiry, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles):
That this House instructs the government to live up to its original commitment by accepting Judge McDonald's decision as announced last Friday that it is the commission itself which has the right to decide what testimony and evidence is to take place in public and what is to be kept in camera.

SALE OF ALCOHOLIC BEVERAGES ON ELECTION DAYS-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent necessity concerning a section of the Canada Elections Act pertaining to the requirement prohibiting the serving of alcoholic beverages in restaurants and the opening of retail liquor stores while a federal election or by-election is in progress, thus resulting, as an example, in the ridiculous situation existing in the Toronto riding of Rosedale, where restaurants may legally serve alcoholic beverages today on the west side of Yonge Street from the waterfront to Merton Street but may not do so on the east side of Yonge Street because it is in Rosedale.
I move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. McKenzie):
That the government immediately bring before the House an amendment to the Canada Elections Act, following the example set by the Ontario Progressive Conservative government with regard to provincial elections, in order to allow licensed establishments, etc., to remain open on federal election days, and thus remove this Victorian anachronism not in accord with present-day thinking.

Mr. Speaker, I rise, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. Due to a two-week strike at the port of Churchill this summer, grain movement through the port will be down by seven million to nine million bushels. This will place the port in a loss position. Therefore, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Neil):
That the government instruct the Wheat Board to use the port of Churchill storage, which will give the farmers a break in increased quotas and place the port in a break-even cash position.

subsubtopic: TESTIMONY BEFORE MCDONALD COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister. In his earlier answers to the Leader of the Opposition, he left the impression that the matter to be resolved in this dispute was the question of accessibility of information which, of course, is irrelevant.
The Prime Minister knows that the contradiction which exists between his position and that of the royal commission concerns the question of publicity-open sessions, or closed. Since, in my view, this goes to the root of the issue, I should like to ask the Prime Minister if he stands by what the former solicitor general said on July 6, 1977, in this House: he said that whether or not the commission would do it in camera or in public depended on the decision of the commission itself, in conformity with its terms of reference and powers. This is contradicted by what the Prime Minister said, when referring to the commission and according to a quote in last Saturday's Ottawa Citizen, as follows:
-shouldn't have the right to tell the public what a minister said to me about the operations of the RCMP-
I ask the Prime Minister: has he, or has he not, contradicted, clearly, the right of the commission to decide whether it is going to have its proceedings in public? If he has as is my view, contradicted this basic principle, will he withdraw that and allow the commission to make its own determination, as was promised at the outset?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: TESTIMONY BEFORE MCDONALD COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the leader of the New Democratic Party says the problem of access is irrelevant. I do not think it is. I think it is very relevant for the people of Canada and members of the House to know that the government is not only, as the commission says, giving everything to them that they have asked for, but we have even given more. We have led them to files; we have shown them things they should know. I think this is very basic to people judging whether the government is trying to cover up or not. We have confidence in the commission and its independence. We have done everything we could to make sure it got what it wanted, and more than what it wanted was in front of it.
The second aspect of the question is, what can be made public? The commission has taken the position in a statement it issued on Friday, and either through coincidence or happenstance I had no knowledge of what the commission was saying on Friday when I was asked a question in the high school. Therefore, my comment was not on what the commission said, even though the Leader of the Opposition said it was published on Saturday. That is pure coincidence. I had no knowledge of what the commission was saying.
What I was saying to a group of students is that the ultimate responsibility in matters of security and in matters of privy council secrecy cannot be discharged by the government. It is an ultimate responsibility that we must bear. I still stand by that, but as regards the operation of the commission, I want to make it quite clear-as the Solicitor General has, as I have, and as former solicitors general have-that we will co-operate

in every way, as the commission says we have, and we do not see any disputes arising. If there are disputes, we will try to resolve them between us, as we have in the past.

subsubtopic: TESTIMONY BEFORE MCDONALD COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I did not, of course, say to the Prime Minister that the question of access was irrelevant to the broad consideration of whether the commission would be able to do its job. Of course it is relevant. I said it was irrelevant to the dispute. The Prime Minister has not clarified that in his answer to me. I should like him to make it very clear. The former solicitor general, Mr. Fox, assured the House that in matters to be decided-whether to be in camera, or not in camera-it was not the government that would decide whether it was on security matters, or other, but it was the commission.
I ask the Prime Minister, now, because according to the statement he made as quoted in the press on Saturday he certainly took a contrary position: is the Prime Minister now assuring the House, and therefore the people of Canada, that the commission will have the right to decide, even on security matters, after it assesses the information in advance, whether testimony or aspects of legal procedures are to be in camera or not. Is the Prime Minister going to say, in certain matters, that the government is still going to insist that it will decide?

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am saying that I know of no case in which there has been a difference of opinion, in fact, with the commission.

About the hypothetical case in the future where the government would try to absolve itself of its responsibility-

subsubtopic: TESTIMONY BEFORE MCDONALD COMMISSION

investigate the possibility of cabinet wrongdoing, a possible illegal wrongdoing.

I have said that we have the ultimate responsibility. I went on to say that we will discharge that responsibility in every way we can to satisfy the commission. I have said in the past that we have succeeded in doing that. Certainly, if the commission finds some evidence of wrongdoing, fraud or crime by some high official, we will not hide behind the Official Secrets Act or anything else. We will find ways of declassifying documents and co-operating with the commission in the future, as we have in the past.
I am just saying that no doctrine can absolve the government of its responsibility for Privy Council secrets. There are cases where we do make those secrets public, and we have done so in the past. We could in the future, if the commission were to argue this was necessary.

subsubtopic: EFFECT OF INCREASED INTEREST RATE-PRESENTATION OF BUDGET
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister. On Friday the thirteenth- a bad luck day for Canada-the Bank of Canada, with the consent of the government, raised the central bank interest rate to 10'A per cent. This is the fifth increase in seven months-a 28 per cent increase since March 9, and the largest single increase at any one time since 1935.
In view of the viciously damaging effects this will have on economic growth in Canada, can the Prime Minister advise the House what the government's plans are to overcome those damaging effects and to reach the 5 per cent growth rate that he promised at Bonn last summer? speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons

subsubtopic: EFFECT OF INCREASED INTEREST RATE-PRESENTATION OF BUDGET

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: EFFECT OF INCREASED INTEREST RATE-PRESENTATION OF BUDGET
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there was a great deal of commentary in that question. Most of it would have been solved for the hon. member if he had read what the governor of the Bank of Canada said when he announced this increase in the bank rate. He said very clearly, at a time when the dollar had been holding steady that day and, I think, even slightly improving, that he suddenly found himself faced with an American bank rate which had increased drastically, and therefore had narrowed the spread between the American and Canadian rates. He responded to that situation in the United States by creating a spread between them which had been reduced by the action in the United States. Therefore, it was not an action based on the performance of the Canadian dollar on that day or days, but it

was based on what happened in the United States: the governor said so in as many words, and I would refer the hon. member to his statement.
As to the question asked by the hon. member, yes, there will be a budget; the Minister of Finance has indicated that it will be brought down in the middle of November.

subsubtopic: EFFECT OF INCREASED INTEREST RATE-PRESENTATION OF BUDGET
speechtext:
Is the Prime Minister saying, then, when he refers to the statement by the governor of the Bank of Canada, that this was done because of the increase in United States interest rates, that Canada is now a prisoner of U.S. interest rates policy, that we no longer control our own monetary policy and that the government is content with that position? Is that the situation? Will the Prime Minister comment on that aspect?
Will he tell us, also, whether a statement is to be made on the present issue of Canada Savings Bonds which is obviously not likely to sell well at an interest rate of 8.9 per cent, with the central bank rate up to 10.5? When will new rates be announced for that issue?

subsubtopic: EFFECT OF INCREASED INTEREST RATE-PRESENTATION OF BUDGET
speechtext: I do not know whether the hon. member is serious in asking that question about our being a prisoner. He must have heard by now that Canada does not operate in a vacuum and that there are other countries in the world whose economic actions influence Canadian bank rates, and so on. There has been traditionally a spread between American and Canadian bank rates, as the hon. member knows or should know. What the governor says is that he is re-establishing that spread after the United States acted in the way it did.

subsubtopic: EFFECT OF INCREASED INTEREST RATE-PRESENTATION OF BUDGET
speechtext: If he is not a prisoner, then, would the Prime Minister explain to the House how he intends to achieve the 5 per cent real growth rate he promised at Bonn; how he proposes to increase our business investment; how we are to improve the economy if the interest rate continues to go up and up? If we are not a prisoner, how is the Prime Minister going to demonstrate that we are not? When will he break these bonds and show us how he is going to bring the country forward economically?

subsubtopic: TESTIMONY BEFORE MCDONALD COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Prime Minister arising out of the first question asked by the Leader of the Opposition in relation to the McDonald royal commission. Bearing in mind that the situation is not hypothetical, as can be seen from the nature of instructions given by the Solicitor General to his counsel and
Oral Questions
made public to the commission, obviously in anticipation of an attempt by government ministers to hide some information, I should like the right hon. gentleman to assure us that when a conflict arises between the government and the royal commission as to whether or not evidence is of a security nature, the government will not make use of the outdated and infamous doctrine of Crown privilege to hide evidence, as President Nixon used executive privilege in the United States.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: TESTIMONY BEFORE MCDONALD COMMISSION
speechtext:
That is a silly question, Mr. Speaker. If the hon. member had taken the trouble to read the statement by the McDonald commission, he would have seen that the commissioners themselves do not make light of what he calls Crown privilege.
It is recognized by anyone who operates in government, or who has any chance of operating in government, that there are some things that are of a nature to be concealed by the state. Let me just quote what the McDonald commission itself says on page 15: they are quoting from a case in 1968, Lord Reid, in the House of Lords: "I do not doubt there are certain classes of documents which ought not to be disclosed whatever the content may be." That is a very clear statement, and this has been a tradition of parliamentary government as long as it has existed. The hon. member pretends that this tradition, this legal doctrine, does not exist. It does-unfortunately for his case.

subsubtopic: TESTIMONY BEFORE MCDONALD COMMISSION
speechtext: Is the Prime Minister not aware that that statement by Lord Reid was related to a decision by the House of Lords that the court would make the final decision with respect to particular evidence, and not the government?

subsubtopic: TESTIMONY BEFORE MCDONALD COMMISSION
speechtext: I am well aware of this case in 1968, but I wonder whether the hon. member is not now changing his whole argument. He is not saying that the McDonald commission should decide; he is saying that the courts should decide. That is exactly what he is saying now, and perhaps that is what the McDonald commission is saying. I see hon. members shaking their heads. Is that not what the hon. member for Peace River has said; that the courts would decide? That is what I am saying, too. There are some cases where privilege may or may not be involved, and it is for the courts to decide whether it is right or not.

subsubtopic: TESTIMONY BEFORE MCDONALD COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is on the same subject and it is directed to the Solicitor General. The mandate which was given to the McDonald royal commission clearly provided, and I am quoting from it, for the commission to "conduct such investigations as, in the opinion of the commissioners, are necessary to determine the extent and prevalence", and so on. That mandate allowed the commission, in its own wisdom, to conduct whatever investigations it deemed were necessary.
Bearing in mind the Prime Minister's statement today, that he intends to continue to rely on the inherent privilege not to release Privy Council secrets-

subsubtopic: TESTIMONY BEFORE MCDONALD COMMISSION
speechtext:
I did not say that.

October 16, 1978

subsubtopic: SALE OF SACCHARIN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is to the Minister of National Health and Welfare. Now that the head of the health protection branch has found that he erred in causing the hysteria and panic among Canadian diabetics and obese people that he did over his 1968 statements about cyclamates causing cancer in rats, can the minister tell this House whether the head of the health protection branch has indicated whether he will allow the minister and members of parliament to advise their constituents that this safe sugar substitute can be used in food and soft drinks?
Further, now that the head of the health protection branch considers cyclamates and saccharin safe for sale at the high price of medical exclusivity in drugstores, will the minister release them to the normal and less costly grocery store outlets?

speakeroldname: Hon. Monique Begin (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: SALE OF SACCHARIN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the recent findings of private laborato-

ries on the exact relationship between cyclamates and cancer have permitted the scientific community to determine the acceptable daily intake of cyclamates for humans, which we did not know some ten years ago when we first restricted cyclamates in order to protect people. Based on that new knowledge we are therefore permitting-and I issued a press release, I think last week-the use of cyclamates in prescription drugs only. The safe daily intake is too small, according to scientific knowledge of today, for me to take any decision to liberalize the use of cyclamates in all soft drinks and diet foods. I am not yet in a position to do that.

subsubtopic: AIRPORTS-EXTENSION OF RUNWAY AT TORONTO
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Transport. The coroner's jury inquiring into the Air Canada crash of last June on runway 23 in Toronto in which two lives were lost has recommended that the runway be extended over a creek at the end of the runway. I would like to ask the minister whether he is going to act on the jury's recommendation. 1 point out to him that the pilot stated that the runway is disastrous.

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto E. Lang (Minister of Transport and Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subsubtopic: AIRPORTS-EXTENSION OF RUNWAY AT TORONTO
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as in every case of a coroner's decision and recommendations, we will look at these seriously, of course. At this point I do not have an analysis of the cost of the recommendation made in that report, and I obviously cannot make a judgment upon it without knowing that.

subsubtopic: AIRPORTS-EXTENSION OF RUNWAY AT TORONTO
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the jury recommended that the runway be extended immediately. If the minister does not have the necessary funds at this point, will he be closing down the runway? The director general of civil aeronautics pointed out in 1976 that there are ten other airports in Canada which are not up to acceptable standards. Have these ten airports been brought up to acceptable standards, and will the minister be closing runway 23?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subsubtopic: AIRPORTS-EXTENSION OF RUNWAY AT TORONTO
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the work of ensuring that airports are safe and that facilities are safe is ongoing. We take a very serious view of the matter, and I can assure the hon. member that in every case where there is any kind of limitation upon a runway or other feature at an airport which causes us concern, steps are taken. Those steps may include limitations on runways or other facilities. They are taken to ensure the complete and adequate safety of the travelling public. That has been done in this case, and if one compares our standards, our runways and our facilities with those in use in countries all over the world, one will find that ours come out very favourably indeed. I think that should be a real reassurance to the travelling public and I do not think we should be overly concerned about the way in which the hon. member has put his question.

The committee was not asked if this was appropriate.

MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE CONSIDERATION OF EVIDENCE IN PUBLIC
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 26. Your Honour, I would say in advance that, whatever other considerations you may have had on this matter, I hope the opportunity for debate during the throne speech debate will not have been among them, because in this particular case, as Your Honour knows, it is the executive branch of government itself that is being called into question, and to rule in favour of the opportunity to debate this matter of fundamental importance to our system of government during the throne speech debate, while providing the opportunity for the executive to participate, would not, of course, obligate it to do so, and, given its past tradition, we could not expect it to enter the debate.
Having said that, I would ask leave to move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), the adjournment of the House, under Standing Order 26, for the purpose of discussing a specific and important matter requiring urgent consideration, namely, the statement by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) made in Ottawa last Friday that it will be the government and not the McDonald commission which decides what matters or evidence are to be considered by the commission in public, the consequences of such a position being completely contrary to the integrity of the commission, which the commission itself recognizes.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE CONSIDERATION OF EVIDENCE IN PUBLIC
speechtext:
Order, please. The hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent) has given the Chair notice of his intention, under the provisions of Standing Order 26, to seek a special debate on the subject he has now put forward.
In answering his preamble I would, of course, want him to observe with me that, even if his argument were to have the full weight he desires, he must recognize at once that he is perfectly correct in that the Chair has no power by which the executive, as he describes it, could be compelled to participate during the throne speech debate in respect of this or any other matter.
The hon. member will recognize at once, of course, that neither does the Chair have the power to compel participation by the same executive in any debate if I were to grant the motion under Standing Order 26. I am not sure that this advances the argument. In either case, members of the executive may or may not participate in any debate, as they see fit, whether the debate is under Standing Order 26, or in respect
October 16, 1978

of the throne speech. Therefore, the conditions seem to me to remain the same.
In any event, and this I suppose will be to the hon. member's regret, the fact is that the very paragraph to which he made reference in his preamble is one that does weigh upon the Chair in deciding whether or not the subject he is putting forward should be debated. Several days remain in the throne speech debate. It is, of course, a very jealously guarded right of any member that he may encompass during the course of discussion any subject which relates to the performance of the government, certainly over the past while, or as intended in the future. Therefore I would have to ignore totally the provisions of that subparagraph of the rule if I were to say on this day that we should set aside a particular aspect of want of confidence in the government in respect of one subject.
I must say that I am also concerned with another aspect, and that is that the Chair must decide whether the matter is urgent in nature. In so doing I cannot brush aside the fact that there is a very strong hypothetical tone to all of these questions that were put today. Everyone will have noticed that the Chair did not intervene on the ground that the questions put sought the intended stance of the government if and when in the future a certain event occurred before the royal commission. Those questions are, by their very nature, hypothetical, and certainly anticipate a situation in the future.
I did not interfere with those questions, for two reasons. First of all, a slight change in the form of the questions would bring them to a present consideration, that is, whether or not the government has formed any plans. In addition, I do not think the Chair ought to intervene where, in circumstances of this sort and of this importance, there is an obvious desire on the part of members of the cabinet to give answers, even though the questions do have a hypothetical tone, as was the case today.
However, I cannot ignore the fact that the statement to which reference has been made is a statement about intended conduct in the future. It has raised concern in the minds of members of the opposition, as expressed by this motion, that in the future the McDonald commission will request certain evidence to be given and members of the cabinet may take a certain stance opposed to that, or different from it.
This has been a matter of dispute today which is also difficult for the Chair. Even if this were not in dispute, the fact remains that the crisis to which reference is made in this motion remains in the future. Until the McDonald commission takes certain steps, and until the cabinet has made certain specific responses, upon which this parliament can focus, indicating that there is in fact a difference between them of a critical nature, I think it would be premature for me to accept the basic proposition that a crisis has been arrived at now which warrants the consideration of this rule, instead of at sometime in the future.
For the two reasons I have cited, I would indicate at this moment that I am not prepared to grant the application pursuant to Standing Order 26.
The Address-Mr. Roche

speechtext:
With our vast resource base, we contribute substantially to the economy of all of Canada. As Canadians first, we Albertans are vitally concerned with the performance of the national economy, for it is only with a strong and vital economy that Alberta or any other province will realize its full potential. The story of Alberta today is one of growth and accomplishment. We are the new builders of Canada. We have the fastest growing gross provincial product in Canada. Per capita spending on education, health, and other social areas is the highest in the country. We have strength and potential and an attractive investment climate. That is why Alberta is now the financial centre of western Canada. Is it any wonder that we attract more than 3,000 newcomers every month, most of them fellow Canadians from other provinces looking for new opportunities?

October 16, 1978
The Address-Mr. Roche
One would think that the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Trudeau) would at least share in the pride of accomplishment of one of the provinces, but the Prime Minister is blind to Alberta. That blindness cannot be corrected, as a careful reading of his speech last Thursday in the throne speech debate reveals. Every reference he made to Alberta was negative. He had nothing good to say about a province that has been succeeding despite the policies of economic discrimination practised by the federal government. The fact is that the Prime Minister cannot stand any province, especially a strong one, standing up for its rights.
When the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) brings to this House his concern for the erosion of provincial rights, and we have certainly seen this in the government constitutional package, the Prime Minister tells him he should be sitting in a provincial legislature, not here. What gall! In that one remark, and his speech is full of examples, the Prime Minister revealed why he should no longer be in charge of Canada: he does not understand that regional growth and strength are what make this country.
The Progressive Conservative leader recognizes that the provinces are partners in confederation, not enemies. And he said clearly in his speech:
There will be times when I am going to have to assert national interests in ways that will not at all please the provinces.
Yet the Prime Minister, who seems to interpret co-operation as subservience, ignored this analysis because he cannot imagine an alternative to himself in protecting national unity. The Progressive Conservative leader knows intuitively that Canada is the sum of its parts; the Prime Minister continues to suffer under the delusion that Ottawa is the country. For the Progressive Conservative leader, the issue is ways to have Canada prosper in all regions, not just certain regions. For the Prime Minister, the issue is battling over who has power and jurisdiction.
In his leader's day speech, the Progressive Conservative leader presented economic and constitutional proposals to truly unite Canada. But the Prime Minister spent the bulk of his speech attacking the Leader of the Opposition and deriding provincial premiers. He has used his histrionic "zap" style once too often. For the Prime Minister, it is not jobs, inflation, the falling dollar, regional growth and national unity that are the problems; it is the man who sits 18 feet across the aisle in the House of Commons, the man whom Canadians are turning to as the next Prime Minister.
The present Prime Minister apparently cannot understand what has gone wrong. What has gone wrong, Mr. Speaker, is that he has lost the trust of Canadians. Under our democratic way of life, trust in government is absolutely basic. No nation can aspire to greatness if its government does not command public respect. "If the people can't trust their government," President Harry Truman declared, "the whole works will fall apart." We may or may not always agree with the decisions of government, but our system demands that we at least have confidence that the government is acting honestly.

Unfortunately, trust in the government of this Prime Minister has deteriorated so seriously that it has become the root cause of much dissatisfaction in Canada today. The cynicism toward Ottawa, found coast to coast, is traceable to the manipulation practised by this government. In fact the issue of trust in the leadership of our country has become the core issue of our time.
A long series of misadventures has characterized this government's decade in office; the Sky Shops affair, dredging contracts, phone calls to judges, questionable payments by Crown corporations, the uranium cartel, a blacklist of extraparliamentary opposition. We have learned to live with these shabby scandals and improprieties. But the government's own sense of morality has been undermined from within. Consequently a weakened commitment to principle for its own sake has infected the larger area of policy formulation. Here the examples become more serious.
The Prime Minister legislated wage and price controls after having campaigned in the 1974 election against them. He forced an abolition bill on the country when the majority of Canadians, fearing that violent crime is out of control, wanted capital punishment retained. Having divided Canadians by a heavy-handed application of the Official Languages Act, he tried to force upon parliament in the last months of his mandate constitutional changes, including diminishment of the monarchy, that are opposed by all ten provincial premiers.
Is it any wonder that people everywhere are asking, "Can Ottawa be trusted?" My answer is that the Ottawa of the present Prime Minister cannot be trusted. This is a government that once paid farmers not to grow wheat, that opened the door to 55,000 abortions per year in the name of "health", that made a welfare scheme out of unemployment insurance. This is the government that gave us LIP and a host of make-work projects that vanished in the night while undermining investor confidence in private industry which creates permanent jobs. And this is the government that attempts to abrogate energy agreements with Alberta, reneged on urban transit assistance to Edmonton, and refused the structural enlargement of the Edmonton international airport urged by the government's own engineers. The grounds for mistrust of the federal government are piling up all around us.
One principle is uppermost in the minds of the government-the principle of holding on to power. The fear of losing power is the reason Canadians have been denied the general election the country needed this fall. Now, in an effort to befog that public opinion, the Prime Minister talks of future referenda as instruments of direct democracy. In my judgment, the direct democracy Canadians want is an election now to throw out this unprincipled and untrustworthy government.
If the government really wanted to change its ways and promote national and economic social progress, it would pay attention to the legitimate evaluations made by Premier Lougheed concerning the Ottawa-Alberta relationship. In his address opening the new session of the Alberta legislature on
October 16, 1978

October 11, Premier Lougheed said that many Albertans look on the federal government "as an adversary rather than an ally." He also said:
Federal policies have been negative and not positive, for young Albertans... in terms of opportunity .. . We are no island here in Alberta. We're part of this country in the fullest sense of the word, and it's simply not possible for us to maintain our prosperity in the face of a sluggish or weak economy in the rest of Canada.
The overwhelming message coming from Alberta is one of frustration with the way the federal government handles federal-provincial relations. It is almost as if the federal government is trying to dig itself out of the economic mess by using Alberta's wealth. And in so doing, Ottawa is affecting Alberta's ability to plan its own economy.
The latest example of this is the attempt to delay the $1 a barrel oil price increase scheduled for January 1. A series of four increases in oil prices was agreed upon between the two levels of government in 1977. On August 1 of this year the federal government approved the last of the increases. By August 26 it had changed its mind, causing great confusion in Alberta. Now the throne speech says negotiations are under way to defer the increase. Is it any wonder that Albertans have become cynical about the government's intentions?
Alberta provides over 85 per cent of Canada's oil and 80 per cent of Canada's natural gas. The only way to bring about self-sufficiency in energy, which is in the national economic interest, is to promote vigorous development, with all the high cost technology that this entails.
Another significant example is the federal government's repeal of the Public Utilities Income Tax Transfer Act in the hastily conceived restraint program last summer. This act provides for a rebate to the provinces of 95 per cent of the federal and provincial income tax collected from privately owned utilities. It was designed to provide equal tax treatment between customers of these privately owned utilities and customers of publicly owned utilities which do not pay income taxes. Alberta is the only province to return this tax to the utilities in full. Repeal of the act will therefore mean increased prices to the consumer, an estimated $25 annual increase per capita.
Albertans, therefore, will be the ones most seriously affected because most of Alberta is serviced by privately owned utilities. Of the estimated $48.9 million which would have been transferred next year, Alberta's share is $33.9 million. Rather than a reduction of federal government spending, this move represents an additional taxation, and Alberta is the primary target. It will have a depressing effect on Alberta industries and agriculture, and will indirectly pass through to higher costs for all consumer goods.
Here we might note the so-called clout of the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner) on behalf of Alberta. When, as the hon. member for Crowfoot, pleading that he could do more for Alberta, he ran across the aisle in lustful pursuit of a Liberal cabinet post, we were told that Albertans would benefit. As the question period revealed last Friday, the minister had no impact whatsoever on his cabinet
The Address-Mr. Roche
colleagues when the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) repealed the Public Utilities Income Tax Transfer Act. No one in Ottawa listens to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce and, as he will find out shortly, his supporters in Crowfoot are becoming hard to find.
As for the Minister of Finance, his action continues the long tradition of doing business with Alberta: decide unilaterally, then consult. The Progressive Conservative way of doing business is: Consult first, then decide.
The Edmonton Chamber of Commerce put the importance of the utilities problem succinctly to the Prime Minister in a letter on October 4, as follows:
The future electric energy projects in Canada require large sums of capital and it can only be generated in a stable environment where the private sector can compete on an equal basis with provincially and municipally owned utilities. This proposed action is in direct contradiction with the announced intentions of your government to reduce the demands on government spending at all levels and discourages the long term planning of the private sector so vital to meet ever growing demands for power.
We are also concerned that this particular action seems to be slanted against Alberta, which province has the largest percentage of its utility services provided by the private sector. We feel that this can be construed as another in a series of actions made against the people of our province; moves which, in the Final analysis, will not be conducive towards the type of atmosphere in which the constitutional debate can best be held.
Incredibly, there was no prior consultation with the provinces before announcing the repeal of the act, or perhaps not so incredible when one considers this government's record over the past year. Sales tax cuts were sprung on the surprised provinces; expenditure cuts were announced without any consultation; constitutional amendments have been reserved for the federal government acting alone.
The western premiers' conference in April was sharply critical of the unilateral and intrusive way in which the sales tax cut was initiated. The joint communique states:
The federal budget directly contradicted the spirit of federal-provincial cooperation and consultation which the February conference (of First Ministers) had been intended to foster and could be prejudicial to ongoing discussions on national unity.
At the February conference, Premier Lougheed called upon the federal government to recognize that its existing policies had not worked and needed to be significantly altered. This required, he said, "not only a change in policies but also a distinct change in attitudes." What the premier was looking for was new economic directions which would help all of Canada to "begin to move ahead again with renewed confidence."
He summarized the Alberta viewpoint on the formulation of a national economic policy as follows: First, the private sector is where the jobs are really created and where the multiplier effect is; second, we have to control the public sector in this country in terms of wage and salary settlements; third, we have to eliminate duplication in levels of government and within governments themselves; fourth, we have got to do more in our country, and press the media to do more,-to recognize the achievers and the doers in Canada today; and fifth, the real key to strengthening the Canadian economy is to encour-

October 16, 1978
The Address-Mr. Roche
age private sector risk investment by developing a climate that is encouraging.
This is also the view of the Progressive Conservative members of parliament from Alberta. For years we have been saying in this chamber that national unity depends on the economic strengthening of all regions and cannot be obtained by linguistic policies alone. We share Premier Lougheed's conviction that a stronger Alberta, and a strengthening of all provinces, are good for a united Canada. The leader of the Progressive Conservative party and the Progressive Conservative premiers have been working together to develop a common approach. But, of course, anyone is out of step except the Prime Minister who marches to the lonely beat of the Ottawa drummer.
Despite the call by the premiers for a co-operative approach, the federal government brought in yet another budget that distorted provincial economic and fiscal priorities, and it proceeded unilaterally with constitutional reform.
Premier Lougheed has rightly noted the deterioration in good relations between Ottawa and Edmonton as a result of the federal government's heavy-handed approach. Recently he said:
We have been making some progress in Alberta and it was in the best interests of Canadians working together with the federal government and other provinces, but we can get pretty disturbed, as we are today, with a series of steps that have occurred in the last number of months-of broken agreements, of tax discrimination towards our province. It is as though they said, 'Well, let's cut Alberta down to size.' There is also a continued intrusion in all provinces and a constitutional bill that literally throws down the gauntlet.
For telling the truth, for standing up to the federal government, Premier Lougheed is derided in this House by the Prime Minister. Instead of belittling the Premier of Alberta, the Prime Minister should be pointing to Peter Lougheed with pride. In Alberta we know that Premier Lougheed is a great Canadian. And Alberta will not tolerate the undermining of this sterling advocate of co-operative federalism.
Let it be said clearly for the nation to hear: Alberta is committed to Canada. In the Alberta Speech from the Throne in March, Lieutenant Governor Steinhauer ably expressed this when he said:
Our citizens are fully committed to a strong and united Canada. The flexibiity of our federal system should prove to be our strongest asset as a new federalism begins to evolve. Alberta will continue to play a leadership role in strengthening the unity of our Confederation.
What Alberta wants to see in any constitutional change is the promotion of Canadian unity, the achievement of the aspirations of the new west, a strengthening of the position of the provinces, and the safeguarding of the traditional and historic rights of the provinces, particularly with regard to natural resource ownership.
The Prime Minister notwithstanding, the message of the real Alberta is starting to be understood in central Canada. I congratulate the Hamilton Spectator for its editorial of October 5 which commended Premier Lougheed for opposing
[Mr. Roche.)
greater concentration of political power in Ottawa. The editorial noted:
The fact is that the economic advance of Alberta is good for all of Canada, very good. And the development of more political power on the prairies would also be good for Canada. Ideally all the provinces from Newfoundland to British Columbia should share Alberta's aspirations and confidence.
What Canadians are looking for is a healthy and hopeful society. We must recover a sense of purpose for our country. The world needs our vigorous participation in economic partnerships.
This past summer I went around the world on a foreign policy mission and I saw the opportunities, and the challenges for Canada in a changing world. We are closing our eyes to problems and opportunities for Canada abroad because we are so beleaguered at home on the economy and national unity questions. We must solve our internal problems so that we can get on with a constructive and responsible role in the modern world. The recovery of trust in Ottawa is essential in this process. Canadians desperately need effective, co-operative leadership, not more political confrontation. Only in this way can our country express fresh recognition of the basic values in life, such as truth, honesty, and decency, that never change.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to participate in this debate in reply to the Speech from the Throne. Particularly I would like to compliment the mover and the seconder, the hon. member for York South (Mrs. Appolloni) and the hon. member for Verdun (Mr. Savard), both of whom gave strong and articulate statements. I was most impressed with the statement made by the hon. member for York South, a colleague of mine who comes from the same region of Canada. Hers was a thoughtful, warm and compassionate statement, not surprising to those who know her as a warm, compassionate, and concerned Canadian.
I was less impressed with the speech which I have just heard made by the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Roche). He has made a number of good speeches in this House and we have listened to many of them with great admiration. This was not his finest hour. Indeed, for a man who is espousing the cause of Canada, it seemed to me to be a speech which was aimed at fanning the flames of resentment and building upon a sense of alienation in the west. I know that alienation is there. I grew up in the west, just as the hon. member did. I probably sense it as well as most people in this House.
I was not impressed when the hon. member used his position as a member representing a very important part of the country to fan those flames and suggest that somehow or other we were not treating one province, the richest province in this country, the same as the others. There was a suggestion that we were trying to take advantage of Alberta through tax discrimination, and I think tax discrimination was the phrase he used. We have introduced tax measures which affect the province of Alberta and its citizens, but those tax measures have been
October 16, 1978

introduced to assist them and other Canadians to develop the resources of Alberta for Albertans, in fact for all Canadians. I am referring to the new measures which were introduced this past year with respect to depletion allowances and other measures aimed at bringing on the tar sands and the heavy oils.
The hon. member referred to the Syncrude project, that gigantic national resource which was formally opened this year, a Canadian first by any standard. But he did not mention that it was only made possible because the federal government provided a particular kind of tax treatment for that project, because the federal government moved in to help salvage the project along with the Alberta government. It was in fact a combined enterprise of the federal government, the Alberta government and the Ontario government which, without the assistance of these governments, would not have taken place. That was not the cast of his remarks. The cast was of grievance, of resentment, of dividing, not building. As I say, it was not his finest hour.
I quote the words of the Governor General in the Speech from the Throne where he stated:
1: Urgent Action Needed
Parliament begins today a new session which will concentrate upon Canada's two most pressing needs. They are the strengthening of our economy, and the renewal of our federation.
Those two inseparable imperatives are different expressions of the same goal: to strengthen Canada through unity: to unify Canada through economic strength.
I do not think we are going to find the clues to those particular policy directions in the sentiments stated and unstated that I listened to in the speech made by the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona.

speechtext:
The two themes of strengthening the economy and of strengthening our country and confederation were themes which were picked up by the Prime Minister in his memorable speech last week.
I would like to add another perspective, a perspective as the minister responsible for energy policy, because no policy area seems to me to be more important to these two objectives than the energy policy area.
Quite simply, our economy, economic security, future economic growth, and future prosperity as Canadians will depend upon adequate and reliable supplies of energy at competitive prices.
Second, our sources of energy and our consumption of energy are often thousands of miles apart in this country. Nowhere is the economic and political interdependence of the regions of Canada more manifested than in the energy policy areas, areas of production, transportation and consumption of oil, natural gas, coal, uranium and hydro power. However, it has not always been that way. That has not always been the perception in Canada.
The Address-Mr. Gillespie
As recently as five years ago, Canadians were unconcerned about security of supply. That was hardly a word that we heard in the lexicon of Canadian economic policy. That was the time when we felt we had lots of cheap energy. The issue was not security of supply. The issue then was: how do we get the United States to take more of it?
That perception started to change in 1973 when the OPEC nations raised the price of oil four times and the Arab OPEC nations decided they would embargo the greatest nation in the world, the United States, that they would cut off supplies to the United States.
Quite clearly, the Arab nations, which produce most of the oil in OPEC, gave the Americans and the industrialized world two simple messages. The first was that the era of cheap energy is over. The second was just as important a message. It was that in the future "you would be unwise to count on us for your energy needs." There have been other events since 1973 and 1974 which have tended to highlight the insecurity of supply to the western world and to Canada.
Venezuelan production, for example, has been declining. The government of Venezuela has decided to cut back on its oil production. There have been some big finds such as the North Sea, Prudhoe Bay, and re-examination of the Mexican reserves, but not many other significant big finds. Big finds have been rare.
At the same time there has been an increasing perception that the technical producibility of existing wells is going to peak within a very few years. The World Energy Conference in their book entitled "World Energy, Looking Ahead to the Year 2020" published in the last few weeks by the Conservation Commission of the World Energy Conference, covered the input of thousands of experts from dozens of countries around the world for a period of three years. It contains the best estimates in the industry, in the countries, the bureaucracies and the universities. It is the most comprehensive that I have seen to date. It indicates that the producibility of world oil reserves will start to decline very shortly after 1985 at a time when the world will continue to be increasing its demand for oil.
During this period of time, as well, we have seen social unrest and tensions between countries in the Middle East start to increase. I refer, of course, to the tragic events in Lebanon, and the assassinations in the two countries to the south of Saudi Arabia, South Yemen and North Yemen, to the events on the Horn of Africa, to the internal events in Iran, to the almost silent takeover from a non-Marxist regime to a Marxist oriented one in Afghanistan, to the PLO, and to the Arab-Israeli conflicts. There is a whole pattern of instability in the Middle East, the centre of the greatest source of world oil.
During this period of time we have also noted a stiffening resistance on the part of Saudi Arabia, the greatest oil producer, to continue its production of oil. This view was put forward again when Ahmed Zaki Yamani, the petroleum minister of mines and resources of Saudi Arabia, was in Canada this summer.

October 16, 1978
The Address-Mr. Gillespie
I have taken a few minutes to put this matter in context. I think it is important that the security of supply arguments be understood by Canadians and all sides of the House. During this period of time, of course, the perception also changed in another very important respect. That was that Canada was no longer a net exporter of oil. Canada had become a net importer. Quite clearly the sense of urgency with respect to security of supply has increased very quickly and very substantially.
Quite simply stated, the major population centres of central and eastern Canada were perceived to be vulnerable as never before. Approximately 50 per cent of the primary energy source of this part of Canada is supplied in the form of oil. That oil has been increasingly imported oil. Without that oil, our economy will not function. Indeed, it will literally run out of gas.
During this period of time there has also been confusion among some people about gluts. There have been temporary gluts because of the Prudhoe Bay find and the discoveries in the North Sea. However, they are not going to answer our problems. The new discoveries in Mexico may help to buy a little time, but that is all they will do, because these discoveries together probably do not add more than a few years to the consumption pattern of the world.
That confusion continues to bedevil the energy policy formula in this country, as it did in the United States. However, there are other reasons for putting this in context, not just for Canadians to appreciate the importance of the issue but to understand the initiatives the federal government has taken and, indeed, to challenge the official opposition to come forward with their own policy positions in these important areas.
As I go through the rest of my remarks there will be a number of cases where I will want to challenge them to respond to important energy issues facing this country at the present time.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
The hon. member says they will tell us after the next election. Judging by the kind of statements his leader made in the House on leaders' day, I think we can expect more. He invited Canadians and members on this side of the House to expect more. He invited us to expect that he is prepared to put his party's position forward on these issues.. We have been waiting a long time to hear from him on some of these issues. We hope we will not have to wait very much longer.
The issue of energy policy is not whether there will be a shortage, nor is it when will that shortage occur. The issue is, given our opportunities and the urgencies facing us, what can Canadians do? What can we in Canada do to protect our own interests, our own economy, integrity, and the interdependence of our own country? What can we do to develop our own energy resources?

We are very fortunate as a country. We have options which most countries lack-large resources in western Canada, in the Arctic and offshore. We believe there is a major role for private industry to play in finding and developing those resources.
We also believe there is a role for the national oil companies in various countries. We believe there is a role for the Canadian national oil company, Petro-Canada, to play in the exploration and development of Canadian resources. But that is not the position of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark). The Leader of the Opposition has clearly stated that he would invite the national oil companies of other countries to come to Canada to look for Canadian resources and develop them, but that he would not permit the Canadian national oil company to do so. He made it clear he would dismantle Petro-Canada. Mr. Speaker, that is an absurd position for any thinking Canadian to take. It would be absurd the eyes of any foreign thinking government.
Can you imagine the President of France saying, "Well, I wonder whether the national oil company of France" which is presently exploring off the coast of Labrador, "would be able to form a joint venture with the Canadian national oil company in the same area in which it is now operating?" Would he not be bound to conclude that were the Conservatives to form the government he would have to find a multinational partner or deal with the oil company of another nation but that he could not deal with a Canadian company in the development of Canada's national resources?
If some other government, for example, the British government through BP, or the German government through its own company, wanted to get into the development of the vast tar sands of western Canada, they could not do so by dealing with a Canadian national oil company; they would probably have to deal with the national oil company of Japan which has already made an application to work out a joint venture with the Canadian national oil company, Petro-Canada.
I think Canadians will increasingly ask what is wrong with having a Canadian national oil company develop our resources. Why would the Leader of the Opposition not wish Canadians to participate in the development of our own country?
I should like to deal briefly before the lunch break with two other important developments which have taken place since the House rose last July. I should like to deal first of all with measures to reduce the inflationary impact of oil price changes, and to follow this with some comments on the measures we have taken to develop security of supply of energy resources for Canadians in the future.
I wish to refer particularly to measures we have in train with respect to certain major capital projects referred to in the Speech from the Throne. I wish to touch on the importance of maximizing eastern Canadian markets in particular for Canadian natural gas as a means of reducing dependence upon foreign imported oil. I should like to deal as well with the
October 16, 1978

program which was introduced in connection with the development of solar energy, an important program which has a strong Canadian orientation looking to the development of Canadian industry and using Canadian firms. This program is in marked contrast to the one which was trotted out-that is probably the most charitable way of putting it-some months ago by opposition spokesmen, a program which seemed to be more concerned with providing tax credits to persons who have installed solar heating some eight years ago than in dealing with the future or with the development of the Canadian industry; nowhere was a preference given to the development of solar systems by Canadians, which is in complete contrast to the approach taken in my party.
The measure to reduce the excise tax on gasoline by three cents will have the effect of enabling consumers to pay a price for gasoline which would be lower than otherwise. It is a measure aimed at trying to contain the price escalation which we became increasingly concerned about as it approached double digit figures. It is aimed at all Canadians.
With respect to the oil price change on January 1, I should like to spend a minute or two discussing the implications, but I shall probably have to do that after the lunch break. However, I want to make it clear that the agreement we have reached with Alberta with respect to the oil price increase on January 1 was conditioned by the level of prices in the United States. Our position was that we have to protect the competitive position of Canadian industry, as well as move prices up in an orderly way to ensure that development will take place and take place expeditiously. We do not think there will be sufficient head room on January 1 for a price increase to take place, but we are saying that in any event we believe it is in the national interest that the price increase should not take place at that time.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to call it one o'clock.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to spend just a moment to recap some of the themes of my earlier remarks. I had been talking about the importance of security of supply. This is a relatively new concept as far as Canadian perceptions are concerned. It is important because we have received a message from the oil exporting countries that we cannot continue to count on their supplies. They are, quite clearly, not prepared to guarantee an ever increasing amount of oil for
The Address-Mr. Gillespie
Canadians and others. We are a net importer of oil, not a net exporter of oil. We have very substantial resources in Canada which we should be developing and, so far as possible, developing ourselves. Yes, we should be developing those resources, with the help of others when we can, and developing those resources by ourselves when we can.
I pointed out that a number of other free enterprise countries around the world also recognize the serious security of supply problem, that they have developed national oil companies to assist them in obtaining security of oil supplies, that many of those national oil companies are active in Canada in an exploration and development way and in some cases in a production way as well, and that the Canadian government formed Petro-Canada to assist in the exploration and development of Canadian resources.
Petro-Canada has been very active in the Arctic and in the offshore. Indeed, last year one half of all the wells drilled in the Arctic and offshore areas of this country were drilled with Petro-Canada participation. However, the position of the Leader of the Opposition is that he would keep those foreign national oil companies in Canada and dismantle the Canadian one. He would go further than that; presumably he would invite those national oil companies which are not now in Canada to come to Canada, but he would dismantle the Canadian national oil company. He would have no answer for the governments of other free enterprise economies when they would say to him that through their national oil companies they would like to deal with the Canadian national oil company in Canada for their purposes and for Canadian purposes.
He would have no answer because he would already have announced, if not already dismantled, the dismantling of the Canadian national oil company. This is a ludicrous position to Canadians. One might also observe that it is a ludicrous position to those outside Canada who would want to do business in Canada. They would ask why the leader of the country, which the Leader of the Opposition hopes to be, has so little faith in Canadians that he would not be prepared to maintain and develop a national oil company as other countries have done for their own security?
I went on to point out very briefly that other free enterprise economies are also heavily involved in the exploration and development of uranium. I referred to Germany, Italy, France, and Spain. Yes, there are companies in Canada with very heavy British government investment as well. There is one national Crown corporation, Eldorado, in which the people of Canada, through the Government of Canada, have an interest. That too, however, is something which the Leader of the Opposition would dismantle or peddle. He has not yet told us how he would deal with it, but he would get rid of it. He seems unable to put Canadian interests first.
It is questionable whether the Leader of the Opposition is a captive of an earlier dogma of the Conservative party or whether he has been talking to interests, perhaps in the uranium industry, who would like to make a bid for the most profitable of the Canadian Crown corporations.

October 16, 1978
The Address-Mr. Gillespie
I was about to go on to the oil pricing question. I want to provide a little background on this because the pricing of oil has always been a trade-off of a number of conflicting interests and objectives. Canadians will remember that we did not move immediately to the international price for oil in 1973-74. Instead, we decided to move up in measured but orderly steps toward world energy prices. We did so because we were concerned about the impact on the economy of such a massive change. We were concerned as well about ensuring a competitive advantage, where possible, for Canadian industry. The Conservative party has yet to state its position with respect to this pricing policy for oil.
As much as possible we have tried to reconcile the interests of the economy, on the one hand, by a pace of change toward international prices which will be slow enough to minimize any adverse impacts, and particularly to contain inflationary pressures. On the other hand, however, we have also tried to move fast enough to produce a favourable conservation impact and favourably stimulate the exploration and development of oil and other petroleum resources in Canada and, as much as possible, to limit budgetary requirements, because the subsidy which has been paid under this program has amounted, or will amount, to better than $5 billion by the end of this fiscal year. This is the subsidy which has been paid-because we import; we are not a net exporter, we are a net importer of oil-to hold down oil prices in a very large section of the country.
We felt that there would not be sufficient head room, that is to say, the difference between the Canadian average price and the American average price would be less than one dollar come January 1-so we took the position that there should not be a one dollar increase come January 1, a position which had been fully discussed and negotiated. Indeed, it was one of the conditions of the oil price increases negotiated a year and a half ago with the producing provinces that if there is not that head room, that there should not be a price increase. In our view there will not be that head room.
We have gone further: we have said that in any event we think it is in the interest of the national economy not to move up that one dollar come January 1. We believe this is a responsible position for the Canadian government to take. We would like to hear from the official opposition, which has been silent on that, as it has been silent on many important and contentious issues. Can the official opposition put its own particular regional concerns behind the national interest?
There are some major capital projects which we hope to complete during the life of this parliament. I am referring, for example, to the Maritime Energy Corporation. Negotiations are continuing favourably, although one must recognize that there are two new leaders in those provinces at the present time, as well as the fact that the third province is involved in a general election. That particular project is important to the maritimes and Canada. It will have to wait just a little longer for fruition. I am hopeful we will be able to bring it off with the cooperation of the leaders of those three provinces. Simi-

larly, the formation of the Lower Churchill Falls Development Corporation in conjunction with the province of Newfoundland has moved along well. We should be in a position to announce the formation of the corporation very soon.
