speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to join with the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) in congratulating the mover (Mrs. Appolloni), and seconder (Mr. Savard), for their very fine statements in the House the other day. I was delighted to listen to what the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie) had to say, as well as what he neglected to say. Particularly I am pleased that he did not make a forecast about the prospects for the Canadian oil and gas industry. Ever since the government has been in power, we have received nothing but different forecasts. Every time the minister speaks, the net result is that we are more confused about the situation.
I was not astonished to hear a restatement in ringing tones of the commitment of the Liberal government that the enterprise system cannot solve the energy problems of this nation. It is a commitment for more government and bigger government all the time.
Many Canadians must find it absolutely incomprehensible that the energy policy of Canada should be one based upon the principle of self-reliance, rather than the principle of self-sufficiency. Surely if we learned anything during the OPEC crisis, it was that we must move as rapidly as possible to this position of self-sufficiency in energy. We are one of the few countries in the world which is capable of achieving a position of self-sufficiency. We have the largest known proven reserves of oil. We have larger proven reserves in our oil sands than the Middle East. It is a measure of the failure of the government that we are not self-sufficient in the production of energy.
I should like to speak for a moment on the contents of the Speech from the Throne and the participation of the Prime Minister the other day. The Speech from the Throne was most unusual and disappointing. Unlike most occasions when the government uses the Speech from the Throne to outline plans for the forthcoming session of parliament, and the participation of the Prime Minister to fill in the details, the government provided us with little vision, and practically nothing was said about the plans for governing this nation during the next year. Moreover, the Prime Minister used his time not to elucidate and expand, but to defend, explain, attack, and condemn, to the point where anyone listening to the debate would think that the Prime Minister had assumed already his position as leader of the opposition.
Perhaps the unusual nature of the government's performance can be explained by the fact that the House of Commons
October 16, 1978

is a political arena as well as a forum for governing, and that we are in the last stages of parliament before the calling of an election. Under such circumstances, the last gasp attempts of a Prime Minister to absolve an administration which is dying, and which, like a sick animal, should be put out of its misery as soon as possible, are understandable. Given the fact that the nation is looking for leadership, is aching to have confidence in its institutions and wants to know what plans this interim government has, clearly there has been a mammoth political miscalculation on the part of the government and the Prime Minister in abdicating the responsibility for providing leadership and offering hope to the people of the country.
Defence of the past is not what the nation is looking for. It is plans for the future and solutions to problems which people are looking for, and deserve to have. Politicians who have been on the hustings during the last few weeks and months know that at the present time Canadians are somewhat fearful of their future. They are distrustful of the inability of their institutions to solve the problems of the day. Probably faith in politicians is at an all-time low. For the Prime Minister to use one of our time-honoured occasions, to attack the opposition, not to put forward ideas and not to say how the government will operate in the forthcoming session, is an additional indication of the inability of the government to lead.
As unusual and misguided as the tactics of the Prime Minister may be, they are understandable at this time in our history. However, what was missing from the Speech from the Throne and the elucidation of the Prime Minister was an appeal and a challenge to Canadians to look at problems as opportunities and to have confidence in their nation. An omission such as this is inexplicable and unforgivable.
I had occasion to look in Bartlett's famous quotations for noteworthy contributions in the House of Commons, and found only the one made by Sir Winston Churchill in the Canadian House of Commons during World War II. Perhaps it is un-Canadian to provide the nation with any resounding statements of aspirations-I do not know. But if ever is a time when Canadians are looking toward the government for leadership, surely it is now. Where in the Speech from the Throne, or in the contribution by the Prime Minister, can an equivalent of John F. Kennedy's ringing declaration of his first inauguration be found? Mr. Kennedy said:
Ask not what your country can do for you but what you can do for your country.
At a time like this, Canadians have a right to expect such statements in the Speech from the Throne or from their Prime Minister. Where can an equivalent of President Roosevelt's comforting words in his first inaugural address be found? He said:
The only thing we have to fear is fear itself.
Or the words of Sir Winston Churchill when he said:
Do not let us speak of darker days; let us speak rather of sterner days.
Surely the essence of leadership is to be able to use the language in a sentence, to infuse the hopes and aspirations of a nation. Is there no one in the office of the Prime Minister who
The Address-Mr. Gillies
is capable of putting together such statements in order to distil for Canadians the leadership they require?
I would not suggest that we only need more rhetoric or more studies. What we really need is action on the pressing problems facing us. Warren Bennis has pointed out in his study entitled "The Unconscious Conspiracy: Why Leaders Can't Lead" the following:
Nothing ensures the status quo so much as putting the best minds and best talents to work diligently on blue ribbon task force committees. For their reports continue to get better as our problems get worse.
In this session of parliament we do not need more studies and more commissions. We require urgent action on parliamentary reform, economic reconstruction, and constitutional reform. We need to get on with the tasks we have been elected to perform-to provide a legislative framework within which people can live with freedom and opportunity.
We got nothing innovative and nothing new from the Prime Minister in his rambling speech. One expected and hoped for much more, because every Canadian who has been following our history knows that the Prime Minister has recently turned his personal attention to the economic problems of our time. This was dramatically illustrated on August 1 when, on his return from Bonn, he personally took hold of the economic management of the country, apparently without extensive consultation, some would say with no consultation whatsoever, with his officials or his colleagues, appearing on national television to announce the new economic policies of the government.
What was indeed lacking and threatening in the speech he made here, which we thought would develop the details of that statement made on television on August 1, was that the government, it is clear, has no fundamental grasp of the interrelationship between the various economic activities that go on in a nation and the need for an interrelated series of policies to solve them.
Unfortunately in his remarks in the House the Prime Minister said absolutely nothing to alleviate the fears of those who believe that economic policy-making in this country has collapsed, that the government has no program for dealing with the problems of high unemployment, has no program for dealing with high inflation, has no program for dealing with the low value dollar, and has no program for approaching the crisis in confidence which is apparent around us.
Indeed, the entire economic portion of the Prime Minister's speech, a speech which was awaited with keen expectation by people both inside and outside Canada so that they could assess the government's plans, was not a speech at all. Instead, it consisted of citations and recitations of statistics which appear to come from OECD press releases, and which were well orchestrated to demonstrate that the Canadian economy was probably outperforming any other economy in the world.
There was no awareness that 900,000 Canadians are out of work, no awareness that Canada has the second highest inflation rate of any industrialized nation of the world, no aware-

October 16, 1978
The Address-Mr. Gillies
ness that the dollar is selling at about 84 cents, no awareness that there is an outflow of capital going on in an unprecedented amount, and no awareness that the general attitude of the people in Canada is that the economy is completely out of control.
It has been long held that statistics can be used to prove anything, and that maxim was never given a greater testing than last Friday when the Prime Minister spoke. How irrelevant to take ten years of statistics to demonstrate, I am not sure what, when we have these problems before us at the present time! How devastating that the Prime Minister, who has taken over and is in charge of economic policy making at the present time, appears to believe that the recitation of statistics for a ten-year period has any relevance whatsoever with what we have deal with in this parliament at the present time!
There is no debate in Canada at the present time about the goals of economic policy making. All parties believe that what we want in this nation is reasonably full employment and relative price stability. What we do have a debate on is how to get there.
The New Democratic Party is convinced that the traditional Keynesian policy of spending more is the way to solve our unemployment problem, to spend our way into prosperity, and if there is something less than full utilization of capacity in our nation, and a short-fall in investments, the government should take up the difference and in this way solve our economic difficulties.
The problem is we know that this, what has become the truly traditional approach, is not working any more, and it has not worked since 1972. The only way that public investment of a greater amount can be financed in Canada at the present time, with the present state of Canadian capital markets, would be with a greater deficit. The government could not finance a greater deficit at the present time and, therefore, would have to print more money. We know that in the structure of the economy we have now, and with the conditions we have now, the only thing that would happen with the printing of more money would be more inflation, and with more inflation there would be less investment, and with less investment there would be more unemployment.
The fact of the matter is that the policy advocated by the NDP, appropriate as it might have been for 1936, and as appropriate as it might have been for some cyclical slowdowns in 1950, is simply inappropriate and would not work under the circumstances we have at the present time. It is somewhat sad to me that a party which has been in the forefront of reform many times would propose such old fashioned, outmoded propositions to deal with our economic problems at the present time. They are almost as unworkable as the nationalization of resources which they have preached since the time of the Regina manifesto.
Unfortunately an analysis of the positions of the present government is more difficult because they are so incoherent one does not really know what they are intended to accom-
[Mr. Gillies.)
plish. Again, the goals are clear. We want to bring about reasonably full employment and relative price stability, but how do we do that?
The government seems to say that what it wants to do is cut, at least in planning if not in reality, its spending plan. Presumably the reason for doing this is to instil confidence in investors, lower the deficit, and slow down the rate of inflation. But at the same time the government raised interest rates. Last Friday it raised interest rates to the highest in this country since, I think, 1934. The result of raising the interest rate is to create unemployment because it slows down the rate of investment. This is exactly the opposite to what the government said it was trying to do with its budget cuts.
The government's stated budget cuts are highly irrational. The government has said, for example, that it wants to increase exports. Our advantage in exports is in respect of many of our basic resource industries. The government cut expenditure on research and development. It has cut expenditures on research in the fishing industry. It seems just incredible it would do this after spending several years negotiating a 200-mile limit in order that we could exploit fisheries. The government now cuts research in that area just when we need it so badly. It has also cut expenditures for research in respect of forestry products and in other areas where we must continue to develop efficient and effective methods if we are going to be able to increase our exports. This makes no sense whatsoever.
There has been no rational explanation on the part of the government as to what kind of deficit it wants. What is the appropriate deficit, the appropriate fiscal stance for this country during the next few years-the next five years, for example? How will it be funded? There are no explanations because there is no policy. Moreover, the government does not seem to have any understanding whatsoever of the fact that a deficit results not only from extravagant government spending but also from a decline in revenues.
The government does not seem to understand that one of the ways to increase revenues is by cutting taxes, strange as that may seem to some. The evidence is in from all over the world now that if you have an intelligent tax cut program which stimulates economic activity your revenues will increase. This has been pointed out by Professor Laffer, and it has been supported by the fact that when President Kennedy adopted tax cuts in the United States in 1960 he converted a federal deficit of $4 billion in 1961 to a surplus of $8 billion in 1965. The government has no policy on taxation in an attempt to stimulate the economy so that revenues will grow again.
The policy of the government in respect of the management of the dollar is so puzzling it defies explanation. Everyone knows that the credibility of this government has been weakened, almost beyond recovery, by the way in which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) has handled the decline in the value of the dollar on foreign exchange markets.
Certainly it is clear, in an economy such as Canada's, where we have 27 per cent of our gross national product generated by foreign trade, compared to 6 per cent in the United States, that whatever happens to the dollar has an immense effect on
October 16, 1978

domestic inflation and on employment. It is simply impossible to make economic policy to achieve full employment and price stability without having a policy about the dollar. Every time our dollar goes down one cent against the American dollar, we have four-tenths of one per cent change in the inflation rate in Canada. Are the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister trying to tell us that the government has no position with respect to the dollar, that any level of the dollar is satisfactory for the making of economic policy in this nation? This is absolutely ludicrous.
If our goals are to have reasonably full employment and reasonable price stability we must have a policy with respect to the value of the dollar. While the government argues that we are increasing our exports through the devaluation of the dollar, it should never forget that this is a very short-run gain. The last country that used this policy for any extensive period of time was Britain, and everyone knows what happened to the British economy from the period 1955 to 1965. In short, because of domestic inflation effects, the advantages that are gained in the export market by the devaluation of the dollar are soon wiped out.
I do not propose to argue today, because it is not the time or place, the merits of a fixed exchange rate versus the idea of a floating rate. Many economists believe that the great depression of the 1930s was caused because of fixed exchange rates when economies were held to the gold standard. Certainly after World War II, when ministers of finance of the world met together at Bretton Woods, it was determined that they would operate with a much more orderly international market. The reality is that the Bretton Woods program for handling international stability is no longer viable. Countries are breaking away from it, and we need new approaches.
Part of that new approach is for countries to demonstrate that they have an understanding of the interrelationship of their currency, if it is an open economy as in our case, and the economic policies that they are trying to propose. For the Minister of Finance of Canada to say that where the dollar is, is irrelevant to economic policymaking in this country, is doing nothing to achieve any gains in this direction. In short, elementary as the lesson seems to be, this government does not seem to understand the monetary, fiscal policy, that is, spending and taxing, and its exchange rate policy, must be integrated and they must work together.
Over the past few years we have experienced exactly the reverse. On the one hand the government does something on exchange rate policy which increases unemployment, then it does something on fiscal policy to decrease unemployment. Then it puts up interest rates by half a per cent, which lowers employment. There has been absolutely no program whatsoever. It is as if from day to day the Mad Hatter, from Alice in Wonderland, were making economic policy in this nation, a policy which can best be summed in Churchill's phrase that the government has, "decided only to be undecided, resolved to be irresolute, adamant for drift, solid for fluidity, all powerful
The Address-Mr. Gillies
to be impotent". It is the best summary one can make of economic policy making at this time in this nation.
The agony of the current economic situation is that it is unnecessary. Canada is a rich country, probably one of the richest in the world in terms of resources and potential. Remember that when the OPEC cut off energy from industrial countries, Germany and Japan did not have any oil at all, and yet they managed to have enormous recoveries and strong economic performances. The only thing we have succeeded at in the past few years is failing.
Why would that be true, Mr. Speaker? Well, there are many reasons. Part of the failure flows from the general inability of the federal government to work constructively with provincial governments toward mutual solutions of problems. Part of it is clearly in the inherent contradictions in the constitution, written 111 years ago, which gives the strong taxing power, and therefore the largest source of revenues, to a central government, but leaves in the hands of the provincial governments the expensive things to pay for, health, education, and welfare. Part of the problem comes from an acceptance on the part of the government in power of spending programs that it has no way of financing and the naive belief that the economy will constantly grow. This is probably based on the euphoric notion that economic growth will always be with us no matter what we do, and possibly in part on a failure to realize that what is a right economic policy for one period may, indeed, be the wrong one for another. Of all these reasons, the latter is often forgotten.
We have been a country locked in policy making based on the programs Lord Keynes developed in and for the 1930s. John Kenneth Galbraith, in his essay "How Keynes Came to America", points out that of all western industrialized nations the most Keynesian is Canada. Tragically, our policy makers have never realized that in a diverse nation such as Canada, with the great differences among our various regions, we need a different approach to our economic policy making. The essence of policy making in this country during the last few decades is that, by changing general tax policies and general expenditure policies, we can achieve the growth we want to have. Under certain circumstances this was true, but in a nation such as ours it is not always true, and it is not true now.
In this country economic policies must be made on the basis that if we make the components strong the total will be strong. What we need to do in this country, and this is more than lip service to some sector analysis, is to have a real belief that if we want to have full employment in Canada and want to have price stability we must be certain that the various sectors of the economy are prosperous. That means doing for the fishing industry what we have to do to make the fishing industry prosperous and doing the same thing for agriculture, manufacturing, and small business. When they are prosperous the nation as a whole will be prosperous. We can no longer go along with the budget making which I have seen in the six years I have been here, where every single budget has been based upon a false perception. Until that changes, we are going to have serious difficulties in this nation.

October 16, 1978
The Address-Mr. Gillies
To solve the economic problems of this country we need not be limited by lack of knowledge. Economists have been much maligned during the past few years, and perhaps properly so. But new economic theory is not needed. What we must have is the political will to do those things which must be done to turn this economy around. We must begin the task of economic reconstruction and development, not only for the obvious reasons of creating the wealth which is available to Canadians, but as a cornerstone for solving our social and constitutional problems.
This country this year is maintaining its record as being among the top one or two countries of the world in the number of days lost through industrial strife, and I wonder why. There are many reasons, but surely one of the most important must be the latent discontent with the management of the economy as a whole. People know, and their common sense tells them, that this is a country that does not have to have high levels of unemployment and inflation, that we should not have underutilization of our resources. They know when they hear of inflation rates of less than 5 per cent in Germany and other industrialized countries, and when they hear of situations where there is full employment of resources in other countries, they know that it does not have to be this way. They know that there has been mismanagement at the top and, they have become discontented and are determined that they will get their share. If they have to strike to do it, they will do it. They are disillusioned and quite willing to question the very social structure of our nation and the way our institutions operate.
That is one of the main reasons why we have so many strikes and lose so much production in this country. It has been said before, and I am sure it is true, that the alienation of the nation is immense. All we have to do is remember that in the province of Quebec we have an elected government that is dedicated to the proposition of taking the people of that province out of confederation. One only needs to go west to see the alienation all the way from Thunder Bay to the Pacific Oceah.
Why should that be, Mr. Speaker, in a nation endowed with the resources and history that we have had in this country? Part of it, as I have suggested, is because of the fact that the economy is not working the way it has previously, and part of it must lie in our constitutional difficulties.
If there is one thing that we must do in this parliament it is to bring in institutional reforms so that we can make parliament operate more effectively. Solving our institutional problems will not mean that all our problems will be solved. They will not, but we must make an attempt to do so and create understanding on the part of all Canadians.
I am speaking for myself but I sense that, particularly among my French Canadian friends, there is often a feeling that those of us not from the province of Quebec may not understand, may not care about what happens in that province. I would remind them, with the best spirit in the world, that the greatest study ever made of American democracy in the 19th
[Mr. Gillies !
century was done by Thomas deTocqueville who did not live in the United States. The social consequences of the policy of the United States of America toward blacks was written by Gunnar Myrdal, a Swede, in his book "The American Dilemma" in 1936. Those of us not from Quebec can also understand the problems of Quebec. I know my colleagues in this party and the leader of this party are bringing insight and understanding to the aspirations of the people of Quebec, even though they may not live there.
I would implore all sides of the House, particularly those responsible for developing policies and constitutional changes, not to ignore what might be said by those who may not come directly from Quebec, because we care, Mr. Speaker. I am sure we care as much as they that this nation survives after 111 years-

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. These are the days for the forecaster of the apocalypse. People as disparate as Robert Heilbronner in his book "An Inquiry Into the Human Prospect", or William Simon in "A Time for Truth", or Richard Goodwin in his analysis of the future of the United States, are saying that the democratic system as we know it is not going to survive unless people have confidence in their institutions.
The institution of parliament is a product of 111 years of history in Canada; it is a product of our history and of what we do, but every institution is also the sum of the people who are in it. I cannot subscribe to the theory that those of us who are privileged to be members of this institution of parliament cannot, in this period of crisis in our nation, make this institution work in such a way that we can solve our problems. Surely we do not want to leave this place thinking that we have not done everything, regardless of our political pursuasion, regardless of our personal interest, to make sure that it rises to the challenge presented by the Canadian people today.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with pleasure that I welcome this opportunity to speak on the Address in reply to the Speech from the Throne, and I want to join the others who have spoken so far to commend the mover (Mrs. Appolloni) and the seconder (Mr. Savard) who did outstanding work.
What can readily be said about the Speech from the Throne is that is is a heap of old statements made by the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) outside the House and before the Speech from the Throne, which really comes down to two main points only, that is, first lower government's spending
October 16, 1978

and, second, the constitutional change being proposed by the government. Apart from that, the most important problems are not mentioned. The economic problem is not mentioned. So we waited for the Prime Minister's speech to see if he could at least explain the Speech from the Throne and make it clearer. Unfortunately, we witnessed a two-hour attack against the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark), but we were not offered any valid solution, any precision as to the attitude taken by the Prime Minister or the government concerning the remedies to be applied to the problems we are now confronted with.
The Prime Minister spent some time asking us to review his scholarly knowledge when he was speaking about experimental and rational psychology and he said that in his opinion the human brain has three different faculties: memory, imagination and intelligence. Lie said the Leader of the Opposition does have some memory despite a few mistakes, that he has plenty of imagination, but as far as intelligence is concerned, it is lacking in his speech.
I think Canadians in general will find it easy to agree with me here and that they recognize that the Prime Minister is indeed an intelligent man. But the fact is his administration lacks imagination and above all memory. The fact that once again the government has increased the rate of interest by three-quarters of one per cent two days after the Speech from the Throne is evidence of a lack of imagination because that was the fifth time the government did that since January. It is a lack of memory as well because such a move has always had the same results. Each time the government thought it would help our economy and each time it has caused a surge in inflation and unemployment.
The Prime Minister had just noted in his speech that the chairman and chief executive of the Royal Bank, Mr. McLaughlin, says we should not be too pessimistic, that things are going fine. If I were the chairman of the Royal Bank, I would certainly have said the same thing. When the government increases the rates by three-quarters of one per cent, the bankers feel allowed to raise theirs by 2 per cent or 3 per cent on the loans they will make. In their place, I say that there is no reason to be pessimistic. But people, the individuals who tomorrow will have to pay 15 per cent interest rather than 12 per cent on their loans, they have grounds to be pessimistic. And the Prime Minister is telling us: things are not that bad, the unemployment rate is going down.
According to Statistics Canada and the latest figures published on October 10-they are always a month old-as of September 16 then, the number of people receiving unemployment insurance benefits had indeed diminished. That is true. On the other hand, what they fail to add is that in some areas like mine, in northwest Quebec where we had 20 per cent of our people unemployed last summer, the unemployment rate
The Address-Mr. G. Caouette
went down to 16 per cent. Some will say: things go better, there are fewer unemployed! There are indeed fewer people who receive unemployment insurance benefits. On the other hand, there is the working population, the percentage of those on the labour market, not the population generally but people working, those who are on the labour market and looking for work. In my area, some 57 per cent of the people indeed are working which means that 43 per cent are unemployed, 16 per cent of whom are drawing unemployment insurance. Consequently, some 30 per cent are unemployed and do not receive any unemployment insurance. Where are they? Are they on social welfare? Is that a valid and buoyant economy, as suggested by the Prime Minister? I would say that we are right in the midst of a depression, but the Prime Minister's response is to say that the Leader of the Opposition lacks intelligence. That was his response in his speech.
In Quebec as a whole, we find 10 per cent unemployed 30 per cent of whom do not draw any unemployment insurance. Can you say then that the economy is booming that business is is thriving and that those who will be compelled to borrow and pay 15 per cent in interest will be happy while the Canadian economy will be expanding? No way.
The lack of imagination and memory of the government squeezes the worker more and more while allowing financiers to tighten their hold on him. Anti-inflation measures which we have lived with were aimed at limiting salary increases for individuals. Lor instance, in my riding and in three others throughout the province of Quebec, when Molson Company employees obtained wage increases, the Anti-Inflation Board came forward with a study and said to these employees: You are not entitled to those higher wages. And then they forced the employees to reimburse the company. That is what the government sitting in front of us is all about! Yes, I say they forced the employees to hand back to the company the increases they had obtained but at the same time this very company was allowed, as were other breweries, and this by order in council, to increase beer prices on the market.
Imagine! They authorize an increase for a big company and afterward crush the worker, even forcing him to give back the increase he has received. This is what the present government has done! What corrective measures have been proposed in the Speech from the Throne? None! Again there is some talk about reductions. In a letter addressed to the provincial premiers, the right hon. Prime Minister informed them of his decision to reduce public spending by $2 billion. But where does he intend to make those cuts? First, we are told that a personnel reduction affecting 5,000 jobs, will take place at least progressively. Will that affect big companies or the financial world? No. The workers will have to bear the consequences of the reduction of 5,000 jobs.
As I have said earlier, high finance has been allowed to boost interest rates. If this is how the Prime Minister wants to cut back $2 billion in government expenditures, I could sug-

October 16, 1978
The Address-Mr. G. Caouette gest to him other ways of saving this $2 billion. My colleague, the hon. member for Abitibi (Mr. Laprise), asked a question concerning the decrease in language training, since 477 Francophones will lose their job in the public service here in Ottawa. The minister's reply was that we had to try and please the other provinces. But we also know that the Liberal party is not very strong in the other provinces. So here are some gifts, because we all know that elections are coming. That is the reason for staff reductions in the areas of language, bilingualism and French positions.
The minister also replied: There is no demand for it. Yet we know that there are 2,000 applications for language training. Still, the minister has the indecency to tell us: There is no demand for it, so it is logical to cut back. Yet, at the very same time the decision is made to do away with 477 of those jobs, we find that some officials of the department are in the process of negotiating contracts with the Berlitz school of languages to give those same courses. That is the attitude of the present government: it would have us believe, on the one hand, that it is reducing the staff to cut down on expenses while, on the other hand, planning additional expenses in another field. We have often seen it happen.
We saw it in the budget of the Minister of Finance last March with regard to the sales tax; we were told that the people would be given goodies, that is a cut in sales tax. After ten weeks of debates in the House of Commons, it was finally discovered that the federal government was giving out $100 provided the provinces increased their own taxes by the same amount. That is making politics on the backs of the provinces. That silly little budget that was brought down at that time offered Quebeckers $85 and $100 to the other provinces. Do you know that, overnight, that increased the national deficit by $11 billion? Do you know that, overnight, the interest on the national debt was being increased by $2 million a day?
When the Prime Minister talks about cutting government spending by $2 billion, my suggestion is one Social Crediters have always made: that government be financed through interest free loans from the Bank of Canada based on Canadian and not American production.
At noon, questions were put to the Prime Minister on the increase of three quarters of one per cent announced last Friday by the governor of the Bank of Canada. The Prime Minister, having no memory, as I suggested earlier, and particularly no imagination, still had the audacity to answer that it was not to solve Canada's economic problem that the governor of the Bank of Canada had decided on that course of action. It was in reaction to the U.S. attitude. Who are the bosses in Canada? Is it the government? Is it Canadians or Americans in front of whom the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) stands on all fours as well as the Prime Minister, as he did this morning? It is the rate increase-and it is a reaction-and it is not a solution to the economic problems, that we know. It is a reaction to the American attitude. That is

the attitude of the government now-flat on all fours before the Americans. That will not solve the problem.
Inflation, government members say, is beyond our control. They are not responsible for it. It is due to the Arabs who increased the price of their oil. It is due to other countries from which we import. We have called many times for a reduction of imports. Then we are told that we must have a trade balance. During that time we, stupid Canadian taxpayers, have to support that policy and reduce our production at home to maintain imports to please other countries and destroy our own production.
I am coming back from the riding of Lotbiniere where an election is under way and a number of furniture industries are closed or must reduce their operations. They are operating at 30 per cent of their capacity. During that time we in Canada bought in 1976, $177 million worth of furniture products from the United States, that is the attitude of the government now. In the footwear industry it is the same thing. For three years we have proposed footwear imports. Finally, the government accepted last winter to impose a quota on imports. Recently the Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport) (Mrs. Campagnolo) took delight in sending every member in this House a letter informing us we had an invitation from the Bata Corporation. They started making sports shoes, which used to be made here, except that the industry was completely destroyed by imports. We welcomed at that point such a step, notwithstanding the fact we had been requesting import curbs for three years. In the other areas, beef, ham, butter, the same thing goes. We are getting millions of pounds of imports from other countries, while we are destroying our own production. Such is the government's attitude. It solves nothing. Neither the Prime Minister nor the throne speech bring any solutions for that.
As I said earlier, the budget brought in by the Minister of Finance in March increased debt interests by $2 million a day with an $11 billion deficit increase. This is no joke. When the Prime Minister tells us government spending is to be cut by $2 billion at the expense of public servants, do you not feel it would make more sense to reduce government expenditures at the expense of financiers, who go on rising their prices, their interest rates instead of saving $2 billion? If tomorrow the government decided to do their own financing, if they financed provinces with loans without interest, this would mean that tomorrow the government would be saving $18 million a day we are paying in interests only on the national debt. And our debt is increasing by $20 million a day. This is not a joke. These debts must be paid by the taxpayers. Canadians have to pay $18 million a day for the bad administration of the government. Do you know that instead of saving $2 billion Canada would have saved $6.7 billion by the end of the year? We could let the Prime Minister have his $2 billion and redistribute the other $4.7 billion in the small business sector to give it a new life, to create employment and to create other production levels to replace those that have been destroyed.
October 16, 1978

Earlier, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie) said that this would help the import of foreign capital, the development of new gas deposits, the establishment in Canada of multinational companies to develop our natural resources and perhaps job creation. There may be some value in having foreigners invest in Canada, but as long as we do not have ourselves the means to buy the production of those machines, what have we gained?
We should therefore start by giving some purchasing power to the individuals. The Conservatives laughed ten years ago when the Social Crediters demanded tax reductions. They found this laughable, but today they are the ones who are demanding what we requested then, who are demanding a tax reduction so as to give a new impetus to the economy and increase individual purchasing power. If I have $5 more to spend, these $5 will certainly result in an additional production, and if all Canadians have more money to spend because they have fewer taxes to pay, they will certainly create a demand for new production, and this will necessarily result in new jobs or a demand for new jobs. This is how we can solve our present economic problem, not by continually allowing inflation to multiply.
It is not necessary to be a genius or an Einstein to understand that if I buy a house tomorrow morning at 5 per cent interest a year, it will take 20 years before the price of my house has doubled. You do not have to be a genius to understand this. If I purchase the same house at 10 per cent interest, its price will be doubled in ten years, which means that in 20 years, it will have increased fourfold, and after this you ask where inflation comes from? The Prime Minister says it does not depend on us but on the Arabs, that we are not responsible. We know that the Liberals are irresponsible, we know that. But when we come to pay 12 per cent, it takes ten years, and then eight years to double the price of a house and soon, next week probably, you will see the rate go up to 15 per cent, which means that it will take six and a half to seven years to double the price of a house. And we ask where inflation comes from? And we do not know where it comes from?
At the present time, because of its approach the government multiplies, creates that inflation; through its policy it allows the Bank of Canada to raise its rates, thereby enabling chartered banks to boost theirs on consumer loans and increase the pressure on the Canadian people to reduce their expenditures. At 15 per cent, people begin to be far less inclined to build themselves a house than before. How much is a $30,000 house going to cost them after 25 years? $89,000! We wonder where inflation comes from just like we wonder about energy. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources talks about the problem of energy. We can see little stickers everywhere on the walls saying "Save energy!"
We still encourage the massive consumption of energy in our cars and heating systems. I raised the issue in 1973 when I was the member for Charlevoix in the House of Commons; I asked the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources: Before talking about an energy crisis, a shortage of raw materials or a
The Address-Mr. G. Caouette shortage of oil in the years to come, at least did you go to the patents office in Ottawa to enquire about the registration of any patent that might reduce gas consumption in our cars or oil consumption in our heating systems? The minister gave me the following answer: No, we did not. This was not interesting. They said to Canadians: Tighten your belts, we are going to increase the price of gas in an attempt to reduce our oil purchases, but we cannot protect the individual or protect our resources by reducing energy losses, it is impossible.
In 1956, as I was 16 years old, I was driving an old wreck. A mechanic had fixed my carburetor so that my old wreck was going 65 miles a gallon, Mr. Speaker. I am' not joking, 65 miles a gallon until that mechanic applied for a patent. The RCMP came and said that the system was dangerous because it was using preheated gas. At that time, I did not know exactly what it meant but I finally discovered that in all planes the fuel is preheated before it reaches the engine. It is not dangerous in a plane with 300 passengers but it is dangerous in a car.
Today, with catalytic systems on cars people are no longer allowed to go anywhere near oil companies' lands as the oil tank 150 feet away might explode because of the high temperature of the converter under the car. That shows how this government is prepared to accept anything: It allows companies to encourage excessive gas consumption in cars so that they make money with such dangerous gadgets as catalytic converters. That is the attitude of the government. Then they come to tell Canadians: You are wasting energy. There are little stickers on walls saying: Turn off the lights, do not over-heat yet at the same time the government does nothing, not even to market patents which have been duly registered in the patent office and make their use mandatory. My predecessor in the riding of Temiscamingue and the House of Commons, Mr. Real Caouette, had been asking in those days for competitions to be held throughout the country for technicians and engineers to find ways to reduce consumption so as to save energy.
One must not penalize individuals but allow them to put their brains to work to find means and solutions to improve everybody's lot. The present government does not see it that way and all it intends to do is to penalize Canadians while putting the blame on others. If there are problems, it is never its fault. It is not responsible for inflation. It is not the government which allows the Bank of Canada to decide anything, it is the United States, the real bosses are the United States. The government has been elected for the fun of it. It has no decisions to make. We have just been treated to a Speech from the Throne in two parts: cutbacks in government spendings and, second, the constitution. It is true that there is a problem of unity in Canada. I listened earlier to the member for Don Valley (Mr. Gillies) expressing his views on the Quebec issue. He was referring to books written in 1936 and dealing then with the American issues and also with Latin America. As to the problem of Quebec, and also Canada in answer to the member for Don Valley and to government
126

October 16, 1978
The Address-Mr. G. Caouette members I would say that in my opinion it is neither a language issue nor a constitutional problem. Indeed the constitution creates frictions but tomorrow I do not know of any Canadian who is going to want the constitution to become his daily bread.
I never heard about one single family going every week to the corner store to buy a new constitution, never. The problem is the right to live honestly and honourably here in Canada. In our provinces it is also the right to live honestly and honourably. That is what Canadians want. Unfortunately, in Quebec many Canadians do not even earn enough money to eat two decent meals a day. The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) said so herself before a group of students recently. There are 600,000 poor in Canada now. They do not even have enough money to eat two decent meals a day. We must admit it, there are people in Quebec who are unhappy, that is true. They do not even have enough money to eat two decent meals a day in French, in Quebec. Is it not terrible, in French, Mr. Speaker? I went to western Canada, on the Vancouver docks where I saw poor people; I went to the maritimes where I saw poor people there also. In Ontario, I went to regions where I also saw poor people who do not have the means to eat two decent meals, not three, we are used to talking about three meals, but here it is not even three, but only two decent meals a day. In other provinces, it is funny, people speak English, it is not terrible? And there are poor people among the English, it is terrible, it is horrible. Is it a language problem? Is it a constitutional problem? It is like I told you: be it in English or in French, nobody wants to eat constitutions, never! Poor people want enough money to go and buy food, for example. That is the problem. It is an economic problem that could be solved by giving to everybody a sufficient income to meet personal needs.

I thank you, Mr. Speaker, as well as all my colleagues. I have only a few more words to say.
Indeed there is a solution to that issue and we should not continue a confrontation between Canadians and we should not say what the Prime Minister said the other day in his speech about the Leader of the Opposition capitulating before the provinces. What we need is a strong government. But we cannot build a strong government without opposing each other. That is not the way. You do not build by confronting people and telling them to toe the line.
A good father does not spend all his time arguing with his children and saying to them: I am the boss and you will do as I say. However, if you have a conciliating father who is prepared to listen to any one of his ten or twelve children or to consider

their needs, I am sure that father will raise a friendly and peaceful family. Anyone who spends all his time confronting his children or his colleagues will surely have the results we have in Canada: discontent in the west, dissatisfaction in central Canada as well as in Atlantic provinces. In his speech, the Prime Minister failed to indicate the solution, and in introducing again Bill C-60, he wants to maintain confrontation.
To conclude my speech, Mr. Speaker, in spite of what government members have to say, the Speech from the Throne does not contain any new or valuable suggestions. The Speech from the Throne will only complicate the complex issues we have to face now, it continues undermining the confidence people may have had in their government. As federal civil servants will have to pay for reduced expenses, that will destroy the confidence civil servants had in government.
Mr. Speaker, let the government start once and for all to recognize the rights of people, their right to earn a normal and valuable living and then, if individuals are to be replaced by machines in industry and find themselves jobless, let the government be intelligent enough then to find ways and means to give those individuals a purchasing power which will allow them to buy this machine-made production. It is precisely what the Social Credit party suggests as a solution to these problems to ensure a guaranteed annual income for everyone so that people will have enough purchasing power.
To conclude, the only suggestion I can make now to the minister and to the government is to stop clouding the issue with a smokescreen, to stop telling us stories and giving us all that hot air. They should start to roll up their sleeves to tackle the economic problems. It is a matter of urgency as more and more people are really fed up to be taken in, really fed up to lose their job and to have to live not even on unemployment but on social welfare.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for York South (Mrs. Appolloni) and the hon. member for Verdun (Mr. Savard) certainly distinguished themselves by the manner in which they moved and seconded the Address in reply to the Speech from the Throne.
The hon. member for York South expressed her love for Canada, her adopted country, and she did so in a most moving way. It was a tonic to hear our country praised for a change- so frequently it seems that Canada is described only in the most negative terms, quite contrary to the evidence around us. Of course there are some problems, and I shall spend most of my allotted time talking about a few of them, but there are many good things to which we can point with pride. I took much delight in the fact that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) devoted part of his speech to doing just that, and doing so most effectively.
I was pleased the hon. member for Verdun used a portion of his speech to talk about the senior citizens. After all, the prosperity and success of modern Canada are in large measure
October 16, 1978

due to their contributions at a time when, as a rule, rewards for achievement were much less than they are today.
The government's New Horizons program has given all hon. members the opportunity to become more closely involved with senior citizens groups, and those of us who have done so are greatly impressed by the way in which these grants are being used, and by the appreciation shown for them. If the government really wants an example of how to carry out a restraint program, it should observe with some care how these senior citizens' organizations take those grants under the New Horizons program and do so very much with them.
When the hon. member for Verdun was speaking, I recalled a visit of mine to his community at the time when he was contesting his by-election. A youth group from Verdun had invited me to participate with it in a seminar on development in northern Canada. The request came at the time when Mr. Justice Berger's report had just been released. I mention this incident only in passing because it illustrated for me that as long as there are Canadians in one part of the country, like Verdun, who take an active interest in and show concern about Canadians in another part of the country, like those living in the Mackenzie Valley, then somehow I feel that we do not need to become unduly disquieted about the depth and strength of this nation's unity.
During the month of August while parliament was in recess, the government announced its determination to reduce its expenditures. At one point, the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Andras) expressed the view that perhaps today in Canada people have become too dependent on government and that they look to government for nearly everything. "What is the government going to do about this? What is the government going to do about that"? I am sure all hon. members have heard that question time after time when they have been in their constituencies. Of course there will always be considerable scope and need for collective action. This is the way in which a civilized nation is nurtured and built. The cost of creating a humane and decent society is considerable. In fact it is immense. At the same time, and in the process, it is also possible for well-meaning governments to assume too much unto themselves and thereby stifle or discourage the initiative of individual persons or of the private sector. Too much involvement of government in people's lives may and, in fact, does, as most of us can testify, cause resentment and bring about a reaction against government generally.
Throughout the 1960s and into the 1970s it is true that governments at all levels increased their shares of the gross national product. It should be noted, however-and the President of the Treasury Board has done this-that increases in government expenditures have come most significantly at the provincial and municipal levels. The figures are there, provided by the President of the Treasury Board, showing that the increase in total government expenditures by the federal government has been much, much less.
The Address-Mr. Penner
Any restraint program, however, must begin with a determination to eliminate waste, extravagance, and inefficiency in government. A restraint policy should not set out to destroy programs, facilities or agencies which are required and essential for the common good, that is, unless or until some private concern is prepared to take over the service and do it as well or perhaps more efficiently at less cost. A case in point is the announcement by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) to axe Canfarm, an important and essential electronic management tool for many farmers. Canfarm has been described as one of the most progressive programs that the government provides in agriculture. It has become indispensable to the most efficient of Canada's farmers.
If the Minister of Agriculture fails to find a private company or organization to take over the Canfarm service, then I think some consideration should be given to doing a number of other things. Consideration should be given to increasing user-fees, which now are really only nominal, amounting to $30 per year per farmer. Perhaps there could be some cutting back on the developmental work which comprises such a large portion of the total program expenses, and possibly the operation at Guelph could be made more efficient. Let the financial burden on the federal government be reduced, yes, but I say to the Minister of Agriculture, do not let Canfarm die.
The decision to close the Petawawa forest experimental station falls into the same category, another possible casualty of government restraint. My colleague, the hon. member for Renfrew North-Nipissing East (Mr. Hopkins), will, I am sure, have much more to say about this particular matter in his speech, and I commend him for his dedicated endeavour to reverse what seems to be a questionable decision.
The forest products industry is the major employer in the constituency which I presently represent. I am advised that this industry directly employs 300,000 people in Canada, and indirectly there are another 700,000 who owe their jobs to forests. Forest products contribute significantly to our merchandise trade surplus-to the extent of $4 billion a year-and the federal government derives revenue from this industry to the extent of $1 billion annually. In the light of these statistics it is easy to understand why people in the industry resent the proposal to close a forest experimental station or a forest lab. In a letter, one of my constituents expressed it this way:
If I had to change my personal budget because of monetary restraints, I would look at unnecessary expenses and tighten regular expenses, but, I would not stop wearing shoes so I couldn't get to work, to save a few dollars.
Forest research in numerous areas is urgently required in order for our Canadian industry to survive. It must survive against competition which is rapidly developing in other countries which have much better climatic conditions than we have, and where trees grow much faster.
The announced government restiaint program is surely a welcome invitation to parliamentary committees to become sharper and more effective in their examination of spending estimates. Those of us who serve on these committees are supposed to be the watchdogs of the public purse. I think that is the way it goes, in political science anyway. Well, if we are
8006S-9'/2

October 16, 1978
The Address-Mr. Penner
the watchdogs, seldom has our bark frightened anyone, and rarely has anyone been bitten for squandering public funds. It seems to me that a time of restraint is a good opportunity for parliamentary committees to prove themselves.
An exercise in restraint is also an opportunity for the government to redirect its efforts toward more desirable social and economic goals. In a time of high unemployment one of those goals must be job creation. In a time of high inflation one of those goals must be to redirect income to where it is most needed, to the elderly and to low-income families. These are measures which we will be debating during this session of parliament.
Above all, restraint will only hurt-and not help-unless the end result is a stimulus to economic growth. Since the early 1970s Canada has been suffering from a very serious lack of economic growth. Advocates of a no-growth or slow-growth economy have been notably silent these past few years. They have been silent because the results of that kind of an economy are not acceptable. The results are a rising rate of unemployment, especially among young people who are the newest entrants into our work force, and very large deficits in our international payments. Canada's current account balance has, with the exception of 1973, deteriorated every year since 1970. The major reason for this deterioration in our current balance is the rising deficit in the service account which escalated from $1.4 billion in 1966 to an estimated $8 billion in 1977. The service account deficit is the consequence of very heavy borrowing during the mid-1970s and an increasing shortfall in our tourist account. The devalued dollar has increased the cost of servicing our foreign debt, but unfortunately it has not generated as much additional tourism in Canada as it was expected to do. I say unfortunately, because the region in northern Ontario which I represent is one of the prime tourist regions of the country.
Looking at our merchandise trade account, the picture is much, much brighter, at least upon first glance. This year, our trade surplus in goods is expected to be $4 billion, which is up from $2.9 billion in 1977. But I would remind hon. members that it is our trade in primary resources and semi-fabricated goods which has made this trade surplus possible. Our trade in finished, manufactured goods or end-products continues to decline. It was minus $3 billion in 1970, and last year it was minus $12 billion. Canadians are buying foreign made goods at the rate of $42 billion a year, which is approximately $2,000 per person, or $8,000 per household in Canada. It is the sale of our wheat, forest products and minerals in large measure which makes it possible for Canadians to buy so many imports, much of which are in the luxury class.
As a member who represents one of the major resource regions of the country, of course I am delighted that our minerals and forest products are helping so much to provide Canadians with a high standard of living. I am pleased that we are able to contribute so significantly to Canada's trade sur-

plus. But there are dangers for us if we continue to rely too extensively on our natural resources to keep us afloat.
The manufacturing trade deficit reveals that there is a serious lack in the processing of our natural resources. Natural resource exports have been a redeeming feature in our merchandise trade account, but selling unprocessed materials abroad also means the exportation of jobs, jobs which we badly need in Canada at the present time. For example, it has been estimated that when we export $1 billion worth of natural resources, we generate 60,000 jobs in Canada. In turn, when we buy $1 billion worth of manufactured goods from abroad, 240,000 jobs are involved. This is the situation in Canada which is leading to more and more discussion by people in the univerisities, by economists and by other groups of concerned citizens, more and more discussion about the need for policies to encourage further processing and manufacturing.
Those of us who live in resource regions favour more on site processing. We would like to see more jobs created in the regions from which the natural resources come. We believe that this is the key to genuine, long term and lasting regional development. Coming from a region which depends heavily upon the forest products industry, I appreciate the positive results which flow from the increased processing of raw materials. For example, increased processing of pulp has meant a steady improvement in Canada's account for fine papers. Imports of fine papers are expected to decline substantially this year, and exports will grow appreciably. Canada's improved performance in the fine papers industry has occurred because of increased rationalization and specialization. Paper mills have concerntrated on fewer grades, weights and colours. Rationalization and specialization seem to point the way toward a more productive and competitive manufacturing sector in Canada. Those who know say that this sector is now plagued by duplication, excess capacity, and short production runs.
A recent visitor to my office put it this way in describing what should be done to improve the industrial situation in Canada. He said:
We are putting our money on too many horses. We should pick the winners.
I would argue that the winners must include those industries most closely connected with the development and processing of our natural resources. Those industries, as well as others, would add value to the raw materials we produce and the energy we consume.
In the report by the Sector Task Force on the Canadian Nonferrous Metals Industry, recently released there were some rather startling figures concerning the value added content in Canada's export of metals. The report indicated that approximately one half of the copper, lead and zinc mined is exported in its concentrate form; only one half is smelted and refined into primary metal. Some two-thirds of the primary aluminum, copper and zinc are exported; only one-third is used in Canada's secondary manufacturing, and over 90 per cent of the nickel produced in Canada is exported.
October 16, 1978

While I have argued this afternoon for policies which would encourage, as a part of our industrial strategy, rationalization, specialization, and incentives for increased processing, I would not favour any policy which would act as a disincentive to mineral exploration and development. Much to the contrary, to discourage resource development would not aid manufacturing. Failure to encourage capital formation for resource development means that capital will go elsewhere in the world, and our Canadian resource regions will remain underpopulated and economically depressed.
Since the three main industries of northern Ontario are forest products, mining and tourism, I was extremely pleased by the announcement of the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner) indicating that there would be increases in economic development programs amounting to $300 million in 1979-80. Approximately $65 million of that total increase will be to provide support for tourism and resource industries. Of equal interest for me was the announcement by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie) which outlined government support of $400 million for renewable energy technology and industries founded on the commercial use of such technology. He stated that over the next five years the government plans to devote a large chunk of this total to the utilization of foreign wastes which are now by-products of the lumber, pulp and paper industries.
With regard to the mining industry, there have been two fairly recent reports pointing to the less than buoyant conditions for the industry in Canada. One report is entitled "The Decline of Small Mineral Enterprises in Ontario". It maintains that higher exploration costs, falling returns, and increased risks have had a negative impact on the small mineral enterprises in the province of Ontario. That report was published by that provinces's ministry of natural resources.
The second report is one of our own. It is the Sector Task Force on the Canadian Nonferrous Metals Industry to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, a report to which I referred earlier. The task force was one of the 23 commissioned after the first ministers' conference last winter to examine various sectors of the economy. The report maintains:
Unless measures are taken by all concerned to revive mining exploration in this country, there will be a spectacular decline in the production in this sector over the balance of the century.
There are some recommendations, one of which has to do with capital formation. It states:
With capital formation the issue of overriding importance, an early resolution of the dispute between the federal and provincial governments over mining taxation would produce more rational tax structures and create an environment more conducive to capital formation.
Secondly, the report recommended:
In order to encourage increased resource processing and trade the report recommends further incentives for research and development.
I was going to comment about Canada's position at the present time with respect to research and development as
The Address-Mr. Penner
compared with that of other countries. However, hon. members are so familiar with these figures that it would be redundant on my part.
I will leave that and move on to the third recommendation in the report, which is as follows:
A problem of increasing importance in the mining industry is labour retention, particularly at Canadian mining operations remote from urban centres. There is often an excessively high turnover rate for the work force in these locations. In order to encourage the movement of people from urban areas in the south to isolated areas in the north, the government should give serious attention to a form of income tax relief for employees in remote areas in Canada who remain on the job for more than two years.
I have made this suggestion in the House before. The response has been that the government, at the federal level, cannot deal with regions, but must deal totally on a national basis. We know that in recent budgets the government has moved more and more toward a recognition that there needs to be special policies for particular regions in order to meet the needs and solve the problems which exist there. I do not think the old argument will stand any longer.
Those who live and work in remote communities located in resource regions are, in general, under-serviced. In some places this is far more serious than in others. Many must travel considerable distances for medical and dental care. Postsecondary education requires moving away from home, and there are additional costs for parents. In view of this additional travel I must not fail to point out to the House that these people pay anywhere from 15 to 20 cents more per gallon of gasoline than do people in urban areas. Yet, the products of our resource regions, as I have demonstrated this afternoon, contribute a disproportionately large amount to the national economy. Our tax system, it seems to me, should provide some tangible rewards for those who work and live in these regions.
If time allows, and I believe it does, I should like to point out that some people in the mining industry have expressed concern about the activities of the Export Development Corporation. Those concerns are based on serious misconceptions as to the purpose and function of the EDC. The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce has pointed out that the corporation's role is to facilitate the sale of Canadian goods and services to foreign buyers. EDC loans are tied directly to the sales of Canadian equipment and services, so they create jobs for Canadians.
Neither the Government of Canada nor the EDC has the power to prevent a sovereign nation from developing its own natural resources. If we do not arrange financing for the sale of our equipment and services, then some other nation most certainly will, some other nation such as Japan, Germany, France, Great Britain or the United States. As the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce has said:
If Canadian exporters are to be prevented from selling to such buyers, we will lose not only their jobs, but tomorrow's competition-and we shall be worse off for it.
To conclude, we are being told today that Canada must learn to live within its means. We must import fewer luxuries, we must buy more Canadian products, we must divert more production facilities to exports, and we must spend on consum-

October 16, 1978
The Address-Mr. Darling
er goods only what has been earned. In the short term, the lower Canadian dollar can help, but in the long haul it will not solve our problems of unemployment, of inflation or of sluggish economic growth. Nor can we expect that our natural resources will help to balance our accounts forever and ever. This simply will not be, and it is time to turn our face to the future.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a privilege to participate in the debate in respect of the Speech from the Throne, such as it was. Before commencing my remarks I should like to congratulate and commend the mover of the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne, the hon. memer for York South (Mrs. Appolloni), and the seconder, the hon. member for Verdun (Mr. Savard).
At the outset I would certainly like to echo the question a vast majority of Canadians are now asking, and that is, which way are we heading? This question has come to haunt an increasing number of Canadians with the entrenchment in power of the Liberal government over the last decade.
Canada is at a unique juncture in its history. We are facing many challenges, with over a million Canadians out of work, a distressingly high inflation rate which threatens to become a double-digit phenomenon, a miserably slow growth rate, impending constitutional changes, and a national unity crisis. One views the state of the nation with grave concern. I must register these concerns even at the risk of being termed an alarmist by government members who prefer not to be reminded of their record over the last ten years of Prime Minister Trudeau's government.
We require renewed faith in the ability of Canadians to surmount any obstacles on the road to making this country an example to the rest of the world. We need dynamism and farsighted leadership to inspire Canadians to place their faith in our country. Lack of effective leadership has led to haphazard and shortsighted policies being pursued by the government. The result of such policies is evident in the economic malaise that afflicts us today, political uncertainty, and an increase in social stress as reflected in the persistent state of labour unrest.
Last week the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) made a flamboyant speech in the House. It was a lot of sound and fury, and I think, as Shakespeare said in one of his plays, it signified nothing. The highly entertaining performance relished by his own party members left many Canadians questioning the seriousness with which the current leadership is viewing the problems facing us.

No one needs to be reminded of the guessing game the Prime Minister engaged in earlier this year about calling an election when he was faced with adverse reports from internal sources which indicated the unpopularity of the Liberal party.
