Would the next speaker from the government side of the House be willing to make a guess and put his seat on the line for the number of seats he will stipulate that his party will win in the by-elections today?
Anyone who examines the record of this country over the past decade would wonder just what is happening and what direction the economy is taking. The most obvious and highly embarrassing situation that confronts us today is the value of our dollar on the world market. This is a vote of non-confidence cast by the international financial community on the policies of the present government. The disastrous economic policies of this government continue to plunge the value of our dollar further downward. The government continues to find scapegoats to blame for the decline, but it would be well advised to examine carefully its own record and policies rather than to blame the Canadian public.
The Canadian dollar has hit an historic low. Surely the Prime Minister will agree that this is not a reflection, as he states, of a "healthy country in a difficult world". The decline of the dollar has led the government to engage in foreign borrowing to prop up its value. It pays out heavily in interest charges which further prevent us from attaining a balance of payments equilibrium.

::

:

October 16, 1978

One obvious advantage of the devaluation of a country's currency is that its goods and services become attractive to foreign markets. This was brought home to me in my own particular riding, in the village of Burks Falls where I live. There is a woodworking industry that is working at full capacity there because a large amount of their production is exported to the United States. But that is the exception to the rule, and there is no question that that firm is doing very well. While in attendance at a social event in the town of Powassan on Saturday night I spoke to a lumberman who also informed me that his firm is doing exceptionally well at this time. As he said, "They are just waiting to grab the lumber as it comes off the tail saw and send it direct to the United States." So, there are some advantages, but in the long run it is not in the best interests of Canada as a whole. Unfortunately, as I mentioned, the value of our dollar has defied traditional economic wisdom in so far as not providing a boost for many more exports than the examples that I gave.
I could go on endlessly listing the failures of this government. For instance, inflation has more than doubled from 4.5 per cent in April, 1968, to almost a double-digit figure. Similarly, housing costs have doubled in the last ten years and the unemployment rate has risen drastically from 4.5 per cent in 1968 to 8.6 per cent in 1978. I am aware that the present minister of employment is greatly concerned about this and is endeavouring to do something to alleviate the situation, and we are hoping that something can be done to turn things around. I am very pessimistic as to what is going to happen during the coming winter.
I mentioned that housing starts are down. The government, in its wisdom, has cut expenditures on a great many departments, something which will make many Canadians very unhappy. I am thinking in particular of those in the low income bracket, who are living in houses which are not in good condition and who had hoped to benefit from the government's current insulation program. The provinces of Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island receive $500 per house under this plan and the people in the other provinces receive $350 for insulation. With the $110 million cut, there will certainly be a great many applications submitted that will have to be turned down. I am still receiving applications from some of my constituents and, of course, I will have to write them in the course of the next day or so telling them to get their applications in in a hurry because the chances are not as good as expected.
Another concern to me is the great exodus of Canadian capital for housing investment in other countries. It is estimated that over $1.4 billion has left Canada for the United States. Much of that money is being invested in apartments and buildings there because Canadian businessmen and developers feel they will get a much better return for their dollar. This is most unfortunate for our country where housing construction is needed, as well as other building construction.
What surprised and further depressed many Canadians was the Speech from the Throne and in particular, the Prime Minister's theatrical performance that failed to provide any
The Address-Mr. Darling
concrete solutions or suggestions to deal with some of these problems. None of the other members of the cabinet have come forth with any policies either. One would have thought that this would be an ideal time for the government to indicate in some small measure what remedies it may be contemplating for our ailing economic situation. Instead, the cabinet and the Prime Minister have engaged in a frantic effort to convince Canadians that all is well, but the Canadian public knows otherwise for they face inflation in the supermarkets every day.
The Speech from the Throne is full of promises. It is littered with the same repetitive and unkept promises that one found in the previous nine Speeches from the Throne. However, it contains no plan of action. On the other hand, I highly commend the leader of my party for delivering a very eloquent address outlining in concrete terms what my party intends to do when elected to govern the country at the next election.
We on this side, for instance, have advocated a proposal to provide tax deductibility of mortgage interest and property taxes on personal residences. I, for one, have long advocated such a move in order to ease the tax burden placed on the individual homeowners.
As reeve of a small community for over a quarter of a century, and as a vice president and member of the executive of the Association of the Ontario Mayors and Reeves, I know that time and time again they have brought in a resolution to the effect that a tax on tax was unfair. The United States have done it for a number of years and, certainly if it is successful there, it can be just as successful here. I would not be surprised that the government, through its lack of policies, ends up by stealing that policy from us. If they do, more power to them.
The Progressive Conservatives have also proposed tax credits for research and development and cutting waste and inefficiency in government. These are, Mr. Speaker, but a few of some very specific proposals put forth by the leader of my party. These policies will be implemented in the very near future when the Canadian public is offered an opportunity to go to the polls to chase out the ineffective Liberal government and replace it with a responsible Progressive Conservative government.
For one who hails from picturesque Parry Sound-Muskoka, it is gratifying to note that one of the promises contained in the throne speech is to provide additional assistance for tourism. I sincerely hope that the promise does not become one of a string of earlier unkept promises. For instance, the government has been promising more aid to small businesses for the last five years. However, by the Prime Minister's own admission, small business is still being strangled in this country; evidence of this is reflected in the 49 per cent increase in business bankruptcies in August over the same month last year.
The hon. member for High Park-Humber Valley (Mr. Jelinek), this party's critic on small business, outlined at some length our position on small business and its importance to the

October 16, 1978
The Address-Mr. Darling
economy. Small business employs over 55 per cent of people in the country and generates over 60 per cent of the gross national product, so it is a most important part of the economy. I wonder how the many small businessmen view the recent increase in the prime rate of the Bank of Canada to 10% per cent today, a jump three quarters of one per cent. That just makes it more difficult to borrow money or, if you can borrow it, it is more difficult to pay it back.
This morning I had a telephone call from the operator of a sawmill in my riding who needs additional financing and is finding it difficult to get. I suggested that he contact the nearest branch of the Federal Business Development Bank where I hope he will be able to make satisfactory arrangements. Its interest rates are not the best, but many Canadians are delighted to be able to deal with it as a lender of last resort.
Tourism is Canada's largest single employer and the sixth largest source of foreign exchange. Furthermore, the combined value of visitor expenditures and domestic travel spending amounts to a $11 billion industry which accounts for 5 per cent of gross national product and yields governments some $5 billion in tax revenues. Yet for too long tourism has been denied the necessary recognition as an important economic and social element in our society.
I have said before, but I will place it on the record again, that I think any department or business that generates $11 billion worth of revenue should be given prominence and, therefore, I feel there should be a minister of state for tourism. Even in this time of cutting back expenditures that would not mean that one additional person need be hired. There are plenty of people in the branch of the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce responsible for tourism who could do an excellent job. Tourism is vital to the economy of Canada and, I must say in all fairness, to the great riding of Parry Sound-Muskoka where it is the main industry.
It is ironic that it was in Bonn earlier this year that the Prime Minister first became fully aware of the seriousness of our domestic problems. The Prime Minister took some heed of the concern expressed by leaders of other industrialized nations about the state of the Canadian economy.
The Prime Minister suddenly became aware of the high rates of unemployment and inflation, and of the astoundingly high federal spending spree. Federal spending has increased by 400 per cent since the present government came to power ten years ago. Upon his return from the Bonn economic summit the Prime Minister hastily arranged to make a nationally televised address to enunciate a new economic policy. The announcement contained the usual promises to do something about everything. It is understood that a majority of the cabinet members were not even consulted before the address. The Prime Minister is not only isolated from the aspirations of Canadians but from his own close cabinet colleagues. Later, in a string of dramatic pronouncements which invoked images of a theatrical performance, about half a dozen cabinet members appeared on stage during the month of August to seek economic credibility. Now that the dust has settled from the

summer activity, Canadians find themselves faced with no brighter economic prospects than before all the August announcements. Once again the government failed to offer any long-term solution or suggestions and most of the cuts announced are to take effect in the 1979-80 fiscal year.
The Prime Minister came to power a decade ago promising a united Canada. Canadians justifiably ask themselves today whether we are any more united or further torn apart.
The Prime Minister wonders why Canadians are questioning his intentions vis-a-vis the monarchy in the package on constitutional reform. When one observes the Prime Minister vacationing in North Africa on a purely private holiday and not at hand to welcome the Queen as the head of state, one questions his real intentions about the kind of role, if any, he would like to assign to Her Majesty the Queen.
The process of constitutional change is a very fundamental one for any nation, with far-reaching effects. It came as a surprise, therefore, when the Prime Minister, in introducing the constitutional proposals, placed a deadline on the passage of these proposals. I commend the joint Senate-House committee which did not agree to head the Prime Minister's authoritarian whims.
A joint effort by the federal-provincial governments is essential to tackle the constitutional issue. Unfortunately, statements by a number of federal cabinet members to the effect that the federal government could act unilaterally in implementing some of the proposals, seriously jeopardize the healthy working relationship that must prevail between the two levels of government. As a result of the statements by the cabinet members, the ten provincial premiers meeting in Regina unanimously denounced the Prime Minister's approach in dealing with the ten provinces in constitutional matters. I believe that the provinces must be included as equal partners in any discussion affecting the future of Canada. The Prime Minister will be well advised not to rush through some haphazardly constructed policies that may come to haunt the nation in the not too distant future. A constitution is meant to unite and inspire a nation. Let us hope to achieve the same in our constitution.
I convey my sincere congratulations to the leader of my party who is engaged in maintaining a sustained dialogue with the provinces. Unfortunately, the Prime Minister finds himself in confrontation with the provinces most of the time. After all the reason may lie in the fact that the Liberals are in power in only one province, and by a mere one seat.
These remarks will not be complete without some reference to the deplorable state of the Post Office. Canadians are once again faced with a nation-wide postal strike. The Post Office, which now ranks as the twelfth largest user of government funds, has, over the years, grown into a monstrous bureaucracy plagued by labour-management problems resulting in crippling strikes at too frequent intervals. The strikes create not only inconvenience but massive economic hardship for small businesses so heavily dependent on the services of the Post Office.
October 16, 1978

The Progressive Conservative party has for long advocated the transformation of the Post Office into a Crown corporation before the Prime Minister consented to the idea in August. It is my sincere hope that the structural change will result in a more efficient operation of a very vital service. One hopes that a settlement will be reached by both parties to the current dispute and thereby avert another strike.
I am well aware that serious talks are going on at the moment between Post Office management and union officials. Let us hope, in the interests of the Canadian public at large, that both sides will give serious consideration to continuing the service, thereby making it unnecessary for this parliament to bring in legislation to keep the CUPW workers at work. If they do go back to work and things are not satisfactory, to put it mildly we will not be getting 100 cents on the dollar from the employees who are back at work because we know that they will not be working as enthusiastically as they would under normal circumstances.
I had the privilege of attending a postal users conference in Toronto during the latter part of September. It was very interesting, as a member of parliament, to hear the many speakers. The figures quoted were really astounding. Those people in attendance numbered some 500 and were the wholesale users of the Post Office. Their business lives depend on an efficient postal service.
I believe a representative of the Bank of Montreal commented on the amount of money paid by them for postal services. The spokesman stated that about two years ago the bank spent $9 million on postage. I believe this year, because of increased rates the amount is up to $12 million, but he mentioned the terrible postal service in operation between Montreal and Toronto. It is so bad the bank has given up on the Post Office. Instead there is now a special courrier who leaves the bank in Montreal with 300 pounds of mail at 3.30 in the afternoon. This mail arrives in Toronto by 9 a.m. the following morning. The bank's representative was asked why the bank did that. He answered that mail between Montreal and Toronto was taking as long as five, six or seven days to reach its destination.
Here we have a very important department of the government which is losing close to $600 million this year. If this department were run efficiently and without confrontation between management and labour, it might be able to recapture a lot of that lost revenue.
Another speaker at this conference was the vice-president of Maclean's who patted the Post Office on the back with one hand and then by saying they gave reasonably good service, he gave them a kick with the other. I believe Maclean's spent $6 million a year on postage. He went on to say that Maclean's spends another $1 million a year for courrier service in order to get their magazines and periodicals to certain key locations to be distributed by the Post Office. One can see that Post Office management could get even more business from that particular user.
The Address-Mr. Anderson
There is no other department of government that is more important to the people of Canada. Certainly National Health and Welfare is a high priority department. However, I believe there are more people concerned with the Post Office and with its efficiency.
I can see that my time is running out. I wish to thank you for your courtesy in allowing me to conclude my remarks.

speechtext:
In this country we do have certain basic freedoms.
People I met this summer on Vancouver Island were quick to point out that they were not against the basic right of people to go on strike, but with the right is a responsibility. People in my area on Vancouver Island were saying that if the Post Office and CUPW were responsible, then obviously they should have the right to strike, and obviously this is a right which should not be taken away from them.
People in Canada over the last several years have come to look at CUPW as an example of all bad that happens in unions because of a series of actions.
During times of relatively high unemployment and during times of concern about the direction our economy is headed, people tend to look at organizations, such as those in Sudbury which recently went on strike, as not being realistic. They tend to look at the labour movement as the culprits in our society. I do not believe they are. I believe the people of Canada would best be served if CUPW were a moderate group of people who could negotiate in a meaningful manner.
I do not think it is meaningful for CUPW to say, for example, that they wish to go from a 40 to a 30-hour week in one fell swoop, and then add approximately 18 hours of travelling time, tea breaks, and a few other breaks as well which would mean that the Government of Canada would have to hire an additional 46,000 workers. If CUPW want to have the support of members of parliament and the people of Canada generally, they will have to be responsible in their demands. I am not opposed to CUPW per se. However, I am opposed to irresponsibility, whether it be on the part of CUPW
134

October 16, 1978
The Address-Mr. Anderson
or the official opposition. Irresponsibility on either count is something with which we all disagree.
Many members have been told at the present time that if the public service unions are not responsible, the people of Canada would like the Government of Canada to take away their right to strike. I am not advocating that. I am saying that if you talk to people across this country, you will hear that said. I think it is wrong. We should not have first and second class citizens in this country, with one group of people having the right to strike but not another.
I fear that CUPW gives a black eye to the labour movement, whether it be private or public, and that it is fermenting disrespect for the labour movement. I do not think the labour movement can afford it at this time. I hope my fear is unfounded. However, from speaking with people in my area, as well as with those in other provinces, I find that subject is raised again and again. They feel that disruptions in our carrier service, police service or postal service, should not be allowed to take place and that legislation should be brought in regarding essential services.
I am not sure that is the answer. I believe it would be more profitable to attempt, through meaningful negotiation with responsible groups, to find solutions that do not cause inconvenience to the public. I hope that union leaders in organizations such as CUPW which have a higher profile recognize the danger they may get into, not only with regard to the right to strike but in another important area. If poor service is provided, less and less people will use it and less and less people will be required. I suppose CUPW could be put into the position of cutting its own throat due to poor service and interruptions in the mail service with private institutions taking their place. I did not want to get into that except to carry on with what was said by the hon. member who preceded me.
I would like to discuss briefly what has happened since August 1 of this year on the return from Bonn of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), who pledged at that time a major re-ordering of government priorities. If I am not mistaken, on August 10 in his national address, the Prime Minister came across saying that new, bold, innovative measures would have to be taken. I could not agree more. I very much support the statement by the Prime Minister that this is the time for bold, new measures to be brought forward.
Mir. Dinsdale: Things are in a mess.

speechtext:
When the group across from me came into the House the other day and politely applauded their leader, I thought they had perhaps adopted a new form of manners which would carry on throughout this session. However, I see they are still unwilling to listen to anyone from the other side of the House. I would ask them to hold their remarks until I

make my few remarks. We would then be pleased to hear them.
In the context of what the Prime Minister said in his address, on August 10 1 wrote to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien). I observed that over the years I have been in parliament, and even before I came here, when ministers of finance came before parliament with measures to last for six months, a year or sometimes two years, it was not in keeping with what we in Canada are facing today.
I think it is a fair criticism of governments past and future, and present I suppose, that they have always taken a short range approach. At the same time, it was not more than a year or two ago that the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) announced to the House a five-year program in which the government would encourage the construction of one million housing units in that period. In other words, he told the construction industry that the Government of Canada was bringing forth a plan which would allow them to dovetail their plans with the five-year plan. That gave the construction industry a certain amount of security with regard to the purchase of equipment and expansion of facilities. They knew there was a five-year direction in which they could go on unimpeded, knowing that we would not change our minds six months or a year later.
That was a very positive statement by the Minister of State for Urban Affairs. For the past two years he has been on target. In fact, he has been above target, which indicates it has been an attainable plan. Also, with various programs, the construction industry, governments, provincial and municipal, are delivering that project. At the end of the five-year period, we will in fact have had one million housing starts.
Something similar took place not too long ago. The Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Buchanan) announced a long-term program for research and development whereby tax credits would be allowed up to 150 per cent. It is to be a 15-year program.
Important as urban affairs, research and development and new housing construction may be, is it any less important for the consumers of Canada, the investors, banks, manufacturers and other segments of our society, to have a plan similar to those brought forward by the two ministers I mentioned? In this way investor confidence and consumer confidence could be established. The government could announce that in a five year period it would come to such and such a point and this is the blueprint to be followed.
I have not been converted overnight to the five-year plans of our socialist friends, the U.S.S.R. and so on. However, I believe this is a day and age when governments can put blueprints before the country, to be discussed as to whether it is the proper direction to be going, and whether the government method of getting there is the correct one. In looking over past parliaments, I have yet to find it the case that a minister of finance or government brought forth that sort of comprehensive plan. It may not be that important to follow exactly a five-year plan. However, everyone would at least know in what direction we are going.
October 16, 1978

One objective that might be considered is for the Government of Canada to strive for a balanced budget at the end of a five-year period. It may be that we cannot achieve such an objective within a one, two or three-year period. However, is it not feasible to say to the people of Canada, our investors and manufacturers, that this is the direction that we want to go and these are the steps we will use to implement our plan? It seems reasonable to have an objective for more than a six-month or one-year period. There would be more confidence in this country if everyone were aware of the objectives we had for our economy. Moreover, business as well as consumer interests could make their plans in keeping with the objectives of the federal government so as to achieve what we all wish to achieve.
It is also obvious to me that in order to accomplish a plan of this sort we require the cooperation not only of provincial governments but also of municipal governments. The opposition does not often mention this, but the provinces and the municipalities spend more of the tax dollar in Canada than does the federal government. I think it is time we recognized that the municipalities do have a role to play in economic planning. After all, they are one of the three partners which, as far as governments are concerned, spend the money. It would be ridiculous to have a five-year program to reduce federal and provincial spending by 5 per cent, for example, if the municipalities were not brought in and did not agree to follow the plan.
I hope the present government or some future government, when discussing the national economy, will arrange for a tripartite meeting which would include not only the provincial governments, God bless them, but also their captives as they are sometimes called, the cities and the municipalities, which in some cases are very important in economic terms. Vancouver, Montreal and Toronto, for instance, spend almost as much as do some of our provinces or territories, yet they are not allowed to take part directly in this sort of enterprise. It would not be a particularly revolutionary idea to arrange for these people to be consulted as to the steps which ought to be taken to improve the national economy.
If we are to aim for a balance between revenue and expenditure over a period of years it will be necessary to identify those projects which are essential to the Government of Canada and determine which can be reduced without causing dislocation unacceptable to the people. It is all very well to talk about balancing budgets and exercising restraint, but every time action is taken by the government in this area our good friends opposite criticize the spending cuts as ill chosen. I think it would be in the best interests of us all to review a number of areas of expenditure with a view to determining whether they could be financed in greater measure by user groups rather than by the federal government. I would give hon. members an example. As one who comes from the boondocks, a small populated centre, I could find it very easy to talk about the Toronto Symphony Orchestra or the Vancouver Symphony Orchestra. I could ask whether the people of Vancouver Island
The Address-Mr. Anderson
were deriving any benefit from these activities. One could say, I suppose, that the people of Canada in general were benefiting, but I suspect it is the people of Toronto or of Montreal or of Vancouver who receive the most benefit from institutions such as these within their areas.
Is it heresy to suggest that those who are the principal beneficiaries should provide the most support? The government can put out seed money, as the Canada Council has done, but must the people of Canada provide the majority of the funding of such organizations for the next 50 years? Is there not a greater community responsibility? In situations where user groups are the main beneficiaries I believe the federal government should say, "We shall continue to make part of the funding available but the majority of money must come from the community. In the absence of support from the community the federal contribution will not continue indefinitely." Maybe the response in the area will tell the government how highly the service or the activity was valued. If people in the area where benefits are received do not wish to support these activities, should the federal government continue to make finance available? One could, of course, apply this principle too narrowly, but there are surely some non-essential services with respect to which a decision could be reached and expenditure reduced over a period of years in the interest of a balanced budget.
Incidentally, I have never heard spokesmen for the official opposition tell us whether they favour a balanced budget. The only programs I have heard of theirs in the last several months are programs which would cost more money and add further to the already high budget deficit. This subject is one upon which the official opposition has been silent in the last six or seven months during which they believed there was to be a federal general election; they never once declared it was a policy of a Conservative party to balance the budget. I am rather surprised at this because the message I have heard from the official opposition seems to be this, "We are the party of financial responsibility, while the Liberals are the spendthrifts and wastrels." The Liberal party has always considered itself financially responsible. At the same time I have never heard a statement from the official opposition that it would be their object, if elected, to bring down a balanced budget within, say, five years.
Does a party of financial responsibility go into an election promising the people of Canada further debt of approximately $4.6 billion? On the other hand, is this government, which is reducing government expenditures, the financial wastrel of this parliament? I can only judge by actions and deeds. I cannot judge by rhetoric. It is of no use to talk restraint when all you can come up with is added debt amounting to $4.6 billion. I suspect that there are people who have watched the charade which has gone on over the last few months.
The Government of Canada has been preaching restraint, not just for three or four months but for the last several years. Our friends in the opposition, who criticize us for throwing
80065 -10'/2

October 16, 1978
The Address-Mr. Anderson
away taxpayers' money, have come up with programs which would cost an additional $4.6 billion. Although I would never accuse hon. members opposite, I suspect that that $4.6 billion program was proposed only as a political ploy in the hope of gathering a few votes from people who have not looked at our budgets. I am rather disappointed that people with apparent capability in financial matters suggest that they might save this country from Liberals who madly throw away money. I do not think my party has ever thought of throwing away money as the Conservatives have. I hope the people of Canada watch, and listen to what is being said, because I suspect that hon. members opposite cannot get away with that any more.
People in Canada are a little too sophisticated to be taken in by this boondoggle which it is patently obvious is designed to do only one thing, and that is to get in and out of an election by making as many promises as possible. I suspect that the people of Canada are not quite naive enough to say that we are spendthrifts when hon. members opposite are prepared to put out some $4 billion with no recovery, and when we should be talking about saving money, not finding new ways to spend money we do not have.
The other boondoggle is the proposed expenditure of $1.6 billion or $2 billion to reduce taxes for homeowners in Canada. If we are serious about helping people-not just owners of big houses who can afford $50,000 mortgages, but also renters and people in many other situations-I hope with the co-operation of all parties we will find an equitable system for all Canadians rather than just for those to whom the Conservative party usually appeals, people on high incomes who probably do not require tax assistance in the first place.
I hope that parliament will continue to assist people through such programs as AEIOP and others. Recently it was proposed that the government provide low income families with $200 a year in addition to $20 a month starting in January of next year. It seems to be reasonable and equitable that people who have the greatest need receive greater government assistance. There is no point for a breadwinner who earns $50,000 a year to receive the same benefit as a family earning $8,000 a year. I am very happy about that proposal of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin). She brought in something everyone said would never be accepted, a means test with regard to the family allowance.
I hope one further step will be contemplated. Although the guaranteed income supplement will be increased by $20 a month starting in January, 1979, perhaps serious thought could be given to the fact that there are people over age 65 who do not require government assistance. If it is our aim that people at lower income levels do not suffer further from disparity between rich and poor, surely this parliament in its wisdom could bring in programs, not to eliminate totally moneys paid to people over 65 who do not require it, but which would be equitable and which would assist those in greater need, and reduce moneys going to people who do not require it.
I do not think that is revolutionary. I have heard people complain that they have paid a lot of money into income tax, that they have employed people, and that they are the ones

who are not getting the benefits. They complain that we always give money to people on welfare and people on unemployment insurance and that those people are the beneficiaries of the system. They complain that they make $100,000 a year and it is all going out to other people. I say that that is garbage, because we have a system which allows people to make $100,000. Our system does not level everyone down with regard to income, as is the case in some other societies.
When a person has made his stake and has done very well in this country, it is two-bitting to say, "So what if that woman's husband left her; give her nothing." It is two-bitting to say, "It is my money you are giving away". I find that to be a contemptible attitude.
Some people who have done well in our system do not recognize the very simple fact of life that it is the system here which has allowed them to do this. The opportunity has been there, and the fact that moneys are taken by way of income tax and in other ways is really not the point in question. I hope that in our society we have enough tolerance to accept the fact that social programs are not demeaning to recipients because they are forced to be recipients.
There is a feeling among some that if a person, through illness or ill fortune, requires assistance, he is somehow taking advantage of the system. I think that for every ten people who would take advantage of the system there are a thousand who would not, and I find it demeaning that some of our citizens, not only in this House but also in other sectors of society, assume that undeserving recipients of assistance are the majority rather than the minority.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Order, please. I regret to interrupt the hon. member but his time has expired.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I must say that it is an interesting challenge to participate in the debate on the Address in reply to the Speech from the Throne in the fourth session of the thirtieth parliament. I really am not going to take any time to comment on the words of the previous speaker, the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Anderson). I was not quite sure what he was protesting about toward the end of his speech. As perhaps with other Liberals from western soil, he certainly gave a great demonstration of why they are an endangered species, especially in terms of messages. Without playing the role of a seer or a prophet, 1 think there will be a message tonight from coast to coast which will show that Canadians have not been fooled by government protestation and declaration.
The government talks about restraint and then cynically selects for cutbacks some of the high profile, very specific programs which receive a lot of press coverage, but in actual terms of savings make little difference in the federal treasury. The hon. member for South Shore (Mr. Crouse) has much more knowledge of fisheries than I. I will not deal with the specifics of some of the protestations or statements of restraint made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and subsequently
October 16, 1978

by other ministers. Contrary to what the hon. member for Comox-Alberni attempted to suggest, my party has been talking about restraint for the last ten years since I and the Prime Minister have been here.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: What have you done?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
It is not what we have done. When one is in opposition he cannot do very much. Canadians will not be fooled by conversion on the road to Damascus. One cannot compare two or three months of speeches since August to several years of very deliberate policy. We have attempted to point out, by criticizing legislative programs, that some of the things we voted on would result in financial ruin. I am sure the message will be loud and clear tonight.
Without being detoured on some of the byways of some of the speeches which have gone before, let me congratulate the mover (Mrs. Appolloni) and the seconder (Mr. Savard) for their addresses in reply to the Speech from the Throne. I found it somewhat ironic that the seconder was the hon. member for Verdun in view of ongoing activities in the Canadian electoral process. Certainly the hon. member for Verdun deserves credit for his participation, but it is somewhat an ironic twist of history that his predecessor is being judged by the people today. The shadow of Verdun will be on some of the results tonight and, like some of the battles of old Verdun, the tale will be told very loud and clear.
The Speech from the Throne and the various speeches of the last few days have provided a contrast between the opening of this fourth session of the thirtieth parliament and that of the third session a year ago. Both speeches took place in the month of October, with autumn leaves, beautiful fall sun, and the painted hills of the Gatineau. Last year we were honoured with the presence of the King and the Queen-

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: King and Queen?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Well, the Queen and the Prince. After the Queen is dead, long live the King. Royalty continues. We had the benefit of Her Majesty and the Prince coming to Parliament Hill in the landau. This caused an air of excitement and anticipation. Regardless of past evasions, we thought the Speech from the Throne by Her Majesty the Queen would be the final act and the final Speech from the Throne, leading into the general election which the country wanted.
I find it somewhat hollow for certain speakers to say, "what are you going to do, why have you not done more?" How can restraint be preached? Perhaps from a bookkeeping point of view certain programs will produce certain dollars in deficit. If a program is carried out as intended and defined, hopefully our stagnant economy will be stimulated. I will not deal with those areas, but I should like to point out that the contrast is invidious.
If one looks at the British history of parliament, he will realize that there has been a long parliament, a short parliament, and a rump parliament. But I do not believe in Canadian history that there has ever been such as lame duck parlia-
The Address-Mr. Nowlan
ment as the present one. We are going through the motions of staying here until the Prime Minister decides to issue the writ. The Prime Minister had more sharps and flats and starts and stops than an organ grinder on a merry-go-round when attempting to make up his mind. A poll from Goldfarb would provide him with a hint, and then he would find out that the hint was not too good. Then he would turn to the Gallup poll for guidance, followed by a return to Goldfarb. He sent Keith Davey to Vancouver, and had someone else fly to Halifax. If the business of the country was not so serious, we could all laugh at it.
One of the greatest testimonies to not calling an election was when finally the Prime Minister indicated that there would be no election and that the House would resume in October. On that day the dollar took one of its largest falls in the decline which has been ongoing for several months. That indicates the confidence of the outside world. It was realized that the chance to restore some confidence to the economy was going to be delayed a further six to eight months while a pantomine was conducted in the form of a forced session of parliament. When the Prime Minister finally decided to play his organ, he indicated that there would be no more flats or sharps; he pulled out the plug and continued the charade.
We have had the benefit of two interesting speeches, those of the Prime Minister and the hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark). Those speeches were diametrically opposed. If one was a man from Mars, perhaps he could be forgiven if he did not appreciate who was the Prime Minister and who was the Leader of the Opposition upon hearing those speeches. There is no doubt that the Prime Minister put on quite a performance in terms of attack, ridicule, and contempt. Years ago I said that the Prime Minister is one of the thespians of the political stage. He makes the bard of old, Mr. William Shakespeare, seem like a piker. He put on a tremendous performance, the purpose of which was twofold. It was to buck up his troops who were feeling somewhat low, with just cause. Also it was to tell a certain lawyer on Bay Street to stay away, that this preserve is still prohibited because the Prime Minister would remain in office for a few more months. He told John Turner to stay away, that he was still in charge. In terms of the morale of his troops in the House and for the benefit of those who were sniffing winds of change, he put on a tremendous performance. From that narrow point of view he deserves credit.
In effect, the hon. Leader of the Opposition came forward with a draft Speech from the Throne in terms of positive things to be done. The Prime Minister's attack on my leader confirmed the fact that he felt endangered and is almost on the endangered species list. The performance of the Prime Minister will not go away, no matter what great theatrical performance follows his. The Prime Minister himself is one of the fundamental issues which confront the country from coast to coast. There are the problems of inflation, the economy, unemployment, and the weak dollar. Also we have a Prime Minister who has been in power for ten years, leading a government which has been in power for 15 years. The federal

October 16, 1978
The Address-Mr. Nowlan
government is the oldest government in the western world in terms of continuity of office. Is it any wonder why Canadians will demonstrate their feelings at the polls? People realize that the federal government can be changed, as is the case with provincial governments and other world governments, if and when a general election is called.
The demonstrations which have occurred in the last few days illustrate my point. Our theatrical Prime Minister over the last ten years has highly personified his office. Whether offshore or onshore, he has performed before the cameras dramatizing his office. I sympathize with hon. members opposite who cannot understand and do not yet believe. Perhaps the results of the by-elections will show them better than I.
The members from Nova Scotia were the last ones to come from the political trenches approximately two or three weeks ago. I do not care about the columnists in Ottawa and the inner sanctum of the ivory tower, but they should realize that in Nova Scotia there was a strong anti-government and anti-Trudeau feeling. If they do not understand that, then they are just whistling Dixie. The longer they whistle Dixie, the better the tune for us to take over when Trudeau, if he is around, does call the next election. What has happened is understandable. This is human nature. My friend, the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Cullen), understands this. He and I came here pretty much at the same time, and we know this has happened before. We know this is historic, that there is precedent for it.
I remember an earlier time when Canadians put their faith and trust in a prime minister who was very colourful. When difficulties arose in a certain economic climate Canadians took out their ire on that prime minister with a vengeance. Between 1962 and 1963 the Conservative party lost more seats than it had previously won, and it dropped from 208 seats down to the minority government of 1963. The same thing is happening again. We have had the great expectations of 1968, the beginning of the love affair on the part of many Canadians, if you want to call it that. Canadians who were not committed to politics then saw the prime minister as a new man, a new politician. That was a love affair, but we all know what happens when a love affair goes sour. Rationale and logic go out the window and are replaced by criticism and complaint. The individual, and sometimes the public collectively, acts in an unreasonable way.
I suggest in all seriousness that is one of the reasons there is an almost virulent anti-prime ministerial mood in some parts of the country today. At one time the feeling was warm and close, almost a love affair; now it has gone sour and people want to get in their licks. I do not know how many people really love the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Stanfield), but when he was leader of the Conservative party no one hated him. There was respect for him from coast to coast.
Seriously, there is a sort of unfortunate feeling in the political domain today that, while the people may have loved the Prime Minister a few years ago, perhaps ten, because of a

multiplicity of factors, including general economic conditions, there is no longer a love affair; and those on the negative side will not go away as a result of a parliamentary theatrical performance on the part of the Prime Minister, even though that performance was a boost to the troops and perhaps accomplished what the Prime Minister intended.
I say no more than that, except that what happened in Nova Scotia was not an aberration. I do not think that what will happen tonight in the by-elections will represent an aberration.
I would almost go so far as to suggest that what will happen in Saskatchewan a few days down the road will not be an aberration. I hope there is another performance by the Prime Minister before the next election in New Brunswick in order that the troops stay bolstered, because I would certainly like the next election to be run against that Thespian north of the 49th parallel, that present incumbent prime minister.
The Prime Minister put on that performance, and at least part of that performance again would explain why the public in Canada is rather negative in its appreciation of his talents. How could a responsible Prime Minister, trying to exert leadership in this country at this particularly difficult time, make the statement he made in his speech that we in Canada "are performing better than most, better than all, actually, if we consider the over-all of total performances"? He then went on to divide up the total performance into job creation, inflation, real income and housing starts.
I do not want to cast stones, but I will use that old maxim that figures do not lie, but sometimes liars figure. In a political, allegorical way, you define your own figures, your own total performances and thereby paint a rosy picture. It does not take the rhetoric of the House of Commons, or any speech from any of us, to point out to you, Mr. Speaker, what you found out when you were home this summer. It certainly does not take a speech from my colleagues here to tell me what I found out when I was at home and in other parts of this country during the summer. We all know that no matter how selectively you define the term, certainly the general confidence of the people in this government and in politicians generally is sadly lacking.
Inflation is historically high in many areas. We have extremely high interest rates, even higher following the announcement over the weekend. The public can no longer be duped. You can cite the job creation programs, you can talk about inflation and real income after taxes, and you can even point out housing starts, as the Prime Minister did; but you cannot fool the public because the people are living with these things every day. Every day the people are having to shell out.
The Prime Minister conned the public once in 1974 when he said there was not to be any control package because inflation was offshore; but then within a year, we heard that famous and memorable Thanksgiving speech on television. He told Canadians, many of whom were eating turkey, or those who could afford it were-he was eating crow and doing a flip-flop-that we were going to have a controls package. The people knew then they were conned but they will not be conned again. They know that these statements of rhetoric represent a
October 16, 1978

con job because they are actually facing and confronting day by day the economic difficulties of life today.
It was only a day after the Prime Minister's speech that someone more knowledgeable of economic figures than I, Mr. Donald McGillivray, the business editor of Southam Press, took the Prime Minister's selective figures and wrote in a most conservative way:
Trudeau is incredibly careless in the conclusions he draws from his numbers.
It is simply untrue to say, as he did, that "Canada, in terms of the employment growth rate, is the best in the world."
According to the statistical Yearbook of the United Nations, 15 countries had faster rates of employment growth between 1970 and 1975.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Which countries?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I have them here. They are Mauritius, Jordan, Malawi, Kenya, Turkey, Syria, South Korea, Malaysia, Yugoslavia, Romania, Spain, Swaziland, Tunisia, Fiji and Pakistan. Let me tell the Minister of Employment and Immigration that this takes us up to 1975. Perhaps those are exotic countries that started from a very slow base, and perhaps it is easy to play with those figures. But this statement was made by the Prime Minister who is supposed to be accepting some responsibility when dealing with these figures, instead of playing footsie with them.
Mr. McGillivray goes on to state:
Since then, Canada's rate of job creation has fallen behind other countries, including the U.S. Statistics published by the Paris-based Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development show that between 1975 and 1977 the U.S. created 6.4 per cent more jobs while Canada was creating only 4.2 per cent more.
He then asks rhetorically how the Prime Minister can cite these numbers to back his claim that we "still lead the world". Then he dissects the process of how the Prime Minister did this, namely by playing with figures. He states:
First, by restricting his "world" to 15 industrial countries and second, by mixing the slow recent rates of job creation with faster rates recorded before 1975.
He then continues by stating:
For proof, Trudeau cited Figures for the period 1968-76. And 1976 was, of course, the year when food prices slumped and gave Canada a relatively good year against inflation. Even so, Canada's performance was so-so, not immensely better.
More recent figures do not bear out the impression that we are doing better at all. The Economist, the British-based journal of business and current affairs, does a regular check on 10 "major economies" including Canada.
They are not the exotic countries which the Prime Minister had fun playing with the other day. This shows that eight of the ten countries, Australia, France, Germany, The Netherlands, Japan, Sweden, the United States and Britain, did better than Canada against inflation in the past year, and that only Italy did worse. My point is that while there was a great theatrical performance the other day, you did not have to question other prime ministers, be they Conservative or Liberal, and their statements when dealing with facts. We have found out to our sorry experience and to even the sorrier, more collective experience of Canadians that we have to question
The Address-Mr. Nowlan
and check the facts and statistics quoted by the Prime Minister.
More serious than just playing with the figures in an attempt to make a parliamentary debating point, is the frame of mind and the premise the Prime Minister reflects when he suggests we are performing better than we actually are. Because if you believe that frame of mind, then how can the Canadian people expect that there will be any change in policies which every objective outside observer has said are bringing economic despair, and in some cases ruin, to a good many parts of this country?
It is the frame of mind of the Prime Minister which has to be indicted here. It is not just three months of preaching restraint that is at issue here. When we go into the election campaign, as eventually we will, at issue will not be just the last three months or the six or seven months before that, it will be the ten-year period. He will not be playing around with different time periods and different countries then; he will be playing with our own country and defining his actions during the ten-year period that he has been in office. That is the time frame which will be relevant to Canadians when it comes to making their decision at the polls.
When he took over the government in April, 1968 unemployment was at the level of 375,000, or a rate of 4.5 per cent. Now it is 8.4 per cent or over 900,000. The youth unemployment rate has gone from 7.4 per cent in that ten-year period to over 14 per cent. These are some of the relevant facts and figures that will have to be considered and will not be easily sloughed off as they were here in parliamentary fashion the other day. The rate of inflation in 1968 was 4.5 per cent; as of August, 1978 it was 9.2 per cent. I could go on on this topic forever.
The unfortunate thing is that the just society of 1968 has become the sick society of today. It is sick on unemployment figures no matter how you count them up. The dollar reflects the sickness in terms of investor confidence outside this country. Some of our modes of transportation are in a sick state as, for example, Air Canada with its labour and management problems. Just today we received notice that the seaway workers are going to strike, and right now, as was pointed out earlier, the postal workers are negotiating in a situation where they may go on strike. You could almost take every facet of our economy-be it interest rates, strikes, inflation, unemployment-and see that in effect we have a thermometer that is registering rather high. It is a sad commentary that the just society has now become the sick society of ten years later, and this is another reason why I would think that the public of Canada wants a chance to make a value judgment on whether to extend the mandate of this government or to give it to some other party that will change the fundamentals of government.
The two speeches given by the leaders were so different. The Leader of the Opposition gave a very controlled, positive and constructive contribution with a few political sallies and barbs from time to time, which we should always have in a partiamentary debate in a political atmosphere. But the Prime Minister had a change in roles. From playing with figures and

October 16, 1978
The Address-Mr. Nowlan
using sleight-of-hand as though he were in a shell game and defining his own time reference in office, he turned to concentrating almost solely, in terms of theatrics, on heaping scorn and contempt on the Leader of the Opposition. Obviously, he feels threatened and can feel the warmth of the Leader of the Opposition's breath on his neck.
Had I been from Mars, I would have wondered if these two men were talking about the same country. It takes me back approximately 119 years to the "Tale of Two Cities" and a fellow called Dickens, who wrote, as many will remember:
It was the best of times, it was the worst of times, it was the age of wisdom, it was the age of foolishness, it was the epoch of belief, it was the epoch of incredulity, it was the season of Light, it was the season of Darkness, it was the spring of hope, it was the winter of despair. We had everything before us, we had nothing before us, we were all going direct to heaven, we were all going direct the other way-in short, the period was so far like the present period that some of its noisiest authorities insisted on its being received for good or for evil in the superlative degree of comparison only.
The comparison of the speeches by the two leaders illustrates in fairly graphic form what Mr. Dickens said 119 years ago in his memorable "Tale of Two Cities". The two different leaders stood in this national forum, but one spoke and addressed his remarks to the problems of the nation and tried to give some examples of where he, had he written the Speech from the Throne or been the leader of the government, would be moving to try, with all the imperfections of any policy- because no policy will bring overnight redress or correction to 15 years of mismanagement, let alone the galloping mismanagement of the past ten years-to put this country on its feet again. The Prime Minister went into his selective figure routine where, by intellectual, dialectical, classical thinking you can prove almost anything. You could prove that the town of Wolfville, which I had the good fortune to come from, in terms of growth is most likely growing faster than the city of Toronto. That is the type of dialectical debating exercise that we got from the Prime Minister the other day. There was nothing in his speech directed to the problems of the nation.
The Speech from the Throne talks about the general state of the economy. We have had some press statements and undoubtedly there will be some bills proposed to plug the dike, like the Dutch boy many years ago, who saw the water starting to come through. There was also mention of the constitution. Unfortunately, Canadians have heard so much about the constitution that many of them are turned off by it. I could make a whole speech on the constitution and Bill C-60 as it then was. Certainly in terms of the economy there is no objective outside observer who does not say that something will have to happen.
The subject of the constitution-and I want to be kind here, for I have not said publicly what my thoughts are on the late, lamented bill, which frankly will not be lamented that much since it died with the old session-you would think would be the Prime Minister's forte since he apparently taught constitutional law at one time. However, in cabinet making it has happened that the person with the expertise makes the worst cabinet minister if he is appointed to the portfolio which is related to his field, because he thinks he knows all the answers.
This can be borne out, for example, where generals have become ministers of defence. Perhaps the Prime Minister has a blind spot. Indeed, I suggest that he has several blind spots in the area that was his professional expertise-the constitution.
