speechtext: Order, please. I regret to interrupt the hon. member but his allotted time has expired. He may continue with the unanimous consent of the House. Is there unanimous consent?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: No.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I find it rather odd to be speaking on a throne speech in this session of this parliament. A few weeks ago I was asked if there was to be a throne speech and a budget in the new session and I said: "Not in my opinion". I thought the government would not want to drop the bills they have on things like constitutional change and that they would not want a throne speech because they did not know where they were going. 1 did not think they would want a budget either because they would not want to make a financial accounting unless they had to. The last session had gone on so long that most of us forgot when the last throne speech was.
Of course, I thought there would be an election last spring. I have never seen such preparation for an election by a government. Everything was arranged. They did not get their bills so far advanced that there had to be discussion of them to the point that opposition might develop. Programs were introduced that could be discussed without a conclusion being reached, so it seemed to me the best possible situation for an election.
When I heard that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) had added six or seven vacant constituencies to the list of by-elections, I was sure there would be a general election, that nobody would be foolish enough to have 10 per cent of the population vote in a mini-election. But all of these things came to pass and here we are in the middle of a throne speech in a new session in the fifth year of a parliament.
I listened to the mover and seconder of the debate on the throne speech and I should like to congratulate them on their presentations. It seemed as if they felt, as I did to some extent, that this is the first session of a new parliament-that this parliament will go on forever. Maybe there will be changes to make that possible and this is the beginning of a new era. They sounded like the speeches of totally new members, although neither of them are and one, I know, has made some very good contributions over the years. But I congratulate them both on their speeches.
Next we heard from the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) and the Prime Minister. I am in complete agreement with those who say the roles have been reversed. It was very surprising how much the Leader of the Opposition has learned about running a government-the necessary finesse, the rhetoric that is necessary to allow him to go in any direction after he finds out what the public will say. The Prime Minister then

October 16, 1978

came along like a schoolboy debating the subject of parliament in high school. In the best tradition of an opposition leader he presented his role in politics.
After travelling around the country, Mr. Speaker, I have come to the conclusion that the only issue that remains for an election is the Prime Minister himself. There are those who think he has done the best he could given the international implications and difficulties being experienced in monetary and fiscal areas throughout the developed and undeveloped world. On those items I think he performed very well, but he must have scared some of the people sitting in their living rooms watching the program, waiting for answers to their problems. They are in a major depression and they do not know what to do about it. They looked for leadership which was not forthcoming; all they got was a tirade saying how bad the other guy was and how bad things were in general.
There are two things that bother the public, Mr. Speaker. The first is the fact that jobs are not available for newcomers on the labour market. Some have been helped to a small degree with make-work projects, but there are no continuing jobs for them. This applies to a large percentage of the age bracket 15 to 24, those just entering the labour market. Some are drop-outs who in the past have been able to find manual work, jobs driving trucks or any job they are equipped for. They are willing and ready to do those jobs but what are they offered? They are sent back to school for retraining and then have to wait till something is available. Sometimes when they enter the labour market they are told they are too highly qualified for the work available and are entitled to more money than an employer can pay. In both cases they are sitting at home waiting for jobs. How long can they wait? I am not sure how long society will allow them to wait and unless there is a great change in our economy they will not find the employment they are trained for.
These young people know that they will be given a hard time by people in the community and that they are going to have difficulty making ends meet. In my community and others some young people have committed suicide because there is just not any future for them and there is no way of getting a living other than stealing or living off their parents. In many cases young people do not want to live off their parents. They did it for years when they felt it was the obligation of the parents to support them, but then they believed they had an obligation to make their own contribution. They are ready to do so but there is no opportunity for them to participate.
Some welfare officials advise young ladies of 18 or 19 years of age to live at home because welfare benefits are not available for them. Just this week I had a case of a father who said to his daughter, "I have six other children to raise; I cannot afford to feed and clothe you and supply you with cigarettes." What is she to do? There is only room for a certain number of prostitutes and there are only some young women who are qualified to be prostitutes. Yet it is the only kind of job that many 17 and 18-year-old girls can get if they leave their community and go to the city. It is not a nice situation but it is part of our society today, as any police
The Address-Mr. Peters
officer will tell you. Where do young ladies go who leave the community? Most of them are found in that profession. It is not entirely their fault. We have a responsibility as well and we are shirking it.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Perhaps there should be a quota system on prostitution.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Perhaps there should be; it depends on the market. It is a free enterprise system and there are a lot of people in that profession who do not want to be but are because there is no alternative. We are not providing opportunities for our young people. I think that is a field in which governments, provincial and federal, have to get directly involved. If there are no jobs, then we should be increasing those kinds of operations that most of us are not completely in favour of but should be looking at, if that is the only alternative left. For example, I think of youth camps or Army training, if that is the only type of training possible. But this winter, with the curtailment of unemployment insurance, and particularly in Ontario where the municipalities themselves quite often make the decision as to how they treat young recipients of welfare, unless parliamentarians do something about the job situation many of the injustices concerning the young will be much greater than before.
I am told that we are in a period of austerity. We are going to cut back on this, and we are going to cut back on that. We have been operating a country for many years on the basis that we were a subsidiary of the United States. The parent company at home could not make enough of the product to sell throughout the world, so they allowed the subsidiary to do some selling as well.
Canada did get into the export market with some manufactured goods and I think we did very well. As soon as there is difficulty in selling manufactured goods, no matter the value of our dollar, the parent company will say: "We want to do the selling; the market is not big enough for you and me, it is only big enough for me." As a result Canadians have not done very well in that regard.
We must think, Mr. Speaker, about some of the things we are doing to provide a better life in this country. All Canadians had better take a look at how we are balancing our trade today. We are balancing our trade today, to the extent we are, by selling raw materials. We are selling our birthright. We are depending on agriculture, on forestry and on mining to balance the budget accounts of our nation. And we are not making it even at that. No other country in the world gives away the amount or resources we give away in return for so little.
I am amused by some of the suggestions 1 hear for increasing production in Canada. It was interesting to note that the government of Ontario and the federal government got together recently. They wanted the new Ford plant built in Canada because it would provide jobs. That is very nice. We would like those jobs and we would like that new plant in Canada but did we really have to provide $75 million to get Ford to come here and help us out?

October 16, 1978
The Address-Mr. Peters
I checked some of the figures published in the Financial Post. I find, looking up these corporations supported by Liber-ils and Conservatives-the free enterprise system-that Ford of Canada actually owns dollar shares worth $8,294,000. Of that number, the United States owns 88.4 per cent, or $7,336,603 worth. In December of 1977, the last available figures, the dividend paid was $8.35 per share or $61,227,235. The amount paid to the American company was 88 per cent, or $61 million.
At the same time as we allow them to transport out of Canada, as a dividend, $61 million plus a few thousand dollars, we allow them to blackmail us into supplying them with a further $75 million. That amounts to a whole year's dividend. We are going to bring that money back in, but since we do not have that money we borrow it from the Americans. We pay interest on money provided to Ford Canada to come back into Canada, though we have already in one year, given them almost sufficient money to have done that themselves had they wished.
The situation is no better in the case of General Motors of Canada. General Motors of Canada has very few shares, some 703,250. These are all held by General Motors Corporation in the United States. Their earnings are $227.24 per share. They paid out a dividend of 53.9 per cent, which is $122.48 per share, with a total of $86 million and some odd going to the United States. What are we going to do with that money, Mr. Speaker? We are not going to let General Motors build a plant in Canada with that money, which they have already taken out of Canada. We are going to give them some more money and use that as a carrot to bring them back into Quebec to build a casting factory in that province. The Quebec government will give them some money and the federal government will give some money.
The Financial Post tells us there is $66,000 in dividends leaving Canada each hour for the United States. This money comes from American owned corporations in Canada. It would seem to me that unless we really loved those Americans a better deal than that could be obtained. Either there would be some way of stopping those dividends from leaving the country or there would be a tax on them.
With that kind of monetary drain out of this country in dividends to Ford and General Motors, we should be able to buy American Motors and set up our own automobile industry in Canada. Maybe they do not produce the best car in the world, but the price is right now. It is likely to go broke in the next few years. Why do we not buy it? It has the patents which are necessary and their cars could be built in Canada and we could use all of the dividends which are going to the United States. Some of them come back to Canada. We could tax those dividends. We could do a lot of things with them.
Recently we decided to cut back, so what did we cut back on? As I said before, there are two things this country is running on as far as exports are concerned. One is mining and the second is forestry. On a television station that I watch I see an advertisement from a lumber company every few days. It says that 23 cents out of every dollar that each Canadian gets comes from the forest industry. It may be right or it may be

wrong, but if it is right 23 cents out of every dollar is a lot of money.
We have cut down the experimental stations in the forest industry. I come from what was one of the best forest areas in Canada. Now there are no trees. We are now cutting about 10 million acres of budworm infected forests and do not have any trees. Canada has never done better in its reforestry program than harvesting one tree out of every ten. We plant ten trees, one lives. If it does not burn down in the next 60 years, someone will harvest it. In my area they are harvesting trees now that are probably not more than six inches at the butt and they are drawing them in tree lengths to Quebec. We in Ontario are so generous we can give them away. Yet we can cut back the stations that are our only hope of developing a perpetual yield forest. It is not like the mines; anyone will tell you that you should plant a tree every time a tree is cut. However, that has not been done. This is a good time to fly over Ontario to see the trees. The leaves cover the ground. It is like a mat. However, in most places there are no trees of any size.
In my area there is a tremendous fight about whether one particular sawmill or the other will get the new cut. Whichever mill gets the new cut will be able to expand; the other will have to close. In other words, there is enough cut for one sawmill, or a little for each of the sawmills to try and get along with.
The forests of Ontario are not being regenerated. This is probably true in British Columbia and, in fact, across the whole of the North American continent. There are no forests for tomorrow. We will be hard pressed to get along for the next ten or 12 years.
A new project has been started. It reminds me of when the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) was minister of agriculture. He talked about the ARDA program, taking eastern Ontario out of farming, where they only farmed stones and little sections, and putting it into forests. I understand that at the experimental stations in Guelph and Petawawa a hybrid tree has been developed that will grow a foot a month.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: The Ontario government did that.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: The Ontario government is the main force behind it, but the federal government is certainly involved in it too.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Don't let her lead you.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
It does not matter who developed it. I could give the name of the man in Guelph who did develop the hybrid poplar tree. The point is that this is an area in which there appears to be a breakthrough. In ten or 12 years you can get a tree the size of a 60-year tree. Therefore, this is not the time to cut off grants to the experimental stations. We would be cutting off our potential for the future in a field where there appears to be some resource. After all, you only need someone with a chainsaw to cut trees which can then be trucked to the
October 16, 1978

United States or somewhere else to help our balance of payments.
All across northern Ontario, including my area, there are headframes and rusty fences indicating where there once was a gold mine. I suppose that 20,000, 30,000 or 40,000 of these operations have been developed over the past 50 or 60 years. Most have a small shaft that goes down 200 or 300 feet. When they were in operation, they operated on a shoestring. Some of these mines operated when gold was $28 an ounce. A lot more operated when it was a maximum $35 an ounce. It is true that wages were not as high then.
Both the forestry and mining industry are labour intensive, other than in areas such as Elliot Lake or Sudbury where very large quantities of ore are taken out. Gold or silver is mined in a vein 40 or 50 feet wide. Therefore, we do not need a great deal of width to extract a considerable quantity of ore. These mines could be developed if there was some leadership given by the federal government. I am not in the position to say what kind of help should be given. Possibly a penny market could be established. There is no question that in most communities the money is available to develop these mines; what is needed is leadership.
Most Liberals have not followed the example of the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Goyer). When he attended a committee meeting not long ago, he was asked by the mining industry to provide gold coins that would contain exactly one ounce of gold with a fineness of .999. I was at that meeting. The minister stated that he would like to have a $100 commemorative coin put out annually but with considerably less gold content than that. However, he agreed with the mining industry he would be willing to have a bullion coin put out. Brokerage and securities people say there is a market for such a coin, one with about twice as much gold as that in production in Canada today. However, the framework to provide such gold coins has not been looked at.
The operation of the gold mines in my area would not require elaborate structures; it would be merely revitalizing a lot of holes already in the ground. A man could mine a few tons per year. In many cases, the gold would be worth $400 or $500 a ton of ore. During the depression, I worked in gold mines for $4.64 a day. Everything has gone up quite a bit since then, but not in proportion to the price of gold today. Today I could get $46 a day, not much in today's terms, working at hard labour in a mine.
People could be found to develop and work in the gold mines in these communities. There are already developed mines that could again be mined. Some of the present mines have extra mining capacity. Kerr Addison Mines in my area is operating at less than 1,000 tons a day, although it has a mill that will handle 5,000 tons.
Not long ago a man who had mined in Boston Creek died. He had operated a mine for ten or 12 years and had made enough money to live on. He went underground, drilled off, blasted, mucked it out, put it in buckets and hauled them to the top. He made enough money to get by for ten or 12 years.
The Address-Mr. Peters
That kind of gold mining is available in literally thousands of places in my constituency. In addition, silver is available.
I suggest the Supreme Court ruling told us something. It told the federal government that it has an obligation to see what happens with gold when it comes out of the ground. In Timmins, Kirkland Lake and Noranda there is an opportunity to create 5,000 jobs within six months. The people there are available and willing to work. Most of them are not qualified to do anything but the job they had been doing for a number of years but which is no longer available.
I now want to deal with the Lakeshore mine. There is more gold in the top 200 feet today than there has been during most of the lifetime of that mine. That gold has increased in value from $35 an ounce to $275 Canadian. Maybe the Americans will only pay $225, but in Canada it is $275 an ounce, almost ten times the amount it was worth when the mine closed.
These mines closed because there was not enough money with which to pay wages, though the most I ever got in the industry was $1.19 an hour in one of the best paid jobs and I really do not think the workers were overpaid. But if you paid the workers ten times that amount today there would still be a good deal left over from the sale of the product; the government could take that gold to any country in the world and get value for it. They could go to Germany or the United States and borrow on the strength of it. Why not develop the gold industry here?
I would have no objection to the federal government setting up a national mining corporation, as did Quebec at the provincial level, paying so much for the gold and getting it processed. I do not care what procedure is followed but I think a country is stupid, stupid, stupid when it fails to take advantage of the price of gold in these circumstances. I am not sure gold will always be at its present price. After all, the world might be broke tomorrow; it is already up to its ears in debt.
A few years ago the United States took out a loan from Germany and agreed to pay back that loan either in gold or in Swiss francs. Several months ago the U.S. Treasury went to Switzerland on bended knees asking the Swiss to put more Swiss francs on the market where the U.S. could buy them to pay off part of this debt. The Swiss authorities declined, saying there were not enough Swiss francs in the world to pay off that particular debt, nor was there enough gold in the U.S. Treasury, or anywhere else where the Americans could get hold of it, to pay that debt off. So, in due course, if the regular procedure is followed, the Germans will own the United States because they will take over its assets by default.
As I was saying, the price of gold may not hold up forever, but right now it is at such a high level that we should be mining it in northern Ontario, in British Columbia and, yes, in the maritimes. I am sure the hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay) could tell us a great deal about the history of the mines which were developed in that province and the reason many of them were unsuccessful, mainly because of the lack of sufficient capital. In those days gold was fetching about

October 16, 1978
The Address-Mr. Peters
$28 an ounce. Today, with the price around $225, even a cow pasture would begin to look good.
It is possible for us to ignore the studies which have been going on at our forestry stations, though we do so at great risk to the future. If present experiments turn out well-of course, there is no guarantee that they will-we can expect a perpetual yield from our forests. Young people today are not as stupid as we were. They believe in the value of preserving the ecology and I am confident they will find ways through experimentation to maintain a perpetual yield from those forests.
The Liberals and the Conservatives are always talking about free enterprise. I am not suggesting that mines should not be managed by free enterprise; my socialist friends would have a fit if gold production were to be nationalized. It has been done before without too much success because the price of gold was not very high and my friends did not think there was very much sense in digging a hole in the ground, taking out the gold and then burying it again in a vault or some place else. Of course, those who need it can use the gold to fill their teeth, though today one has to be very rich to afford gold fillings in teeth; I suppose people can only afford to have them gold plated. But surely we can find a way of helping to develop Canadian gold mines if only for the purpose of providing employment. Even if we are interested in helping our southern friends-we help them by sending our savings down there and by allowing them to put up factories in our country and take out the dividends-there are some things we can do very well here; for example, long-distance transmission of electricity.

speechtext: I will only take half a minute more, Mr. Speaker. I was pointing out that we do have certain resources in this country, that we had better quit playing around and make sure that we use them. I told some of my young people who are smart at developing things that they would be able to get a grant for development of solar energy, but when I sent them all the information they found that without a "gross" of half a million there was no point in even applying for a grant. Mr. Speaker, development in this country will come as a result of innovations by young people with knowledge of these subjects, not from companies of size. Let us begin doing the things we can do best, and develop skills and resources internationally, particularly in mining and forestry because those industries could employ a lot of people.
