speechtext: Order, please. At six o'clock the hon. member for Cochrane (Mr. Stewart) had the floor.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first I would like to join with those who spoke before me in congratulating the mover and seconder in this debate. In particular I would like to underline the important contribution made by the hon. member for York South (Mrs. Appolloni) and her courage in expressing her opinion regarding respect for the lives of the unborn. I agree with her stand and I congratulate her.
The main concern in our country today is the economy. Reasons for the difficulty facing us are many and varied, but there is no doubt that work loss caused by strikes and so-called working to rule must bear a good share of the blame. We have seen what has happened in England and in Italy as a result of frequent work stoppages. Surely no loyal Canadian can wish for the same thing here.
In August the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said that Canadians are fed up with the nonsense going on in the Post Office. I can say without a doubt that my constituents are fed up and, indeed, so are many, many others who have spoken to me on this subject. In fact, the attitude of many Canadians is "fire the bastards"! While I can understand this kind of frustration, I do not personally advocate mass suspension; but it is obvious to me that a much tougher stand has to be taken, and this stand must extend to all essential services.
I do not know who coined the phrase "the right to strike". How can it be called a right to disrupt a country? Some people refer to the right to strike in the same way they talk about the right to free speech and the right to freedom of expression. The term I prefer to use is the "option to strike," and I say there should be no such option, at least in essential services.
1 think an analogy can be made between a strike and a declaration of war, because in both cases they are a last resort when everything else has failed. In addition, they both create a great deal of disruption, one destroying the physical environment and the other creating havoc within the economy.
I have always felt that a strike should be the very last resort, but in recent years it has become far less than that and is used even as a tool for arbitration. Obviously, something had to be done to change the present system because it simply does not work.
Perhaps strikes have become outmoded. Perhaps they should be set aside in favour of some other means of settling labour disputes. Indeed, the prominent American labour leader, George Meany, said a few years ago that strikes no longer served the purpose they had in the past and were becoming obsolete. It is abundantly clear to me that strikes serve no useful purpose when regarded in the over-all context of the disruption that is created in our country as a result. If we do not go as far as doing away with strikes entirely, the least this
October 16, 1978

parliament can do, if it is to act responsibly, is to legislate against strikes within the public service and in other essential services to Canadians.
When a strike or walk-out causes a necessary industry or service to grind to a halt, the public indicates its displeasure. However, too often the degree of their disgust is strictly proportional to their own discomfort or loss. Too few citizens think or feel beyond their momentary personal or family inconvenience.
The average resident of Montreal or Winnipeg, for example, fails to realize how much more terrible an interruption of rail-ferry service becomes for the people of Prince Edward Island, Newfoundland or Vancouver Island than for himself. If he lives in Nova Scotia or Alberta, he may not think about how interruption of air freight in the Northwest Territories or to the isolated settlements of James Bay and Hudson Bay may threaten the health and the very lives of those in the hinterlands.
The householder of Saskatoon and Fredericton does not get terribly upset if the sanitation work forces of Hamilton stay at home so that garbage piles into hills while flies and rats hold festival. If he lives in Toronto, suspension of electric or gas service to Hull, Quebec or Vancouver is not nearly as despicable a thing as the same thing happening in his own city. What is it to Mr. Average Citizen in Charlottetown or Victoria if a strike of telephone operators cuts off emergency messages to doctors, hospitals, ambulances, firefighters or police in North Bay or Windsor? Does it matter if a business in St. John's or another in Calgary is forced to close its doors and send its employees home because a postal strike has suspended transmission or sortation of mail?
If the significance of an industrial dispute weakens with its distance from home base, one should not be surprised that remoteness in economic terms is even less well realized. Interruption of stevedores' work in Thunder Bay or pilots' duties on the St. Lawrence seaway may cause grain to choke elevators and pile up on farms. Beyond that it may wreck an international agreement with Great Britain or China, or it may even bring hunger closer to helpless millions on the other side of the world.
Every disruption of utility or production line inevitably and inescapably raises the cost of goods and services throughout the whole market area, usually beyond that area, and prices rise with costs. Reduction or disappearance of income in any segment of the economy results in the slowing of business, an increase in unemployment, the disappearance of profits which would otherwise be available for investment in expansion of existing enterprises or the founding of new ones. New cost burdens are thrown on the welfare apparatus of municipal, provincial and federal governments, forthwith translated into bigger levies upon every taxpayer. The strike to obtain higher wages simultaneously and inevitably is accompanied by higher costs and higher taxes, leading to the next round of demands and strikes.
The Address-Mr. R. Stewart
Are we in Canada waiting for a general strike which strangles the entire population before doing something about it? Are we to endure forever this pattern of big or little blows, of short or prolonged agonies? Are we to endure everyone facing another work stoppage? Are we to endure some new example of injustice hitting first one group of workers, then some employers, then whole communities of consumers, and even the entire nation?
Most Canadians would agree that when a nationwide strike cuts a service from the Atlantic to the Pacific, the government has to step in. Indeed, any hesitancy on our part would be regarded as weakness by the majority of Canadians. Quite aside from the widespread hardship for the whole population which may be imposed by a work stoppage in a vital industry or service, also the following should be considered. It is ridiculous that the practice should have grown up in this country of meeting the more serious crises by the adoption of special legislation put before a specially convened session of parliament or legislature. Surely it should be beneath the dignity and reputation of a sovereign state that the parliament of Canada should be summoned to end a railway strike or an air controllers strike; that the legislature of the province of Quebec should be convened to get teachers and public servants back to work or the government of the province of Ontario should end a transportation paralysis. Laws should provide a structure within which foreseeable disputes can be settled in a just and orderly manner; they should not be improvised to meet sudden emergency.
The laws of the modern state may not yet give adequate support to unions seeking to fulfil their functions under such conditions, but constantly they are being improved as experience accumulates and as a clearer concept of social justice is achieved. Present standards have not been reached easily. Unions look back upon a history of struggle against odds. However, unions are long passed the stage when they should feel threatened, harassed or unprotected. Now they are part of the establishment, whether they wish to admit it or not. They are not government and should never be permitted to act as if they were.
The state is the instrument which serves the entire society. The whole society must guard jealously against being used by non-political powers, wealth, labour unions or pressure groups based on religion, sex, race, ancestry, professionalism, education, or by the idle, the criminal and the violent. The point is that unions are no longer oppressed but are a part of the estblishment. They can even look down on the non-union labour in some instances. In the over-all picture the only group that is sacrosanct is the whole of society, for whom the political state must be able to speak and act.
It follows then that the state must limit the powers of the corporations so that its citizens may remain politically free. Similarly, it must limit the power of worker organizations to whom some of these citizens belong. No class or group within our nation should be in a position from which it can hold the whole population or large segments of it to ransom. Unions

October 16, 1978
The Address-Mr. R. Stewart
must be controlled for precisely the same reasons that corporate entities within society must be controlled-so that they may not obtain a stranglehold upon the political organism which alone must think, speak and act for all.
Those who find their jobs eliminated by the cessation of essential operations, who find their costs skyrocketing as efficient industrial and merchant activities are halted, and those who find health and education threatened for themselves, their families and neighbours by disputes utterly beyond their control, can find protection only in their instrument and servant- the state or government. Unemployment, reduction of food supplies, a halt in the building of homes, are just as painful if they result from union action or are imposed by slum landlords or corporations.
If we were looking for a place to lay the blame for labour problems, one could blame the government, management or unions. Regardless of whose fault it is, the important thing is to find a solution, one which is better than what we have at present. I believe the solution is known and it can be imposed justly. The way to impose it is through the control of law. On this matter I wish to quote Abraham Lincoln as follows:
The reign of law and the maintenance of the machinery for the administration of justice, inadequate as they are, are man's only possible defence against the reign of violence, tyranny and unqualified injustice. Without these the weak man and society as a whole become prey to the unscrupulous and the strong; the individual becomes the victim of the mob.
I repeat, the rule of law is the only way to a solution. There is scarcely any activity of men and women in society which is not brought within the scope of law. Whether it be the quality of food or clothing bought for the family, a commercial form of recreation, the manufacture, sale and purchase of vehicles, all aspects of housing or the production of utilities, all are within the ambit of law.
Codes set standards of health and working conditions, outlaw discrimination, provide a structure of rights for unions and their members, establish obligations for employers, set out procedures for negotiation and conciliation. But strangely when it comes to strike action, the one form of action which affects every man, woman and child in a multitude of ways, it substitutes anarchy for order and actually legalizes a form of blackmail aimed at employers, fellow workers, the state and the whole of society; it is left completely open-ended.
Outside of criminals, it is difficult to think of any segment of society which is not brought under the control of law. It seems odd that whenever we discover leaks in the structure of protective law, such as juries or other public bodies, an attempt is made to plug the leak. But in the case of strikes, it seems that society simply stumbles on from one strike crisis to another.
At the beginning of my remarks I indicated that all strikes should be brought within the rule of law in the same way as other activities which affect society. But all strikes are not equal in importance and a least those which affect society seriously should be brought under the law. To categorize that which is an essential service is relatively easy. They include all industries and services, the uninterrupted maintenance of

which has become essential to the survival of the modern western community. Those industries and services which are categorized by law as being essential to society would not be permitted to strike.
Compulsory arbitration may be anathema to all orthodox unionists. But since the existing methods have not worked, it is time that we choose this course and stick by it. The fact is that our society has continued to take great risks in permitting services and industries, which are vital to survival, to be interrupted time after time, while the dangers and costs of interruption multiply.
It is immaterial whether the fault lies with the employer, the employee or the government. The time has come to call a halt to disruption. No one should be compelled to work in essential occupations, but if one prefers to do so one must forgo the option to strike in return for compensations guaranteed by law and administered by arbitration courts which are as far above influence and interests as are the skilled courts of criminal jurisdiction.
It deserves to be repeated that while social action of this sort may have a shock effect, it is really not sudden or revolutionary. We have been moving gradually along a straight path for many years. That path has had to be cleared of trees and underbrush like any other pioneer road in new country. The route has had to be explored and blazed before it could be cleared. But it has been apparent to any discerning eye that the path is marked "Law" with a capital "L" and that the destination point is "Justice" with a capital "J".
For labour peace and social order the price which unions in the essential services must pay is the relinquishment of the so-called right to strike. The price which management must pay is a levelling up of compensation, not only in dollar terms but in guarantees of job security. Both labour and management must learn to live with compulsory arbitration as the seal of the customary processes of negotiation, conciliation, mediation and procedural rules. All elements, including society, will be rewarded by escaping the incalculable costs and the ever-threatening hazard of periodic interruption of production and distribution.
Other reforms must follow and I should like to mention some of them briefly. One is mobility of labour. If a large and important class of workers is to be deprived of its major escape valve, job security alone is not sufficient compensation. It must also have improved opportunity to move into different types of work. Some of this mobility is already in place and is facilitated by such things as retraining programs, employment finding organizations and by means of the payment of costs of moving to new occupations. Such programs must be sufficient so that a worker feels confident of being made mobile.
The second pathway to be brushed and paved follows as a corollary to the first. A worker moving from one job to another must be assured of the portability of his pension rights, whether he moves into a new type of work or into another
October 16, 1978

province. Considerable progress has taken place in Canada already but the provinces which have not acted must do so to assure the maintenance of full pension rights.
It is time that new methods be put into practice for the settlement of labour-management relations. I contend that to strike is not the God-given right that some people advocate. If society suffers to the extent that it has in some countries, let us learn from the mistakes of others and establish a system of arbitration which will obviate work stoppages in the future. There may be circumstances in which the strike weapon is a legitimate one, but others in which its use is a crime. In the case of essential services, such as the postal service, it is a crime and should be treated accordingly.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the outset, of course, I want to congratulate the hon. members for York South (Mrs. Appolloni) and Verdun (Mr. Savard), respectively the mover and seconder of this Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne. They have done an admirable job under difficult circumstances I would say, sir. I also wish, as other members have done, to pay very sincere tribute to His Excellency the Governor General and his good wife who have carried out, with such distinction and warmth, their responsibilities during their term of office.
This particular Speech from the Throne was almost obsolete, I would suggest with deference, about 30 minutes after its release. Talk about a sense of deja vu; this particular one in its antecedents and in its premises simply cries out for non-acceptance and for scepticism. It does little to meet the challenges of our country. It does little to meet the needs of our country. Nor does it signal the end of the posturing and the economic failure of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau).
I was very interested in the remarks of my friend who just spoke. He castigated big labour, he castigated big business, but he ignored the biggest villain of all in this country at the present time, and that is big government; a government which has failed so signally to protect its citizens from the excesses of either big labour or big business. It is obvious that the Prime Minister in his visit to Bonn, Washington and other places did not really learn anything as far as the need for a different posture in his approach to leading this country is concerned.
He and his cabinet should refer to a very interesting book written by a former secretary of the treasury of the United States, Mr. William Simon, called "A Time for Truth". Mr. Simon points out that the reason for discussing economic issues is not to inspire a national passion for bookkeeping, but to inspire a national awareness of the connection between economic and political freedom. The connection is real and it is unbreakable, and to lose one is to lose the other.
In this country that is exactly what is happening to a government that favours manipulation and intervention. They are creating economic alternatives which are practically inescapable. Such government can confiscate, it can redistribute what is confiscated, it can spend more than it possesses, but there is one thing it cannot do, and that is produce wealth. That is what this government has not yet learned. It has not
The Address-Mr. MacKay
yet learned that the productive partner in our society is the private sector.
The government has maintained, belatedly, that the private sector does have some responsibilities, and the private sector does have the capacity to produce wealth and to spark a recovery in this country. But the economic climate that has developed under the Prime Minister and his cohorts, a climate which is so terrible and has resulted in such unprecedented high interest rates and deficits, is one which discourages and not encourages the private sector, which this country and this government belatedly is now depending on to right the harm it has done over the last ten years.
The cutting of taxes and the untangling of red tape is absolutely essential if we are to make any progress. One possible answer lies in the theory of potential budgeting. That is one possible answer to these difficulties. Governments must rearrange their priorities. They must consider the necessity in some cases of spending money in order to make money. The difficulty is, this government has been spending money for all the wrong reasons. There is a big difference between buying a Cadillac and buying a dump truck. With one you can make money and deliver something of value. With the other you can drive around, perhaps back and forth to the House of Commons or to your place of business, but that really does not do very much for the economy, unless you are pushing a consumer economy and trying to consume energy.
You can spend money wisely to make money. You can reduce taxes and get more revenues as a result. President Kennedy proved this when he, over the objections of many of his financial people, reduced taxes in the United States by approximately $10 billion and was rewarded by almost double that in increased revenue.
The Chancellor of Germany, Ludwig Erhard, quickly realized after the last war that if you reduce taxes to an acceptable level it will produce an unprecedented response from the people. Andrew Mellon did the same thing in the 1920s in the United States. This government is absolutely incapable of recognizing that it is taxing our people right into the ground. This government does not even have much interest in indexing the capital gains tax, or experimenting with any of the equity that is possible when taking a look at our tax system. All this government can do is have a Pavlovian response when someone on this side of the House puts forward some positive theories in this regard.
It is very amusing to see what happens when the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) try to counter the criticism. I think sometimes that the Prime Minister must be a bit of a baseball player. He is leaving his Minister of Finance in the House of Commons under considerable fire from the heavy hitters and the arbitragists in the financial centres of the world while that gentleman throws his verbal knuckle balls around the House of Commons and gets wracked up and our poor economy sinks lower and lower, just like the batting averages of some players in the World Series. I

October 16, 1978
The Address-Mr. MacKay
would not want to try to negotiate next year's salary on the batting averages in the economic league of either the Prime Minister or the Minister of Finance. The only thing we can be thankful for is that he is not a playing coach and tried to assume the portfolio himself; otherwise we would probably be even worse off.
The concerns of this country, as reflected from the part of Canada that I come from, are growing steadily more pronounced. We have not seen anything constructive being done to cure our transportation inequities, and we have not seen any responsible capital intensive projects of a major nature to help us. Little has been said about a corridor road, although Maine, an idea which has been brought up from time to time-it has been brought up, in order to be fair, by members on the other side as well-a road which would, by its very nature, cut a couple of hundred miles off the journey and greatly improve our accessibility to markets in central Canada. Such a road could be built in partnership with our friends in the United States and do a great deal to help our economy and to straighten out inequities in a very practical way.
We should have had a far greater and more gracious acceptance of our historic rights for our offshore resources than we have had. Under some prodding the government finally conceded that Nova Scotia could have three-quarters, subject to certain of their own claims coming off the top. This is absolute nonsense and a denial of the rights and the traditions of Atlantic Canada.
For example, the province of Newfoundland is a province that has the capability, right, capacity and historic claim to its offshore resources. This government, however, will not even concede that, subject to the powers of the National Energy Board, national energy policy, environmental standards within a federal jurisdiction, the province of Newfoundland has the right to proceed on its own level to develop and exploit these resources, knowing full well that that province, as my own province of Nova Scotia, can handle this development far better than a centralist government. To make matters even worse, the government does not appear to be willing to apply customs and immigration and other federal statutes to the point where it is protecting the rights of Newfoundlanders, against off-shore drilling, particularly at this time, for the benefit of inshore workers and producers of local products. It is nothing less than a disgrace.
As far as the fishing industry is concerned in Atlantic Canada, time after time the member for South Shore (Mr. Crouse) has pointed out to this government the ludicrousness of its policies, the inequity of its quotas, the fallacies of the ICNAF arrangement, and that hundreds of thousands of tons of the very best fish in the world are being dumped by fishing captains to avoid these silly laws. The government has refused to listen to the hon. member despite the fact that he is one of the few members in this House who has the practical experience to back up what he is saying. He has actually operated a fishing fleet and therefore knows of what he speaks; but these people opposite still do not listen.

Regional disparity in the past has been a buzz word with this government. In some of the Speeches from the Throne in the not too distant past, it has been said that there is no higher priority than solving regional disparity. Well, Mr. Speaker, one would never know that. As the failure to solve regional disparities becomes more and more manifest, so does the mention of its continuing support become less and less obvious in successive Speeches from the Throne. Right now we have energy costs that are almost prohibitive for any industry that would seek to establish itself there, yet this government up to this point has not been willing to press ahead with any meaningful, large capital cost projects that would see as their objective the solving of this problem by making it possible to take in electrical energy from parts of Canada where it is available by means of a national power grid.
This government has commissioned yet another study of Fundy tidal power. I do not know how many studies we have had, but it is good business for the consultants and that is about all. That is another sore point, consultants. For the money this government spends on consultants, we could probably fuel an economic recovery in at least one of the Atlantic provinces on that expenditure alone, which sometimes has approached $1 billion on an average over the last few years. This government absolutely refuses to spend its money and marshal its priorities in a way that is good for the country.
The Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) is an interesting man for he is practically a one-man cabinet. He is minister in charge of the Wheat Board, Minister of Justice and Minister of Transport. The people of Canada have not seen an act like that since Harpo, Groucho and Chico Marx, and he has done it all by himself, just he and his JetStar. The Minister of Transport and his departmental associates have paid out, for example, over $1.5 million, as evidenced in a belated answer I received to a question on the order paper that is over a year old, to consultants, Phillip Binehaker and his group and a well known Toronto law firm, for some work having to do with the Pickering airport.
They are still beavering away at this project, despite the fact that the government of Ontario and the people of Toronto have indicated that they do not want another Mirabel, a monstrosity that not only is an economic drain, having run up a deficit since it opened at the average of approximately $40 million a year, and which is an international model of how not to build an airport. This may result in the closing down and curtailing of a perfectly good airport in Montreal which continues to make money. That kind of use of our tax revenues and how to get value for money spent is what is causing a great deal of the difficulty in the past ten years in those areas of the country where there is a real need for sound infrastructures. Such examples as the corridor road, the development of minerals offshore and improvements that are required in our fishing industry are only a few of the projects that could have been funded.
The government, despite pleading from their own members as well as members on this side, has steadily refused to provide even the most rudimentary of amenities to the fishing industry,
October 16, 1978

as the hon. member for South Shore I am sure will agree. They could in a few of the communities around our coastlines put in a few slipways, a few lights on the wharves, a few things to hoist heavy crates off boats, and this would do a tremendous amount.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: A little more dredging.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Yes, a little more dredging. That is another story-the millions and millions of dollars over the years that were wasted on dredging. We wonder if the dredging in some cases was ever done, but that matter is being proceeded within the courts, and perhaps some day we will have the answers.
There is no point in going on ad nauseam about examples of government waste, but the refusal of the government to come to grips or even to admit that this is occurring is a reason for the tremendous animosity that is building up, not just toward unions and business, as my friend from Cochrane (Mr. Stewart) said, but toward the government itself.
The Minister of Public Works (Mr. Buchanan) said today in the House that he is quite satisfied with the report of the standing committee on finance in the other place, as if that report justified and vindicated the things that his department was doing. He must be either so unaware of the practical realities or so regimented that he does not understand what is going on in his own department. Let me put on record some of the statements made before the committee which took a look at the Les Terrasses de la Chaudiere project, which is only one of many projects that one could choose. Page 90 of the Senate report states that the Department of Public Works-
-with the approval of the Treasury Board, failed to observe precautions taken as a regular course in all other projects for the acquisition of space... The committee's inquiry into the details brought out evidence that these agreements have committed DPW to pay rates for the space involved well beyond the prevailing private sector level.
It states also on page 89:
The committee's inquiry into the details of the four lease-purchase agreements made in the Ottawa-Hull area brought out evidence that these agreements have committed Public Works to paying rates for this space well beyond the prevailing private sector level. The two agreements for the buildings in Hull have brought the department's judgment into question in parliament and the press. In entering into them the department, with the approval of the Treasury Board, failed to observe precautions taken as a regular course in all other projects for the acquisition of space. No tenders were called and proposals made by the owners for space not yet in existence were accepted.
If that kind of commentary can be interpreted as a vote of confidence in a department, then there must be a new standard of acceptance.
As far as matters of security are concerned, the government has again failed to be honest with the people; they have failed over the years and months to answer a very simple, rudimentary question about what they intend to do with this iniquitous section 41(2) of the Federal Court Act. This section has become so infamous that it really does sanction executive privilege without judicial review in this country. Sum it up anyway you like, that is the bottom line. Any country that would allow a statute like that to remain on its statute books in
The Address-Mr. MacKay
times like these, having consulted and been in touch with the attorneys general of the provinces, as the former minister of justice indicated to me in this chamber that he had, and without making some modification to it, has got to be extremely unrealistic and insensitive.
This government has not lived up to its responsibilities in the way that the Canadian people have a right to expect. Rather, it has shilly-shallied, delayed and asked people to have confidence. What the government is really saying is, "Let us be your confidence men." There is no reason why they should extend this parliament-if they had any confidence in themselves. If they had real confidence they would have called an election. The fact that we are in this chamber at this time indicates their tremendous lack of confidence in themselves.
How can the people of Canada extend to this Prime Minister that which he appears to want more than anything else-a mandate to change our constitution? Supposing someone hired the Prime Minister to run a large business-and I do not think many people would-and then over the last few years the corporation had systematically fallen into a deficit position- had lost large markets, good will, its credit rating had been damaged, its retained earnings depleted. In other words, it had been weakened to the point that its stock in the business community was in the same state as our dollar is in the international community. Then he came up with the great idea of radically changing the way of doing business. He proposed to computerize everything, change the distribution methods, turn the thing upside down and make a lot of money, saying, "I want you to have faith in me." If he had done a good job during the past ten years and had increased the retained earnings, held his own in a challenging market and demonstrated a grasp of practical realities, then I think one would be justified in saying, "It sounds unorthodox and it is untried, but based on your past record, we have confidence and we will authorize you to take us into these uncharted waters."
I can see you doing that, Mr. Speaker, because you are logical, reasonable and an admirable individual, but I cannot see our permitting anyone with his record to do anything further, he having demonstrated his incompetence under the present set-up. Yet that basically is what the Prime Minister is asking the people of Canada to do.
His reach for constitutional reform is frustrated by his lack of grasp of practical realities. That is the greatest frustration that I think the Prime Minister and this government will have to face. They have failed miserably in their stated objective of reducing regional disparity and of bringing us a more open society. They have even welched on the solemn commitment to do something about the War Measures Act. I believe the anniversary of that infamous occasion is today. A solemn commitment was made that it would be discussed in this House and steps taken to do away with it, but as usual nothing has come of it. Yet the Prime Minister and his government are asking the people of Canada and members of this place to trust them to lead us into uncharted waters and change the very basis, in many respects, of our constitution.

October 16, 1978
The Address-Mr. Lee
If the government wanted to do something constructive and work with the other place, they should take one step at a time. First of all, they could make the Senate an elected body and no one would quarrel with that. At one time the United States Senate was an appointed body but it ran into difficulties in the early part of this century. It is now a very admirable institution and I suspect part of the reason is that it has become an elected body.
I sincerely hope that in the few months left in this parliament the government will bring forward some concrete legislation which will be handled with dispatch. We on this side would be pleased to do that. Mention was made today of the Bank Act which needs to be reviewed and I think the government and the Prime Minister would find us very co-operative in that regard.
Many other things need to be done, such as tax reform. Let us experiment a little with reducing or at least indexing some of the capital gains taxes which are the noxious glue gumming up the wheels of free enterprise in this country. We cannot afford a capital gains tax in this country. Anyone who has examined it can see that it is a regressive tax which stops people from taking a chance and doing things which they could do with a more reasonable approach to taxation.
The government could recognize that many people who purchase stocks in Canadian companies wish to provide for their retirement or to educate their children and should deal with them differently from the speculators who deal in nonCanadian securities. Instead of that, the Prime Minister, as he clings to office for the last few months, is going to continue to be obsessed by his constitutional pretentions. As far as I can see he has never demonstrated that he is particularly qualified for this task. Certainly some of his colleagues and some distinguished senators from his party have been most savage in their criticism of what he is attempting to do.
I would hope that his proven lack of capacity to lead this country along the road to success and prosperity which some of his own predecessors in his party who held the highest office predicted for us will be a strong warning, a red flag and all the other warnings that are necessary to the people of this country and members of this place so that they will not permit him, of all people to vary our constitution. Let us wait until we have a new parliament, a new leader, a new prime minister; let us wait until the present cabinet, which, as someone said, is probably the largest collection of pygmies outside the Belgian Congo, has had to go to the people and try to get another mandate. Let us then talk about making changes to this constitution of ours.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would first like to extend my sincere congratulations to the mover and seconder of the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne. Having had the distinct honour and privilege of doing so myself, I know how proud their constituents must feel in

having their members move and second the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne. It is a privilege not only in recognition of the hon. member for York South (Mrs. Appol-loni) and the hon. member for Verdun (Mr. Savard) of their own particular talents and capabilities. It is a distinct recognition of the particular constituencies and people they have the honour to represent in the House of Commons.
I also extend greetings on behalf of my constituents to His Excellency the Governor General and his wife on the excellent Speech from the Throne. I wish him well. I hope he will be able to continue in his portfolio and that we will not be seeing the end of the fine work he has done in serving Canada over the past few years.
It was very interesting to listen to the speeches delivered last Thursday by the leaders of the various political parties. I listened very attentively to the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark), the leader of the New Democratic Party the spokesman on behalf of the Social Credit party and, of course, the leader of our party, the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau).
There is no question that the Prime Minister did an excellent job. It showed this country and those in this House that he is truly a leader of distinction. He showed in which direction this country should go. The economic program and the discussion about the constitution and national unity were excellent. His speech really hit the nerve of what Canadians want to hear.
The speech by the Leader of the Opposition was rather interesting. He raised the spectre of many old scandals about which we have heard off and on over the past few years. All the opposition wants to do is talk about scandals.
We in this country have a unique and sound tradition with regard to our judicial system, how it is thought of and how we approach it. A person is always thought to be innocent until proven guilty. The Leader of the Opposition raised the old problem of Sky Shops and Senator Giguere. He stood trial and was cleared, yet the Leader of the Opposition raised the matter again. I sat in amazement. These people talk about our very fine traditions and what is fair. However, in his speech the Leader of the Opposition did not once mention that Senator Giguere had been cleared.
The Leader of the Opposition talked about the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. As Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General, I had first-hand experience with the way the opposition attacked the government on this matter. They talked at great length about the need for a royal commission and the rightness of the Keable commission in the province of Quebec. When evidence brought forward showed there was need for a royal commission, one was established. During the fall and summer the opposition attacked the government, saying that all it had done was create a royal commission to cover up and that it was not going to do the job. They even questioned the appointment of the head of that commission, Justice McDonald, a very fine person.
October 16, 1978

The opposition has attacked the government with regard to the independence of the judiciary. I recall the so-called alleged judges affair. There they attacked the independence of a member of the judiciary, Justice McDonald of the Supreme Court of Alberta. I really wonder about the duplicity of the kinds of arguments raised by the official opposition. They must realize that once a person is appointed to the judiciary, we have to respect him as an independent person.
During the alleged judges affair, there was lecture upon lecture and question after question in question period about how the government was upsetting the independence of the judiciary, tampering with their integrity and the principle of independence of the judiciary. The official opposition keeps coming down on one side of an issue and then on the other, as it suits them.
The whole issue of the RCMP is an excellent point. It is a very fine institution in this country, well respected in Canada and throughout the world. The opposition soon found that the people in this country were asking what they, the opposition, were doing. They were told that they could not win elections and gain power by riding on the backs of the RCMP. Canadians were telling them to cool off.
For the last while, the opposition have not been attacking the RCMP. I think the opposition found that by attacking that institution they were attacking the men and women who make up the RCMP, some very fine people. I have had the opportunity of meeting members of the RCMP in the smaller communities in my province, the Northwest Territories and the Yukon. They not only perform the duties of the police force but become involved in the community. One often finds the local constable directly involved in community affairs by acting as coach of the local baseball or hockey team. They help to solve the serious problems of juvenile delinquency in the communities. They are involved in diverse programs. This is what the opposition members faced when they returned home.
By attacking this very fine institution, the opposition found they were attacking the people. When they were told they were not going to be elected by attacking the RCMP, they backed off. We have not heard much complaint about the RCMP from the opposition recently.
We have heard about any number of scandals from the official opposition in the four years I have been here. The hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay) said that the government could put forward a big economic program if it tallied up all the dollars that have been spent on consultants. At the same time the opposition complains that the government does not listen enough to outside people, that it listens too much to the civil servants.
The Leader of the Opposition complained about the so-called elite in the Prime Minister's office running this country. I wish the opposition would make up their minds. Which side are they on? Are they saying the government should not listen to anyone other than civil servants? There are many good deputy ministers who are advising the government. Are they saying we should not have outside consultants, people
The Address-Mr. Lee
who are expert in their field and close to the regions or specific problems they are asked to deal with?
On one hand the Leader of the Opposition says that all we have is a group of elitists in the Prime Minister's office who are running the country. I really do not understand this. The opposition comes down on one side of an issue and then within a month, week, day or even an hour comes down on the other side.
This is the party which hopes to replace us in leading and governing this country, but I certainly do not think it will. We hear members of the official opposition complaining about the restraint program announced by the government in August and discussed in great detail in the Speech from the Throne. They say it is not a real program but just cynical politics to gain votes, yet I have heard a number of opposition members who represent constituencies in my province complaining about some of the cuts. I have heard them complain about how the cuts will affect the province of British Columbia. They have complained about cuts with respect to weather ships. I have heard opposition members from the Atlantic provinces complaining about cuts which will affect weather reports there. In my own city I have heard opposition members complaining about the cuts because they will affect federal programs, particularly public works projects. There will be cutbacks with respect to the federal government building which is planned to be built in the federal riding of Vancouver Centre. These are the same people who talk about cynicism and about the government restraint program not being a real program, yet they ask why we are cutting this and that.
We talk about tightening up unemployment insurance, and hon. members opposite ask why. 1 remember that they often used to complain that it was too generous, but now we are cutting back. Perhaps we were too generous, so now we are trying to divert some of those funds to job creation programs. In this regard members of the official opposition and of the New Democratic Party complain that we are being too tough.
I think that the government's program boils down to three R's, restraint, reallocation and renewal. Restraint means even tighter controls on government spending. We have slashed $500 million from current expenditures while slicing another $2 billion from next year's budget. As well as making government leaner and more efficient, our belt-tightening exercise will leave more resources with the private sector for job creation.
This is exactly what the hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay) was talking about. He says we are not leaving enough to private enterprise not allowing private enterprise to produce. He says that private enterprise is the one sector which truly generates wealth and that we should allow it a little more freedom. The hon. member talked about indexing the capital gains tax. Why not examine the possibility of eliminating the tax entirely? Why even talk about the question of indexation? Why not examine the recommendation of the Bryce commission which talked about the elimination of the

October 16, 1978
The Address-Mr. Lee
capital gains tax? Hon. members opposite like to tinker around. They like to be on the one side as well as the other. Perhaps they should decide whether they do want elimination of the capital gains tax.
The second of the three Rs of the federal government program is reallocation. Within our reduced budget we are taking away $1 billion from certain departments and programs in order to spend it where the present need is greatest. I think this will mean more jobs for the unemployed, more help for elderly Canadians with low incomes, more help for low and middle-income families with children and a faster growing economy.
The government's economic package does not signal a radical departure from previous policies. I think it has been labelled by members of the official opposition and by some members of the media as a deathbed conversion.
At a convention of my own party I once delivered a speech about restraint, and I can see that since 1975 the government has followed a program of restraint. It has limited increases in government expenditures to a level below the rate of growth of the gross national product. In the same period we have fought inflation in order to cushion the most vulnerable of our citizens against the ravages of inflation. Finally, we have given a high priority to economic growth and the creation of jobs for our young people. What cutback and reallocations really represent is a strengthening of existing programs and a reaffirmation of our long-standing goals.
I listened with great attentiveness to the hon. member for Central Nova when he spoke about turning everything back to free enterprise. I do not think we have really had free enterprise in this country, unless the free enterprise about which members of the official opposition are talking is the free enterprise of the days of the robber barons or the Carnegies. 1 do not think I particularly want to return to that era. In that era free enterprise did not really care about the working people. Working people did not have pensions or health plans. When people were unemployed, there was no such thing ar unemployment insurance.
This is the kind of thing which leads me to think that members of the official opposition want to throw out the baby with the bath water. They want to turn to the old, free-style free enterprise where the needs of average working people are forgotten. Such needs are medicare, unemployment insurance and the job-creation programs which this government has undertaken and, 1 think, very effectively. I do not know what members of the opposition are attacking when they ask for more cutbacks and more restraint. I think if we were to do things the way they want us to, we would throw the country into a tailspin and cause a recession the likes of which this country has never seen.
Members of the official opposition talk about redistribution of income. They talk about their mortgage plan. I must agree that the principle behind the plan is not bad, but judging by the way the hon. members opposite are talking about it, the program would be ludicrous. I come from a working man's riding, and I do not see anything in the plan to help working

people. Many people in my riding are renters. The program would do nothing to help them. How would it help people who rent? Should those people not be allowed to deduct something from their incomes? Should they not be allowed to deduct part of the payments they make to their landlords?
Because of the marginal rates and the effective rates in our Income Tax Act, those on higher level incomes usually receive a better advantage from any proposal which does not really take into account the effect of marginal and effective rates. That is why the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) announced changes to the family allowance and tax credit of S200 per child per year.
I remember reading about this in the Carter royal commission report as well as in the report of the Advisory Council to the Department of National Health and Welfare. The Carter commission and the advisory council were involved in the area of national welfare, and they advised the government that it should implement a tax credit program.
We do not find that in the program of the official opposition. It is very clear that the proposals of the official opposition would not help people on low and middle incomes. Those at the top who earn $50,000 and who have large mortgages would really be laughing, but the proposals of the official opposition would not help the average working Canadian. The mortgage interest deduction program has to be the greatest political gimmick I have ever seen.
1 remember explaining to some people in my riding the effect this program would have and how it would not really help them. They were quite amazed. They said, "Perhaps this is really an election gimmick". That is what many people really think when they study the proposal of the official opposition. There are many people in my riding who cannot afford down payments, and 1 do not think the program would help them.
In the process of trimming our budget and redistributing dollars it is clear that some very good programs will suffer. We do not like to cut back on those programs, but we should redirect our tax dollars to areas of the greatest need. We have no choice.
I have spoken about the family allowance. We are cutting it from approximately $25 per month to $20. I think that is a positive step, when we take into account the tax credit of $200 per child for those families which earn $18,000 or less. For those families which earn more than $18,000 the tax credit will not be as high. I think this is an excellent way to approach the matter. The approach should be to help those who really need help. If we are to use the family allowance program effectively in this time of restraint, we must reduce monthly payments to some families. The monthly cheques will still go out to every family with children, but in a reduced amount- $20 per month per child instead of the current $25.
The money saved by that reduction will finance a refundable tax credit of $200 a year for each child under the age of 18, in cases where the family income is below $18,000. Above
October 16, 1978

$18,000, the amount of the credit will diminish and gradually disappear in the high-income brackets. That credit will be paid to the mother of the family, effective January 1979, and it will be paid even in cases where the family pays no income tax. While the greatest benefit will go to the 1.5 million children who live in poor Canadian families, the tax credit will also provide greater assistance to middle-income families in caring for their children.
Our unemployment insurance measures tell the same story. We are reducing the benefits of the program and tightening up its administration. But with the money saved, we are offering enriched incentives to the private sector to create permanent jobs. Young people have trouble finding jobs because of their lack of experience; the federal government will now pay the cost of a $1.50 an hour wage subsidy to those employers willing to take a chance on hiring a young worker. We will also give a subsidy to business to train the workers it needs. We are aiming to have these measures in place before winter.
And we have other proposals, likewise aimed at combatting inflation, fostering economic growth, or improving the lot of needy Canadians. The old age pension supplement will rise by $20 per month per household from January, 1979. An additional $300 million has been alloted for industrial development. The federal excise tax on gasoline has been cut by three cents per gallon. Postal service will be improved by the Post Office's conversion into a Crown corporation. Taken together, these initiatives and announcements add up to a comprehensive agenda of economic and social action.
This brings me to the third R, renewal. Our economic program aims at something beyond more jobs, better social services and leaner government. Ultimately, we are seeking to establish a renewal, a strengthening of confidence in this country and its future.
Canada still has boundless potential in its natural resources, its skilled manpower and it growing industrial might. We also have a solid record of past economic performance. Whether the measurement is the rate of growth in employment, the number of new homes, or the increase in real disposable income, Canada comes out first among the western industrialized nations in over-all performance. Nothing but a lack of confidence can hold us back from economic recovery.
Spending restraint and the reallocation of existing resources are now fact. What remains is for Canadians everywhere, in their response to the government's new economic program, to display the renewed confidence which will allow them to achieve the future they deserve.
The other issue I would like to spend a few moments talking about concerns the area of constitutional change. During the summer, along with colleagues from all sides of the House I served on the special joint committee of the House and the Senate with respect to the constitutional proposals. 1 think it was a very interesting exercise and I think it is noteworthy that the committee was able to come down with what I think is a unanimous report in some aspects, shedding light on how it feels about constitutional change and constitutional proposals.
The Address-Mr. Lee
I listened to the hon. member from Central Nova saying there was no urgent need to change our constitution. Well, I think there is. I think we have to demonstrate to the people of this country that parliament is not going to stand by and maintain the status quo. 1 can see the hon. member across from me shaking his head. They keep on saying we are going about this the wrong way, that we should not just be making changes with respect to institutions but that we should also be talking about the division of powers.
The premier of my own province, British Columbia, delivered a speech last spring, in May of 1977, to the Canadian Men's Club in Vancouver. He said-and I believe my memory serves me correctly-that the two most important and urgent problems facing this country were the national economy and the question of constitutional reform. In that speech, Premier Bennett went on at great length to express the view that we did not really need wholesale changes affecting the division of powers; and what we need is a change in our institutions to ensure that the various regions within our country, and the west in particular, do have the power and the ability to influence what is going on within Canada by changing federal institutions. He agreed that maybe we should change the upper chamber as it is not really doing the job of properly reflecting regional interests and regional needs.
As for the particular proposal of the government with respect to the House of the Federation, which was tabled for discussion purposes only, I certainly do not think that proposal is that sound. But it started off a very good discussion on how we could change federal institutions to meet the needs of the west and of the Atlantic provices so that we would get away from this feeling of alienation, this feeling that there is too much power within central Canada.
That was certainly brought out by the people who spoke and testified before the committee and in particular by the representatives of the Canada West Foundation. I think they are a very articulate and good group headed up by Mr. Stanley Roberts, the former vice president of Simon Fraser University of my home province. What he was saying was: Yes, we realize that this government has in fact taken into account the various regional interests. Whether through appointments to various quasi-judicial bodies like the CRTC, the Canadian Transport Commission or administrative bodies, or with respect to appointments to the cabinet, we do take into account regional interest. But he was saying that it is the appearances that have to be changed and that institutions like the upper chamber really have to reflect truly regional interests within this country. He said after having attended a number of symposiums in major centres across western Canada-in Winnipeg, Banff, Calgary and Victoria-that most people did not like the concept of the House of the Federation in that members of various provincial governments, whether they be premiers or ministers or delegates of those governments, could come down to Ottawa and in effect block or veto legislation passed by the House of Commons, a body which is elected on the basis of a national mandate at each federal election.

October 16, 1978
The Address-Mr. McKenzie
This is exactly what the concept of the House of the Federation really amounts to. It is unacceptable that an upper chamber, particularly one made up of people who represent the various provinces could come here and block federal legislation passed by the House of Commons consisting of people who represent the will of this country. I think it was Professor Mcquinney, one of the witnesses who testified before the committee, who called it the "Bundestag caper". He said that provinces like the province of British Columbia were not really addressing themselves to the issue. He also pointed out that one of the constitutional courts in Germany held that the Bundestag really was not a bicameral house in a true federal state, that it was only an extension of the executive form of government.
I think the area in which we should work much more closely is that of having proper and full discussion at the first ministers level. Provincial governments are elected to represent provinces. The Prime Minister very adequately pointed out last Thursday that as the Prime Minister he is elected to represent the nation as a whole. That is the area upon which we should concentrate.
Some of the other witnesses who testified before the committee indicated that in times of war, at the end of war or in times of great need or emergency all the component parts of the constitution can be changed, whether it is the actual make-up of government or the division of powers. Many of the witnesses said that the government is taking the right approach by adopting a rather pragmatic approach to the entire issue of constitutional reform. It is dealing with the issues of institutional reform, the upper chamber, the constitution of Canada, the charter of human rights, and then seeking a consensus respecting the division of powers.
I see that my allotted time has expired.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity of entering into this debate. I am very disappointed that the debate has reached such a low level. Of course, this trend was commenced by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) last week when he used selective statistics and handed out false information.
The hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Lee) was respected on this side of the House, but this evening he has completely destroyed any respect members on this side had for him, especially after such a ridiculous speech. He touched upon Sky Shops as if it was a mischievous matter raised by the Conservative party. The Quebec government laid charges against four men. There have been court cases, and Senator Giguere has been acquitted, which acquittal is being appealed by the government of Quebec. If the hon. member thinks this man is making any contribution in the Senate, I advise him to look at Senate Hansard. In the ten years he has been a Senator, he has done absolutely nothing other than being involved in the Sky Shops matter. I will not defend anyone like that, and I do not know why the hon. member would.
There are three ongoing inquiries into the RCMP. They were not instigated by the Conservative party; they were instigated by other governments. Obviously there is something wrong when the hon. member indicates that the Royal Canadian Mounted Police are against us. Those statements are completely false.

I have many friends in the RCMP. I should like to tell the hon. member about the RCMP. Representatives of that force came to my home in 1968. They wondered what was happening in the country because the Liberal leader was to become the Prime Minister of Canada. They could see Trudeaumania occurring and they said, "What on earth is happening in this country? Is a man with that background going to become Prime Minister?" The RCMP has not forgotten that.
The hon. member for Vancouver East expressed concern about bringing expenditures into account. On February 7, 1978, we presented a motion in the House to review the entire government structure, to bring in sunset laws, and to make every government department justify their existence in order to conduct proper examinations and bring expenditures under control. I suggest the hon. member read the speeches in that debate. Every one of your members over there, including the NDP, ridiculed that debate. You are no more interested in bringing expenditures under control than flying to the moon. You are such an irresponsible group that you changed the rules in 1968.

speechtext: Order, please. I regret to interrupt the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. McKenzie) but I would suggest that he direct his comments to the Chair.
