speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I apologize for that. I will direct my comments through Your Honour. Of course we have no control over expenditures. This is due to legislation brought in by the Liberal government in 1968. At that time they stopped proper examination of government expenditures and reduced the role of parliament to the point where government estimates were not examined properly. This legislation was rammed through the House of Commons under closure by the Liberal government. My party did not support that particular motion.
Today we are in such a financial mess that the Auditor General has indicated that he cannot certify the accounts. This has resulted in the necessity for a Comptroller General, which will cost the Canadian taxpayers $6 million. That department will be set up in order to find out where the money is going, yet the hon. member for Vancouver East told us that the government is interested in controlling expenditures, as well as speaking other silly nonsense.
He mentioned the mortgage interest deductibility program. The manner in which that program has been criticized by the
[Mr. Lee.)
October 16, 1978

Prime Minister and other government members is very interesting. It is evident that we have come up with something good. A similar program is working in the United States and Great Britain. Why on earth cannot it work in Canada?
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) was out in Winnipeg making a series of irresponsible statements concerning the mortgage deductibility program. I should like to make a few comments regarding the financing of such a program. The minister indicated that the federal budget deficit was expected to reach $11 billion this year and perhaps go as high as $15 billion. He wondered how we could afford a new program at this time. We stated that a Progressive Conservative government would offset the cost of these major tax incentives by instituting a program of restraint to reduce current government spending.
On February 2, 1978, we raised this matter but it was opposed by the New Democratic Party. The privatization of Petro-Can will result in the sale of assets with a current book value of $900 million. Also that will result in an end to advances to Petro-Can which amount to $200 million a year.
Also we mentioned that there was no need for the Department of Urban Affairs. We are not backing down on that suggestion. That would result in a saving of another $20 million.
The Liberal government stated that the program made no provision for Canadians who are not home owners. Because mortgage interest and property taxes are deductible business expenses for landlords, renters already receive these benefits. The majority of Canadians aspire to owning their own home. We want to assist Canadians in buying their own home. Young married couples want to own their own home. They do not want to live in apartment complexes all their lives. The rich are able to buy homes. It is the low income earners who are unable to buy homes. Renting for many, especially the young, is viewed as a temporary condition until they can afford to purchase. This program will make the dreams of these renters come true. Renters should realize some spin-off benefit from the program.
As middle income Canadians encouraged by the tax deductions move into their own homes, the amount of rental accommodation will be increased, thus removing some of the pressure from renters. We have come up with a program that will be worked out with the provinces, though certainly some technical aspects will have to be worked out. It is a plan designed to help people purchase homes. The hon. member for Vancouver East has ridiculed this plan in his riding, yet he offered no alternative.
Also the Liberal government indicated that the program benefits only the rich. The tax proposals are not intended as a social program. Their primary purpose is to provide a major economic stimulus in order to get the Canadian economy going again at a satisfactory rate. From time to time we will outline more detail, but I have touched briefly upon the matter now.
We can obtain money in order to finance this program by a reduction of consulting and other contracts which have risen
The Address-Mr. McKenzie
by 650 per cent, or $1.4 billion a year. Canada has the benefit of having approximately half a million public servants who have some of the finest brains in the country. They are educated and have degrees, yet $1.4 billion a year is spent on outside consultants. This work could be done within the public service. Perhaps some highly specialized consulting work will have to be done by consultants outside the public service, but a lot of money can be saved in that area.
In the area of information and advertising, expenditures have increased by 100 per cent, or $180 million a year. I would suggest that propaganda would be a better term to describe this area. We do not need all this advertising. This is another area where we could find some money for the program.
During the 1975-77 period the administrative and other operating costs of the government increased by 45 per cent. If during that period the Trudeau government had lived by its own AIB guidelines, its own spending would have been $3 billion less in 1977. What on earth is this government doing with operating costs going up 45 per cent? Hon. members opposite stand here and tell us what brilliant administrators they are. If they are brilliant administrators the costs would not be increasing to the extent of 45 per cent.
A PC government will cut the waste and inefficiency from government operating costs without reducing efficient service to the public. If hon. members want to find out about waste and mismanagement I suggest they just read the Auditor General's reports. On and on this goes.
I am not going to read out our whole program tonight, but there is another point I want to make. The PC program of tax deductibility for mortgage interest and property taxes would be of particular benefit to the Canadian housing industry where unemployment is currently running at double the national average. Housing starts this year are running at 230,000 units, yet the Canadian house building industry has a proven capacity of producing at least 275,000 starts a year without significant pressure on housing prices. By stimulating demand to at least that proven capacity the PC program would generate 75,000 new jobs. What has that to do with a program for the rich?
Let me say to renters and everybody else in this country that unemployment here is costing Canadian taxpayers a great deal. Whether one lives in a home, rents or lives in a hotel, unemployment is costing $8 billion a year. I am quite sure that many renters would like to pay a lot less to welfare and UIC programs.
Members on the Liberal side have said that house prices would inevitably rise with our mortgage tax deductibility program. A colleague has just informed me that this mortgage deductibility program has been in effect in the United States for the last 40 years and the price for a house there is a lot less. Let me give an example. A Winnipeg home must have a basement and be properly built for a particular climate. The same home in North Dakota or Minnesota costs $10,000 to $20,000 less, and they have had this program in being for

October 16, 1978
The Address-Mr. McKenzie
years. But in this regard we have had absolute nonsense from the government side.
At the present time there are 70,000 unsold homes in Canada. Is that not some record? Have we heard one speech from the other side since last week saying what the Liberals are going to do about those 70,000 unsold homes? Some builders in my riding have held these unsold homes for a year or a year and a half. They are going bankrupt. Isn't that wonderful? What is this government going to do about it? I suggest it will do absolutely nothing. We have come up with a program; let us get it off the ground, get it going and do something.
As usual, the Liberal party is divided all over the place. I have an article here from Montreal which indicates that the Liberal candidate in Westmount likes this Tory policy. I understand there are two or three others in Toronto and one in St. Boniface who support the policy. Someone referred to the former mayor of Toronto in relation to housing. I recall that gentleman coming down here and appearing before a parliamentary committee in respect of housing and urban affairs. That is a man very concerned with housing and he appeared before this parliamentary committee with a lot of constructive ideas regarding housing. Thank God he is going to be here in this House to make his contribution in respect of housing in Canada.
At the commencement of my remarks I referred to the climate of the debate, and what a sorry thing it was that the Prime Minister is leading by giving us a lot of false statistics. It is incredible that the man in the number one position in Canada, the leader of the government and the country, would make a speech at this particular time using a lot of improper statistics.
This whole matter was covered very well by Don McGilliv-ray of Southam News Service. I have mentioned a lot of the false information being spread about our mortgage interest deductibility program. Let me read what Mr. McGillivray has said in reference to the Prime Minister's speech:
Trudeau is incredibly careless in the conclusions he draws from his numbers.
It is simply untrue to say, as he did, that "Canada, in terms of the employment growth rate, is the best in the world."
According to the statistical Yearbook of the United Nations, 15 countries had faster rates of employment growth between 1970 and 1975. Those were years when jobs were appearing in Canada faster than they have since, but Mauritius, Jordan, Malawi, Kenya, Turkey, Syria, South Korea, Malaysia, Yugoslavia, Romania, Spain, Swaziland, Tunisia, Fiji and Pakistan did better.
Since then, Canada's rate of job creation has failed behind other countries, including the U.S. Statistics published by the Paris-based Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development show that between 1975 and 1977 the U.S. created 6.4 per cent more jobs while Canada was creating only 4.2 per cent more.
How then, can the prime minister cite numbers to back his claim that we "still lead the world"? First, by restricting his "world" to 15 industrial countries and second, by mixing the slow recent rates of job creation with faster rates recorded before 1975.
Has Canada really done "immensely better" against inflation than most of the other industrialized countries?
For proof, Trudeau cited Figures for the period 1968-76. And 1976 was, of course, the year when food prices slumped and gave Canada a relatively good
year against inflation. Even so, Canada's performance was so-so, not immensely better.
More recent figures do not bear out the impression that we are doing better at all. The Economist, the British-based journal of business and current affairs, does a regular check on 10 "major economies" including Canada. This shows that eight of the 10-Australia, France, Germany, The Netherlands, Japan, Sweden, the U.S. and Britain-did better than Canada against inflation in the past year. Only Italy did worse.
The Prime Minister stood up in this House and told us we are licking inflation. Mr. McGillivray concluded by stating:
But perhaps we should not expect Trudeau to be candid.
But it does seem that a prime minister who sets out to correct the "absolute falsehoods" uttered about the economy by the opposition leader should avoid the tricks described in a book like How to Lie with Statistics.
How can we have any credibility at all in any the government's proposals to cure unemployment or anything else?
Then we heard the ramblings of the hon. member for Crowfoot, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner). Good heavens, I remember his speeches and statements about the 92-cent dollar. He was raving in here about how we could not live with a 92-cent dollar. Now he says that the 84-cent dollar is the greatest thing that ever happened to Canada. I don't know, but I think I would call him the Christine Jorgensen of Canadian politics. I have never seen such a transformation in my life. I do not know how he lives with himself.
Let me read a very interesting statement made this week by the British secretary of state for trade who talked about the British experience with the devalued dollar. He said:
The British experience with a falling currency is that it helps trade but with "serious costs" in rising domestic inflation-
While Dell refused to comment directly on Canadian dollar problems here, he said the declining value of the British pound in the mid-1970s "did give us certain advantages and competitiveness" in trade. "But there are costs in this and serious costs," he said to reporters after talking with federal ministers. Among these are costs of inflation caused by depreciation. It is better if one can be less dependent on the price factor in selling one's goods and services and more dependent on quality.
We want our dollar to be worth a dollar, or at least within a couple of cents either way.
I read with great interest the statement made by the premiers last August at their conference in Regina. They seemed to identify all the problems and wanted to take some particular action, but so far no action has been taken on the recommendations. The bulletin from the Manitoba Information Services Branch says:
The provincial premiers reviewed the state of the Canadian economy and the progress which they had made towards achieving the goals established at last year's conference in St. Andrews, New Brunswick.
They noted that as provincial governments they had made some fair degree of progress in the areas which they had established as important in coming to grips with the dual problem of unemployment and inflation.
The provinces had restrained their operating expenditures, with the growth of provincial expenditures falling below that of the federal government.
Provincial public sector wage and salary settlements have been comparable to or less than those in the private sector.

October 16, 1978

The premiers also stated that they urged the development of a joint national economic strategy.
The February conference was a step in this process. The premiers reaffirmed their commitment to the principles agreed to but expressed their concerns about the lack of progress on specific policy directions and projects also agreed to.
It would have been wonderful if this government had dealt with the issues raised by the premiers at this conference in August, Mr. Speaker, instead of spending the last few months debating the constitution. You could debate the constitution for the next 20 years but it is not going to create one job or stop the best of money from leaving Canada. It will not correct the debt or do anything. These are things that should be debated these next few months by the federal government and the premiers. The bulletin goes on:
The premiers agreed that the review promised by the federal government in February should proceed and be concluded with dispatch.
We have seen no dispatch at all, Mr. Speaker.
The premiers also came up with an excellent suggestion in regard to UIC:
The premiers agreed that the UIC Act be changed, if necessary, to provide for new uses of UIC funds which would be more conducive to job creation. In this respect they urged the federal government to co-operate with the provinces, in devising more creative use of the UIC funds.
This is an excellent suggestion and I am sure that we all support it, but nothing is being done about it. We, the opposition party, support it and all the premiers support it, but where is the leadership from the government? It goes on to say:
They agreed that, for instance, where a temporary economic crisis disrupts employment patterns, a strategic disbursement of unemployment insurance moneys could maintain a work force intact and hasten its re-employment.
The premiers also agreed that there should be an immediate program of restraint and proper management of our financial affairs. This was even agreed to by the NDP premier of Saskatchewan.
I would like to give an example of what happens when expenditures are brought under control and waste is eliminated along with mismanagement. We have experienced this in Manitoba over the past year. Before I begin to explain how we have made such a successful gain in the economic scene in Manitoba, I just want to point out the figures for September. They showed that there was a 35 per cent increase in unemployment. This is some kind of phenomenon for Manitoba. In September, 1977, unemployment was up by 29 per cent, but it is just for this particular month that this happens, and I cannot explain it fully.
The poor economic performance of 1978 has its basis in the economic environment established by the previous NDP government. A poor performance for this year was forecast in November, 1977 by the Conference Board, with the dismal economic performance of the first three quarters laying the groundwork. The groundwork of our problems was laid by the previous NDP government and has nothing to do with what the present Conservative government is doing in Manitoba.
This research completely counters the false statements the federal members of the NDP have been making about the
The Address-Mr. McKenzie
economic conditions in Manitoba. The Conference Board has said:
As the Manitoba economy has borne more than its share of the general national economic slowdown in 1977, the 1978 projections show a recovery that is significantly weaker than that for the nation.
There are two variables which affect the level of unemployment in an economy. One variable, labour force growth, is not controllable. The other variable, employment growth, is influenced by economic performance.
I have just received a note on how things are going in the riding of St. Boniface tonight. The NDP spent most of their campaign on attacking the present Conservative government of Manitoba, but I would like to point out right now that the Conservative candidate is 2,100 votes ahead.
The memorandum which I have been referring to goes on to say:
The Manitoba labour force has grown by 18,000 in the past year-a growth rate above the national average, and far greater than had been experienced in any of the NDP years. This factor is not controllable.
Employment growth is controllable. Employment in the past year has grown by 10,000 jobs. Employment growth in the last four years of the NDP government averaged only 3,000 per year. This year's job performance is actually better than was forecast by the Conference Board.
So, by properly controlling your expenditures and cutting out a lot of wasteful programs, the private sector can be attracted to invest once again in the province. In the last year of the NDP government, 6,000 manufacturing jobs were lost. There was a loss of 5,000 jobs in transportation and communications. The 6,000 lost manufacturing jobs have been more than regained, for manufacturing employment is up by 8,000 over this time last year.
That is quite an enviable record for just one year considering what the Conservative government inherited after eight years of complete mismanagement of Manitoba's affairs. Of course, we have another parallel in this House with the present government. When the NDP was first elected, the Manitoba unemployment rate was 2.6 per cent. Within a year it had jumped to 6.4 per cent. The first year of NDP government in Manitoba was a disaster in terms of unemployment as the 8,000 jobless in June, 1969 almost tripled to 22,000 in June, 1970. They did not waste any time in destroying the economic situation in Manitoba.
The NDP also talk about the fact there is no building or construction going on in Manitoba, that everything has ground to a halt. I would like to point out that $300 million worth of construction permits have been issued so far this year. The city building permits department has reported that it issued $40.2 million worth of permits last month, a 69 per cent increase over $23.8 million total for September, 1977. This is an enviable record in just one year, and it shows what can be done. If this government, adopted these policies you can imagine what an enviable position we would be in today, Mr. Speaker.
I would like to explain why we have such a high unemployment rate in this country and such a high level of investment leaving it. According to figures published in the first quarter.

The Address-Mr. Hopkins

I have some statistics here, Mr. Speaker, provided to me by a financial consultant who assisted some 24 businesses to move out of Manitoba. He says that countries, or for that matter provinces, which have nationalistic, leftist or extremely strong bureaucratic tendencies make striving and successful entrepreneurs feel uncomfortable. That also described this government. It is why we have such a mass exodus of business and investment money from Canada. This financial expert stated that the movement of this $40 million out of Manitoba would cost the province 4,000 jobs. When I spoke to him last week, he said the trend is definitely changing. The provinces are not going to correct this situation by themselves but will need co-operation from the federal government.
The Prime Minister and members of the government who have spoken in this debate have upbraided us for having the audacity to criticize the government. I challenge anyone to show me a document that supports this government. Even the Senate is issuing studies describing its failures, and that goes for a lot of Liberal senators too. Everybody in Canada is writing some sort of document to support the things we have been saying for the last five years. Newspaper articles and statistical information offered by experts around the country confirm what we have been saying-that this government s handling of the economic problems of Canada is a disgrace.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all I would like to take this opportunity to congratulate the mover and the seconder of the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne.
Tonight I want to say something about rural development in Canada. We live in an urbanized society today. Cities are growing larger and larger and unless we develop the rural communities into places where people can live without the need and high cost of law and order, as is required in highly urbanized or centralized areas, we are going to pay the price in
years to come in the same way as the Chicagos, the Detroits, the New Yorks and the Bostons are paying the price today.
Our nation was built on three main staples-the fur trade, the timber trade, and wheat. Since then it has bloomed in many different directions and to a large degree we are now a technological nation, particularly in the field of electronics.
The region I come from, the upper Ottawa Valley, was one of the original fur-producing areas. It was also among the first of the timber-producing regions. Parts of the valley can grow wheat and other parts are good only for forest lands. Agriculture, forestry and small community development are therefore of great interest to me. The tall pines, the spruce, the hemlocks and the hardwood stands are part of the proud heritage of eastern Ontario and western Quebec.
After the turn of the century when the "boom timber days" were declining, a great vacuum grew in the economy. The forest industry continued at a reduced level of production and the federal government moved in to take up some of the slack. In 1907, Camp Petawawa was established under the Laurier government. The land was purchased from local farmers, many of their ancestors had come to cut the pine off the sand and rock of the uppermost valley area, and had stayed to farm as best they could.
There are some interesting stories about this in the upper valley. During the days when the military were having firing practice they would move families out of the farm houses to what is now known as the historical Matawa Trail along the Ottawa River. Then they would fix up the houses and move the families back in for the night.
In 1909, settlers were totally moved off this land. There is an interesting editorial in one of the local newspapers of that time which says what an economic disaster it would be to have this farm community moved off what was Camp Petawawa, because it would be a great detriment to the business of merchants in the nearby town of Pembroke. Today, about 10,000 people have replaced those farmers whose families were moved on to better nearby lands with their families.
Mr. Speaker, may I call it ten o'clock.
